Homage to the venerable gurus.
The *Śaivakālaviveka*:

Having prostrated before the Supreme Lord with a heart slowed by devotion, we shall now discern the time for rites beginning with the plowing [of the ground] and ending with the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*). (1)

One should avoid the Sun, Maitra (Anurādhā), Maghā, Aśvinī, Rohiṇī, Svātī, Mṛgaśiras, Puṣya, Āśleṣā, Hasta, the three Uttarās, Revatī, Puṣya, and the two Aśvins; as well as the fourth, ninth, twelfth, penultimate, and eighth lunar days.
Having abandoned these clusters of defects, one should choose a fixed or dual sign and the bright fortnight.
Venus, Mercury, Jupiter, and the Sun are to be accepted for plowing, as are the day-dignities (dṛḍhorā) and so forth. || 2 ||
First, the guide should examine the ground by its taste, smell, and color, as well as by means of the soil,
water, and other such signs.
One should also perform propitiatory rites with devotion for the sake of auspiciousness. || 3 ||

On days corresponding to the asterisms of Puṣya, Hasta, Mṛgaśiras, Maghā, Aśvinī, Svāti, Citrā, Anurādhā, Mūla, Jyeṣṭhā, Ārdrā, Śravaṇā, Dhaniṣṭhā, and Anurādhā, and during the northern transit of the sun (uttarāyaṇa),
one should avoid the movable signs of the zodiac in the months of Māgha, Āṣāḍha, Kārttika, and Nabhas (Śrāvaṇa).
Having avoided the days of Mars and Saturn, as well as unfavorable lunar days, the preceptor should install the Vāstu.

During the six months of the northern course of the sun, when the moon is in the asterisms of Citrā, Mṛgaśiras, Svātī, Śravaṇa, the three Uttarās, Revatī, Anurādhā, Maghā, Hasta, Rohiṇī, or Puṣya; and when the sign is Taurus, Pisces, Aquarius, Virgo, or Capricorn— one should proceed upon an auspicious occasion.
Having carefully examined it by its color and other qualities, let either a stone or wood be taken.
In a sacrificial session (*satra*), in the assembly of the ignorant (*bālasabhā*) and other such places, at the site of a stone sacrifice (*upalayajña*), during the ritual sprinkling (*samprokṣaṇa*),
in the rite of installing a *liṅga* or a jeweled pavilion (*ratnamaṇḍapa*), in the laying of the foundation (*garbha-saṃsthāpana*),
in every rite of consecration (*pratiṣṭhita-vidhi*), and for the purpose of dance on the stage (*raṅga*), [the following] should be performed.
According to the Vāstu-pūjā-āgama, that [worship] is for the delight of all the deities residing in the dwelling place.
One should perform [the rites] during all Śiva-activities, such as the festival procedures, ablutions, consecrations, and sprinklings;
prior to that, on the ninth, seventh, fifth, or third [lunar day]—
Who indeed has performed this act of sprouting instantly, both by night and by day? (7)
The best [time for consecration] is said to be when the sun is in its northern course during the first year after the previous [consecration],
provided the month is other than Māgha and the lunar day is auspicious;
one should perform the installation during stable *horās*, *drekkāṇas*, and *navāṃśas*, together with favorable *karaṇas*.
And on an auspicious day when the moon is in the constellation Puṣya, one should especially enter the temple of Śiva or other such places.
When the sign (liṅga) called "Bāla" has been described according to the sequence of the two [types], the beginning, and the interval, they say that here it is twofold; they declare it to be tenfold:

the image (bimba), the water-pot (kumbha), the cloth (paṭa), the painting (citra), the mirror (ādarśa), the fine brush (sukūrca), the mandala, the earth (mahī), the sandals (pādukā), and the first [two].
The time for worship has been stated according to the root [text], but others know it to be otherwise according to the relative degree [of capacity]. || 9 ||

Likewise, it should be performed during the northern solstice (udagayana), excluding the month of Māgha, as well as the Riktā tithis, the eighth lunar day (aṣṭamī), the first lunar day (pratipad), and the change of the moon (parvan).
One must also avoid days when malefic planets aspect the [ascendant] or its portions, as well as the days of the blind and the one-eyed.
The installation of Śiva should take place during the asterisms of Pātā, Avyoga, Amṛta, and Bhāni.

The installation of a Śiva-liṅga should be performed on a day when the moon is in the asterisms of Puṣya, Āditi (Pūrvaphalgunī), Mṛgaśiras, Śiva (Ārdrā), Tiṣya (Puṣya), Mitra (Anurādhā), Aśvinī, Viṣṇu (Śravaṇa), Svātī, Hasta, or one of the three Uttaras;
provided that the signs of Sagittarius and Aries are avoided, as well as those occupied by Mercury, Jupiter, the Moon, and Venus.
The procedure for the rising of the decan (drekāṇa) and the aspect should be performed within one's own navāṃśas and horās.
In the asterisms of Savitṛ, Āditya, Candra, Uttara-pavana, Surācārya, Vaidhṛti, and Pauṣṇa;

in dual-natured or very stable signs; and when the eighth house is pure—one should install a liṅga fashioned from pearls, rubies, sapphires, and other gems, or made from materials such as bamboo or minerals.
Teachers of pure intellect may also establish forms representing the creation, preservation, and dissolution of the universe. || 12 ||
One should perform the installation of Vighneśa under the asterisms of Prajāpati, Āditya, Hasta, Uttarās, Puṣya, Svātī, and Revatī,
in a pure eighth abode.
One should form the heaps, excluding those known as the movable signs. || 13 ||

Having abandoned the faults of the asterisms Jyeṣṭhā, the three beginning with Ārdrā (Ārdrā, Punarvasu, Puṣya), Nairṛta (Aśleṣā), Sārpa (Āśleṣā), Raudra (Ārdrā), Aindrāgna (Jyeṣṭhā), Vāruṇa (Śatabhiṣaj), Vasu (Dhaniṣṭhā), Bhāgnibha (Pūrvabhādrapadā), Dhanus, Carabha (Pūrvaphalgunī), and Mandamukha (Mṛgaśīrṣa).
One should perform the installation of Guha during the beginnings of auspicious degrees.
In the asterisms of Hasta, Mṛgaśīrṣa, Punarvasu, Anurādhā, Citrā, Puṣya, Uttaraphalgunī, Śravaṇa, Uttarāṣāḍhā, and Revatī;
when the eighth house is pure; and when there is a conjunction with a fixed (sthirā) ascendant.
The virtuous proclaim this as the installation of Gaurī. || 15 ||
During the five *ghaṭikās* immediately following dawn, known as the *brāhma-muhūrta*,
one who has abandoned sleep, whose heart is pure, and whose mind meditates upon the lotus-feet of the Lord,
should perform purification, the cleansing of teeth and mouth, bathing, and the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyā*).
Then, for the sake of bringing security to the world, one should cause this to be performed with the five kinds of musical instruments. || 16 ||
This [time], known as day and night, is established through the sequence beginning with exhalation (*ucchvāsa*) and so forth;

its eight junctions (*sandhi*) are declared in the Śiva doctrine, and worship is prescribed during all of them. O Śambhu, this worship is renowned as being of nine kinds—consisting of the superior, excellent, and lower sequences—or even fivefold.
The daily worship, the occasional worship, that performed according to the rules, and the optional worship performed at will; || 17 ||

"Experts and authoritative teachers have declared that expiatory rites (prāyaścitta) are thus of four kinds: obligatory (nitya), optional (kāmya), occasional (naimittika), and those for the fulfillment of a specific injunction."
Because it is an eternal constituent part, this purifier is eternal. || 18 ||

The three months beginning with Āṣāḍha, as declared in the Śiva tradition, are excellent, middling, and inferior respectively; and within the bright and dark fortnights, the eighth lunar day (Aṣṭamī) is the auspicious date for enjoyment and liberation. These [months] are to be accepted when they coincide with the rising and setting of the sun, in which case the Pavitraka rite should be performed in due order.
Beginning with the sixth lunar day, one should perform the rites in the respective residences according to the rules of observance, excluding the intercalary month.

The month called saura is declared to be of two kinds: subtle and gross. The subtle one begins with Aries (meṣa), while the other is said to begin from the month of Mārgaśīrṣa or from the Puṣya nakṣatra.
[One should avoid] the lunar mansion of the month, the Śiva-bhedana yoga, the equinoxes, the parvan days, and the two eclipses.
One should worship Śiva with the substances prescribed for those [deities] during the transits of the planets, the lunar mansions, and so forth.

If two transits (saṃkrānti) occur in one month, they should both be performed on the same day; however, if they fall on two different days, the one occurring during the day is auspicious, provided it is beyond the time specified [for the previous]. Furthermore, if the preceding transit is joined with an auspicious conjunction (puṇyayoga), or if it coincides with the transit of the sun (saṃkrānti) or the rising of Rāhu (rāhūdaya), [it is likewise auspicious].
Having discarded [the previous materials] on the preceding day and consecrated them, it should take place after the daily worship on the following day. || 21 ||

The asterisms Sāvitra, Vedha, Harivāruṇa, Pauṣṇa, Anurādha, Uttara-māruta, Guru, Indu, Saumya, and Uśas are recommended as the days and divisions of time for the rite of conception (garbhādhāna). || 22 ||
When the embryo has become manifest, one should perform the *puṃsavana* rite in the third month under the asterism Puṣya or when the moon is in the sign of Leo;
it is auspicious when performed during the rising of Venus, Jupiter, Mercury, or the Moon in the eighth lunar mansion from the woman's natal star.
The sages have declared here that the rite of *sīmanta* (parting the hair) for a Śaiva should be performed under the asterisms of Puṣya, Āditi (Punarvasu), Mṛgaśiras, Hasta, Viṣṇu (Śravaṇa),
and the three Uttarās; on an auspicious lunar day, in the fourth or sixth month, avoiding the months of Leo and Scorpio, and when the ascendant is pure and conjoined with an auspicious eighth house.
On the eighth day of the waning moon, there is worship of Viṣṇu.
With a mind delighted at the birth of a son, having quickly performed the birth-rite (jātakarma) under the asterisms of Svāti, Śroṇā, Aditi, Śatabhiṣaj,
Saumya, Mūla, or the Uttarās; or under Ārya, Pauṣṇa, Ambuja, or Bhavakara— one should perform the highly praised rite of naming (nāmakaraṇa).
Then, on the eleventh or twelfth day, the preceptor should perform the naming ceremony according to the prescribed rules.

The rite of departure (*niṣkrāma-karma*) should be performed under the asterisms of Aśvinī, Śravaṇa, Āditya, Vasu, Marut, Maitra, Citrā, Uttarā-phalgunī, Indu (Mṛgaśiras), Brāhma (Rohiṇī), Pauṣṇa (Revatī), Savitṛ (Hasta), Varuṇa (Śatabhiṣaj), and Aryamā (Phalgunī);
when the day is pure, in the tenth house, at an auspicious moment (*muhūrta*), and in a favorable *lagna*.
In the fourth month, the auspicious rite for children is prescribed according to the rules.

In the sixth month, during an auspicious moment (muhūrta) presided over by the Moon, the gods, Varuṇa, the Aśvins, Prajāpati, and the Daśa, one should perform the rite of first feeding solid food (annaprāśana) for the child when the [lunar] day is pure. || 27 ||

In the third year, under the asterisms of Vasu (Dhaniṣṭhā), Pauṣṇa (Revatī), Puṣya, Punarvasu, Saumya (Mṛgaśiras), Kar (Hasta), Aśvinī, Tvāṣṭra (Citrā), and Harā (Ārdrā)— provided they are in their eighth position and pure— one should perform the *nāndīmukha* and *caula* rites.

For the Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas respectively, at the proper time— beginning from the eighth month of pregnancy and during the fertile period— one should perform [the rite] under the asterisms of Puṣya, Anurādhā, Svāti, Aditi (Punarvasu), Tvaṣṭṛ (Citrā), the Moon (Mṛgaśiras), Savitṛ (Hasta),
the three northern asterisms, or when the Sun is in Taurus, Gemini, Virgo, Cancer, or Sagittarius.
In the sign of Pisces, one should perform the initiation (upanayana) for those who possess the eighth purification, starting from sixteen years of age. || 29 ||
All months except Māgha and Proṣṭhapada; the asterisms Rohiṇī, Revatī, the three Uttarās, Maghā, Mṛgaśīrṣa, Svātī, Anurādhā, Hasta, and Jyeṣṭhā;
the pure seventh lunar day; and the zodiacal signs Leo, Capricorn, Taurus, Virgo, Libra, and Cancer.
In the phrase "the jar has a handle," those with faces turned upwards are recommended by the wise for marriage.

Having recognized the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) through the signs manifested in the disciple who has approached him, the Guru should repeatedly perform the rite of initiation (*dīkṣāvidhi*) here in this world— either in the highest or the middling manner—
in the prescribed locations during the months of Caitra, Māgha, or Kārttika, or under the asterisms of Śravaṇa, Hasta, Svātī, Revatī, Mūla, or the Uttarās.
In the signs of Diti, Ārdrā, and Mitra, as well as in fixed and dual signs, there is no [inauspicious] time for one desiring liberation. || 31 ||

In the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, when the final [tithi] of the bright fortnight is joined with a favorable yoga, it is auspicious; if this same [yoga] occurs on the first day of the following pair of days, that day is indeed superior.
In the case of equality [of yogas], the former is preferred; otherwise, in the ocean [of time], the lunar day (tithi) is the criterion, while elsewhere the asterism (nakṣatra) is so—thus says Guru.
Having distinguished the months, asterisms, and so forth, one should perform that ninefold festival of Maheśa.
On the fifth lunar day, on the ninth lunar day (the day of Śiva), on the two festival days (parvan), during a solar or lunar transit (saṃkrānti),
during a solar or lunar eclipse, and at the solstices and equinoxes, the fruit [of the rite] shall be manifold; likewise during the rites of initiation (dīkṣā),
installation (sthāpana), festivals, and sacrifices, as well as during consecrations (samprokṣaṇa) and when portents (utpāta) occur.
On one's own birth-star (nakṣatra), during the practice of the mantra and so forth, one should bathe Śaṅkara with water-pots.

During a famine, at an ill omen, in the fear arising from fever or the mouth-born [pestilence], when the plague has broken out, during earthquakes, the burning of the quarters, and so forth; for the purpose of victory, for the sake of rain in the month of Tapasya,
in the months of Caitra or Vaiśākha, under a lunar mansion that produces kings, and on the new moon day— [The rites should be performed.]
And on the fifth lunar day and others, as well as on the days of the Moon, Venus, and Jupiter, one should perform the cold-water rite (*śītakumbha*).

When the sun has moved to the northern direction, on an auspicious lunar day, for the conquest of cruel untimely death, for the destruction of enemies’ afflictions, for the victory over [hostile] planets, and even for the accomplishment of all desired goals;
on the birth-day of kings, at the time of their consecration, and also at the beginning and end of battle—
On those days joined with auspicious yogas, the preceptor should perform the worship of the birth-star.
It is likewise for the purpose of rain, for the rite of destroying untimely death, for the destruction of pestilence,
for relief from the affliction of malevolent planets, for the rite of victory even over a formidable enemy,
for kings to conquer their foes, for the pacification of fevers and the like, and for the peace of villages and so forth.
In the Āgama, the worship of the day is prescribed for the sake of accomplishing the performer's desired goal.
At the time of a king's consecration, during the birth asterism of the monarch, in the middle of the two fortnights even when they are near their end,
or at the conclusion of a battle, or when joined with an auspicious yoga.
The Nakṣatrayāga is declared for the accomplishment of all goals.
On the birthday of the Lord of all the earth, on the day of the month’s asterism being Ārdrā, during the two junctions of the lunar fortnights, during eclipses of the moon or sun,
during the transits [of the sun], on the eighth day, on the day preceding a lunar festival, during the two solstices and the two equinoxes, or at other auspicious times.
Having performed the preliminary consecration during the night according to the stainless ritual rules, one should perform the auspicious worship. || 38 ||
In every month, Saturdays, Tuesdays, and Sundays are considered superior, middling, and inferior respectively;

furthermore, the middle and penultimate lunar days, the third, the ninth, and the new moon (darśa) are to be avoided. For the performer, the rising [of planets] on a day with a favorable asterism for birth, excluding the last quarter and the three nāḍīs [following it], is auspicious.
In the morning, at the conclusion of the daily worship, one should perform the secret worship (channapūjā) of the beloved Gaṇapati.
At the commencement of war, during the oppression by an enemy, in times of drought or the onset of heat-related epidemics,
and upon the outbreak of disease, one should practice that which is taught in the scriptures.
The preceptor performed the milk-bath for Śaṅkara.
Even at a time conjoined with the birth asterism of the king’s consecration, or at the beginning or end of a battle, or during the time of ritual worship and the like,
or on other auspicious days, one should [perform this] before the morning twilight.
Having performed this, one should carry out the ritual consecration with jars for Paraśiva.
It may be that during the four months beginning with Āśvina,
on the auspicious day of one’s birth asterism or birth month,
or on an extremely wonderful or marvelous day in the middle of the dark fortnight, [the rite should be performed].
The offering of a stream of ghee should be performed according to the rules for Giriśa. || 42 ||
If the Kṛṣṇāṣṭamī is pierced by the following [tithi] or the preceding one, it is certainly to be accepted for the worship of Śiva during the first watch of the night;
provided there is equality [of duration], the one pierced by the preceding tithi is to be taken.
In the months, at the beginning of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, [one should worship] Tripurā at the conclusion of the Jaya festival. || 43 ||

In the month of Caitra, during the bright fortnights of both Jyeṣṭha and Tapas (Āṣāḍha), one should avoid the six lunar days beginning with the ninth; likewise, in the dark fortnight, one should avoid the first four lunar days. Furthermore, one must avoid the three weekdays beginning with Friday (Bhṛgu).
Regarding the piercing (vedha) of the needle: it is auspicious when performed under the Puṣya, Maghā, Uttarās, Aśvinī, and Śravaṇa nakṣatras, and under a favorable yoga.
One should perform the release of the planet during the signs of Aries, Cancer, Leo, and Aquarius.
On the eighth lunar day of the asterisms of Rājārka (Pūrvaphalgunī), Ṣaḍaśīti, Śiva, Hari, and Brahmā;
likewise on the new moon, during solar and lunar eclipses, and during the Citrā asterism in Caitra,
as well as on Phalgunī in the month of Phālguna— bathing Śiva with musk is thus prescribed.
It bestows all desired fruits, grants victory, and yields the fruit of sacrifices performed in all ritual assemblies. || 45 ||

On the day of the *Amṛtasiddhi-yoga* of Lord Īśa, on the new moon (*darśa*), during the transit of the sun (*saṅkrānti*), on one's own birth asterism (*janmarkṣa*), on the middle lunar days of the fortnight, and on the lunar day sacred to Śiva,
the Preceptor [should perform the rite] with forty-nine conchs of superior, middling, and inferior quality.
One should bathe Śaṅkara with a hundred or even a thousand of all desired things.
Under Rohiṇī, the two Anilas (Svātī and Anurādhā), the Guru-nakṣatra (Pūrvaphalgunī), Hasta, and Maitrarkṣaka (Anurādhā);
on days honored by the Moon, Āditya (the Sun), Budha (Mercury), and Asura (Venus); during solar and lunar eclipses;
on the fifth lunar day, as well as on the two junctions of the fortnights (parvan); and at the beginning and end of the month and its asterism.
One should perform worship for the sake of desired objects during the final and middle parts of the two fortnights and the two solstices.
When the sun had thus entered its northern course, O King, during the asterisms favorable to the sacrificer,
the crown was placed for the sake of auspiciousness at both the beginning and the end of the battle.
One should give [the gift] on auspicious days during the bright fortnight. || 48 ||

Thus, for the pleasure of those whose intellects are skilled in ritual action, he has composed these Śaiva Āgamas— oceans churned from the mouths of the Kāmika and other scriptures— just as [the gods churned the ocean] for the sake of the deities;
and this heart-pleasing nectar of the discernment of time has been constantly obtained.
May you not be like those extremely crooked asuras, wicked men who perceive only faults. || 49 ||
The root verses of the *Śaivakālaviveka* are complete,
together with the commentary composed by Gaṇapatibhaṭṭa.
I take refuge in Him who is the natural outflow of compassion, who wanders in the forest of liberation,
whose body is dark like a monsoon cloud, and whose face is like that of a young elephant.

He was like an infant nourished by the breast-milk of the Daughter of the Snowy Mountain, who, resting upon the couch of the Vedas, was being suckled by her mouth while scattering [the milk] along with its meaning.
The supreme reality of the Lord is devoid of beginning and end;
it is the support of all sciences, yet itself without support and immutable.
I perpetually prostrate before the Lord of Ambikā, the Sovereign, whose form is wondrous and who is an ocean of the waters of infinite bliss and consciousness. 4.

A treasury of all noble qualities, proficient in the essential principles of all the great scriptures, having attained clarity of intellect through familiarity with the practice of conduct, yoga, and ritual action,
he was the expounder of the entire great system of the Vedas applied to the worship of the Self.
There dwells in Vyāghrapurī a sage named Vedajñāna, who is highly honored. || 5 ||
The *Śaivācāraviveka*, the *Ātmayajana*, the *Śaivapratiṣṭhāvidhi*,
the *Bhāṣāmañjarikā*, the *Aruṇācalamahātīrthasthalīvaibhava*,
and the pure ritual procedure (*kriyā*) consisting of an explanation of the collection of specific principles taught in the Siddhānta.
The sage named Nigamajñāna composed this Ratnollekha.

Now, the author, for the sake of completing his work without obstacles, in order to observe the conduct of the learned, and for the sake of its widespread propagation, first performs an auspicious rite in the form of a salutation to his chosen deity and then declares his intended undertaking.
Root Text:
Having prostrated before the Supreme Lord with a mind slow with devotion, we shall now analyze the period beginning from the plowing and ending with the consecration ceremony. (1)

Regarding the word "bhaktyā" (with devotion): [he refers to] that Supreme Śiva who is the witness of the fivefold cosmic acts of the Supreme Lord; for He is supreme because He alone is the bestower of grace upon all.
Having bowed down to Him with a mind slowed by devotion—that is, with an internal organ rippled by the contemplation of devotion—by this [act of salutation].

Thus, the threefold nature of salutation—consisting of body, speech, and mind—is also stated, because such a state of being alone is the cause of the three types of salutation. However, in the absence of such devotion, even that [salutation] takes the form of a mere avoidance of salutation. This has been illustrated by the masters of poetics (*alaṅkārikas*) in the following manner:

Salutations to those few who have realized the underlying connection— that the *kartṛ* (agent) possesses two dots at the beginning of the line, while the *karman* (object) possesses a dot at its head.
"O Poet Bilhaṇa, you exert yourself only among those who compose verses whose flaws are worn away by the whetting-stone of thousands of texts. Thus [it is said].

p. 3) The period from plowing to the consecration (pratiṣṭhā): the time for the collection of ritual acts beginning with plowing and ending with the consecration is being analyzed—specifically demonstrated—by us.
The use of the plural "by us" refers to the many scriptural statements residing within our hearts. Now, [one might ask], it is of many kinds...

If it is argued that this commencement of the treatise is redundant— since the specific requirements for time regarding the network of ritual acts have already been established by the multitude of astrological texts, and since they have also been set forth in various places in the *Kāmika* and other Āgamas at the appropriate occasions for ritual action— the answer is: true, [but] regarding the prescription of time...

Since these matters, such as the determination of time, are common to all [traditions] and have been demonstrated here and there in the *Kāmika* and other Āgamas, they are difficult to grasp in their scattered state; therefore, this work is commenced for the sake of facilitating the understanding of practitioners. Thus, [the sequence beginning with] plowing and so forth—[is not purposeless].

Regarding the phrase "ending with the consecration" (*pratiṣṭhāntam*): the time of that consecration which has cultivation as its beginning, as well as the time for the obligatory (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), and optional (*kāmya*) rites, are both intended here. If it is asked, "Since time is without beginning or end, it is difficult to discern; how, then, can there be a method for discerning time?"—it is true.

Although undivided Great Time (*mahākāla*) is difficult to grasp, time as delimited by moments (*truṭi*) and so forth must be defined; otherwise, since the entire web of actions depends upon their respective times, there would follow the undesirable consequence of the cessation of all worldly transaction. Thus it has been stated in the *Matanga-pārameśvara*:
O Brahmin, although time in this flow of time is immeasurable, it is nevertheless described for the purpose of establishing its divisions; it is the domain of the *truṭi* and other such units.
Now, the entire sequence beginning with the *kalā* shall be declared to you according to calculation: a *truṭi* is said to be a fraction of the blink of an eye for a person at rest. (3)
Because it is exceedingly subtle, it is to be grasped; that which transcends it is not perceived.
A minute division called *truṭi* is subtle, and a *lava* is said to be twice that. (4)
Two *lava*s constitute a *nimeṣa*; fifteen of these constitute a *kāṣṭhā*;
thirty *kāṣṭhā*s constitute a *vāhā*; and thirty *vāhā*s are explained as a *muhūrta*.
O observer of noble vows, that which is known in this world as a muhūrta consists of thirty of those [nimeshas];
it is declared in this Pārameśvara Tantra to be one day and night.
A fortnight (pakṣa) is to be known as consisting of fifteen units within the cycle of day and night;
two fortnights are recorded as a month (māsa), and two months are declared to be a season (ṛtu).
O best of sages, a northern course (ayana) arises from three seasons,
and a year is defined by two such courses.
"According to the vision of reality, three hundred and sixty solar years of those belonging to the human race are said to constitute one year of the celestial dwellers. (9)
Likewise, in the *Suprabheda*:
"The cool season (*śiśira*), spring (*vasanta*), summer (*grīṣma*), the rainy season (*prāvṛṭ*), autumn (*śarad*), and winter (*hemanta*)—these are proclaimed as the six seasons. (10)
The two months of Māgha and Phālguna are Śiśira, consisting of Tapas and Tapasya;
and the two months of Caitra and Vaiśākha are Vasanta, known as Madhu and Mādhava.
The seasons of Jyeṣṭha and Āṣāḍha are known as Grīṣma (summer), while Śuci and Śukra are remembered as the two months [of that season].
The seasons called Śravaṇa and Bhādra are designated as Nabhas and Nabhasya, respectively. || 12 ||
The two months of autumn are Śaradi and Paurja; these are Āśvayuja and Kārtika.
p. 5) "The winter season consists of a thousand [years] for each; those two, Mārgaśīrṣa and Puṣya, are traditionally known as such.
The southern course should be understood as the night of the gods, while the northern course is their day. (13)

And so it is stated in the *Jñānaratnāvalī*: "One day and night of humans would be one *ghaṭikā* for the ancestors (*pitṛs*). Thirty such *ghaṭikās* constitute a day and night; the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*) would be their daytime."

One should know that the night is the dark fortnight; that constitutes a day and a night for the ancestors. The new moon (amāvāsyā) is the morning twilight, and the eighth lunar day (aṣṭamī) would be midday.
"The afternoon of the full moon day, as well as the eighth part of the day at sunset. Thus it is said.
Now, for the sake of thoroughly understanding the subsequent judicial procedure, the deities of the lunar mansions as described in the *Suprabheda* are stated:
Kṛttikā has Agni as its deity; Prajāpati is the deity of Rohiṇī;
Mṛgaśiras is declared to belong to Soma; and Śiva is remembered as the deity of Ārdrā.
Punarvasu belongs to the Ādityas, while Bṛhaspati is the deity of Puṣya;
Āśleṣā has the serpents as its presiding deities, and likewise, the Pitṛs are the deities of Maghā.
For Bhaga is indeed [the deity] of Phalgunī, and Aryaman of Uttaraphalgunī;
Hasta is said to belong to Savitṛ, and it is honored in all undertakings.
Tvaṣṭṛ is the deity of Citrā, while Vāyu is the deity of Svātī;
Indra and Agni are the deities of Viśākhā, and Mitra is the deity of Anurādhā.
Indra is likewise for Jyeṣṭhā, and Niṛti for Mūla;
Pūrvāṣāḍhā is said to belong to the Waters (Āpa), and these are to be avoided in the rite of installation.
Viśvedevas preside over Uttarāṣāḍhā, while Brahmā presides over Abhijit.
Hari is the presiding deity of Śravaṇa, and likewise the Vasus of Śraviṣṭhā;
Varuṇa is the deity of Śatabhiṣak, while Aja is proclaimed as the deity of Pūrvaproṣṭhapada.
Ahirbudhnya is declared to be the deity of Uttaraproṣṭhapada.

Pūṣan is the presiding deity of Revatī, the two Aśvins are the presiding deities of the Aśvinī asterism, and Yama is the presiding deity of Bharaṇī; such are the presiding deities of the asterisms. Thus it is said.

If it is objected: "Where there is no contradiction between what is stated in the *Jyotiṣa* and what is stated in the *Āgama*, there is no superiority [of one over the other]. But where there is a contradiction, what is the recourse? It is replied: In the case of a contradiction between what is stated in the *Jyotiṣa* and what is stated in the *Āgama*, one should set aside what is stated in the *Jyotiṣa* and accept only what is stated in the *Āgama*. Thus it has been said in the *Bodhāyana-smṛti*:

"Wherever a contradiction is observed between what is stated in astrology and what is stated in the Āgamas, one should indeed set aside what is stated in astrology and practice according to what is stated in the Āgamas. Thus it is said.
In reality, however, there is no contradiction whatsoever between the Śaiva Tantra and other Tantras;
where a sense of contradiction appears, that is solely the fault of the speaker.
Thus it has been stated in the Mataṅgapārameśvara:
However, when a meaning is here subsumed in contradiction with its own specific system,
that should be understood as a mere verbal mockery resulting from the weakness of the teacher's reasoning.
In whatever place, in whatever manner appropriate, and by whichever path,
that which can be brought forth— let it be investigated in exactly that way.
"O best of sages, if the entire system is of the nature of Śiva because it is non-contradictory, then it must be taught by the teacher in that way and not otherwise. (p. 7)
Nor, then, should it be said that there is a contradiction with the *Bodhāyana* [Smṛti], for that [text] concerns only what appears on the surface;
moreover, because the Śaiva Tantra was composed by the Omniscient One, it is the most excellent of all.
Now, therein, first of all, regarding the entire network of Śaiva rituals, such as the *ālayas* and so forth...
Since the rite begins with plowing and consecration, he first states the time for plowing—
the root verse says: Maitra (Anurādhā), Āditya (Pūrvaphalgunī), Maghā, Aśvin (Aśvinī), Padmaja (Rohiṇī), Marut (Svātī), Saumya (Mṛgaśiras), Īśa (Ārdrā), and Hastottarā (Uttaraphalgunī).
The asterism Pauṣṇa (Revatī), Puṣya, the fourth, ninth, twelfth, penultimate, and eighth lunar days.

Having abandoned the groups of malefic planets, one should take a stable, even sign, and a bright fortnight; Venus, Mercury, Jupiter, and the Sun are to be accepted for ploughing, as are the Ghorā and other [auspicious] days.

Regarding "Maitrī": Now, he states the lunar mansions (*nakṣatras*) for the first task there, namely plowing. Maitra is Anurādhā; Āditya is Punarvasu; Maghā is well-known; Aśvi is Aśvinī; Padmaja is Rohiṇī; Marut is Svātī; Saumya is Mṛgaśirā; Īśa is Ārdrā; Hasta is well-known; and the Uttarās—

The three *uttara* constellations—Uttaraphalgunī, Uttarāṣāḍhā, and Uttaraproṣṭhapadā; Pauṣṇa (Revatī); Puṣya, which is well-known; and Hari (Śravaṇa)—these fifteen constellations are to be employed for plowing.
Thus it is stated in the *Karṣaṇapaṭala* of the *Suprabheda*:
Tiṣya, Śravaṇa, Hasta, Ārdrā, Maitra, Āditya, and Maghā; likewise Prājāpatya, Aśvayuḥ, Svātī, Saumya, Pauṣṇa, and the three Uttarās.

Now, he states the rule for the lunar days (tithis) by way of those to be avoided: having abandoned the fourth (turīyā), the penultimate (upāntyā—the fourteenth), and the fourth, ninth, twelfth, fourteenth, and eighth, the others are to be accepted; this is the meaning.
As it is stated in the *Suprabheda*: "The second, the third, the fifth, the sixth and seventh,
the tenth, the eleventh, the first, and the thirteenth."
"But the lunar days, especially the full moon day in the bright fortnight," so it is said.

The meaning is that one should abandon the groups of defects—such as *avayoga* and others—which will be described immediately below, and instead adopt the excellent conjunctions (*suyoga*) and so forth that are about to be mentioned. The bright fortnight (*sitapakṣa*), i.e., the waxing moon, should also be adopted. Now, he states the zodiac signs: fixed (*sthira*), dual (*yugala*), and movable (*cara*) signs—the fixed, dual-natured, and movable signs.
And those [planets] are to be accepted except for the one in Sagittarius. This too has been stated in the *Suprabheda*: "The movable signs are to be excluded;
the remaining ones are to be accepted, with the exception of Sagittarius."
"Venus, Mercury, Jupiter, and so forth—the days, aspects, *horās*, and so on, of Venus, Mercury, and Jupiter. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the *drekkāṇas*, degrees, and others are included.
This too has been stated in that very same [work]:
The days of Mercury, Venus, and Jupiter are indeed the best, and not others;
the decans, navāṃśas, and horās of these [planets] are desired for observation.
"Having abandoned the arising of the moon there, and for others in both cases as well. (p. 9)
In the *Santānasaṃhitā*, the retrograde motion (*mauḍhya*) of Jupiter and Venus is also mentioned, as follows:
"During the setting of Venus and likewise during the setting of Jupiter, one should avoid plowing and other such activities; even those already performed will perish."
The Sun, Moon, Saturn, and Mars, when situated in the third, sixth, or eleventh houses, bestow auspicious results;
however, these same planets, if they have entered the ascendant (lagna), bestow inauspicious results.
Thus it is said in the *Suprabheda*:
On a day occupied by malefic planets, it causes affliction from disease here;
however, the Moon, Sun, Saturn, and Mars are auspicious when situated in the third, sixth, or eleventh houses.
Those same planets, when situated in the ascendant, cause disease, grief, and fear;
however, all of them, when occupying the eighth house, bestow security, health, and prosperity.
Bhargava (Venus), situated in the sixth, seventh, or tenth house, is said to cause fear;
likewise, Jupiter, situated in the ninth, second, seventh, or fifth house, brings about auspiciousness.
The Moon is declared to be a bestower of great happiness when situated in the second or the fifth house. Thus it is said.

Furthermore, the auspicious conjunctions (*suyoga*), inauspicious conjunctions (*avayoga*), and so forth, pertaining to the days of the week, lunar dates (*tithi*), and asterisms (*nakṣatra*) are also demonstrated therein.
For example:
"Sunday is auspicious when conjoined with Revatī, Hasta, and the three Uttarās."
Saturday is declared auspicious when conjoined with the asterisms Svātī or Rohiṇī.
The second lunar day joined with Mercury, the sixth joined with Jupiter,
and the eleventh joined with the Moon indeed cause affliction to the vital breaths.
The constellation Puṣya, when conjoined with the seventh lunar day (Saptamī), burns up one's progeny like fire;
likewise, Monday is inauspicious when joined with Uttarāṣāḍhā.

One should avoid the *viṣṭi* yoga, the *sthūṇā* asterisms, the *dhana* asterisms, the *gaṇḍa* portions, and the *gulika* periods; as well as on cloudy days, during the burning of the quarters, during earthquakes, and when there is a fierce wind.
It is taught that an inauspicious omen occurs when there is the sound of a thunderbolt;
likewise, during a solar transit, an eclipse, and at the solstices and equinoxes.
During festivals, at times of propitiation, and also at the commencement of the sixty-fourth year-cycle (Ṣaḍaśītimukha).
If one should act out of delusion, it will surely cause the destruction of the builder's dwelling. Thus it is said.

Having thus explained the time for plowing, and since plowing depends upon ground that bestows auspiciousness, and because it must follow the examination of the ground and be governed by the proper time, the teacher describes the examination of the ground:
"First, the teacher, having examined the ground— "

By means of taste, smell, and even color, as well as by clay, water, and so forth, or even by their causal characteristics— if these are inauspicious, one should diligently perform a rite of pacification (śānti). || 3 ||

Regarding the phrase "having examined": first, the preceptor should examine the ground by means of its taste, smell, color, soil, water, and other such signs. In that regard, in the chapter on the examination of the ground (*bhūparīkṣāpaṭala*) in the *Kāmika*, the nature of the ground is defined through the classification of the ground as belonging to Śiva, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Indra, or the Bull (Nandin).
The twelvefold nature is stated through the divisions of Bhautika, Āsura, Paiśāca, Rākṣasa, Vāyavya, Vāruṇa, and Āgneya.
That is as follows:
The Śaiva, the Brāhma, the Vāstu, the Vaiṣṇava, and the Aindra;
as well as the Aukṣa, the Bhautika, the Āsura, and the Piśācaka.
And likewise the Rākṣasa, Vāyavya, Vāruṇa, and Āgneyaka [marriages]. Thus it is said.
The formal definition of these characteristics is also established in that very same place, as follows:
"The best of teachers should recognize the various types of ground by these characteristics:
the *karṇikāra*, *arjuna*, *aśvattha*, *kapittha*, *aśoka*, and *ghātakī* [trees]."
Or likewise, the earth with land-lotuses, *tulasī*, and *dūrvā*;
or with *viṣṇukrānti*, *akhukarṇa*, *śālmalī*, mountain [soil], and *sārivā*.
That auspicious earth belonging to Śiva is graced by pigeons, parrots, and swans,
as well as by bilva, palāśa, darbha, and kuśa grass, and likewise by deer.
The earth, when offered with fragrant oblation materials, is considered auspicious and bestowing of blessings;
likewise, it is so when offered with *tinduka*, *tintriṇī*, *karañja*, and *veṇu* wood.
That land which is endowed with cotton plants, arka, and japā flowers; with swans, birds, and deer; and likewise with thornless trees.
The earth is declared to belong to Viṣṇu; it bestows valor and heroism upon men.
It is likewise adorned with kadali, panasa, āmra, punnāga, and vakula trees.

The earth is considered to belong to the Vaiśyas through pāṭala and sinduvāra flowers, as well as through āmalaka fruits; it is considered to belong to the Śūdras through blue lotuses (indīvara) and aindrī plants.
Rich with the fragrance of *pāṭala* and *agaru*, it bestows abundance of wealth and grain;
likewise, with *aṅkola*, *dhava*, *mandāra*, and *nakula* trees.
The earth is considered to have been sprinkled by hares, iguanas, cakora birds, and trees;
it bestows valor and heroism, and grants the abundance of prosperous progeny.
Nirguṇḍī, mādhavī, dūrvā, svaṅkola, and likewise kiṃśuka,
along with mallikā, karavīra, and madhūka, are considered bhotikī.
It bestows food and nourishment upon men, and is permeated with the scent of ashes;
it abounds with marking-nut trees, great trees, wicked creatures, and onions.
The ground of the Asuras, filled with Kirātas, cocks, vultures, serpents, and rogues, brings about war; yet that which is endowed with the fragrance of Pathyā is auspicious.
Likewise, the ground was covered with *śālmalī* trees, *vakula*, and *vibhītaka* trees;
and it was further filled with *ślaiṣmātaka* trees, asses, camels, jackals, and boars.
Filled with Caṇḍālas and Pulindas and pervaded by a foul stench,
this is recorded in the scripture as the Piśāca age, accompanied by universal destruction.
[The wind] is like outcasts, poison, and thieves, and likewise causes diseases such as those of the head; enriched with the scent of pepper and molasses, that Rākṣasī wind brings about consumption.
That which is crowded with packs of jackals, filled with crickets, and strewn with gravel is called Vāyavī; it bestows suffering and poverty.
That ground which is surrounded by clusters [of trees], where the *vārūṇī* plant yields all accomplishments,
or which is joined with *snuhī*, *śleṣmātaka*, and other such small thorny shrubs;
The saline soil is devoid of water and is fiery, destroying everything;
that which is in the region of Śiva is declared to belong to Śiva, and that in the region of Viṣṇu belongs to Viṣṇu.

In the region of Brahmā, the ground should be Brāhmī; for those such as Brahmins, the ground suitable for Śaivas should be Śaivī. For a Brahmin, the Śaivī ground is superior, while the Vaiṣṇavī ground is suitable for the Brāhmī [rite].

The *aikṣī* (sugarcane-based) is prescribed for Kṣatriyas, the *bhautikī* (fermented grain-based) is considered for Śūdras, and the *vāruṇī* (liquor made from grapes or similar fruits) is recommended for all; or rather, all [types] are considered suitable for everyone.
"The land of the Piśācas, the land of the Asuras, and that which is considered the land of the Rākṣasas,

as well as that which is declared here to belong to the outcastes (antyajas) and that which has been cultivated by hundreds [of people], and the land enjoyed by cows while grazing— all such land may be acquired after a year of possession. Thus it is said.
The threefold classification according to the distinctions of marshy (*anūpa*), dry (*jāṅgala*), and intermediate (*sādhāraṇa*) lands is also explained in that very same work.
Now, regarding examination by colors, the *Suprabheda* states:
"White, red, yellow, and black earth belongs to the Brāhmaṇas and the other castes respectively."
The Brāhmaṇa woman bestows liberation, and likewise, the Kṣatriya woman bestows victory.
"The Vaiśya woman is the giver of land, while the Śūdra woman is the giver of sons. Thus it is said.
And regarding examination by means of tastes, it is said in the *Mayamata*:
"The earth that possesses all six tastes— bitter, pungent, astringent, salty, sour, and sweet— is the bestower of all prosperity."
Regarding the examination by means of scents, the *Mayamata* states:
"With the scents of the *punnāga*, the *jāti*, the lotus, and the *dhānyapāṭala*, [the earth] is excellent when endowed with the scent of livestock; it causes all seeds to sprout."
"That which has the scent of honey, ghee, or molasses, or that which smells of oil or blood,
or that which smells like a corpse, urine, or sugarcane— such a *sādhara* is condemned by the wise."
Regarding the examination of the soil, the *Suprabheda* states: "One should dig a hole in the ground knee-deep and fill that pit with the excavated earth;
if the soil exceeds [the original level], the ground is excellent; if it is equal, it is middling."
"Those who know the scriptures understand that a deficient [sacrifice] should be avoided according to the ancient rule. Thus it is said.
Regarding the examination by water, it is stated in the *Kāmika*:
"When the pit is being filled with water from a jar containing flowers,
water that swirls clockwise and has calm bubbles is auspicious."
"A flower with its face turned upward is best, not one with its face turned downward. Thus it is said.
By the word "etcetera," examination by means of seeds is also intended, as stated in the *Kāmika*:
"On whichever ground sprouts of mustard or sesame seeds sown grow within three nights, that ground bestows auspiciousness."
In the *Ajita*, another method of examination is also stated: "One should trample with the right foot while reciting the mantra;
if, during that trampling, the ground resounds deeply and remains firm."
She is to be embraced. Thus.
In the *Kāmika*: "A site sloping toward the east and north is excellent; one sloping in all directions is mediocre.
Even that [mediocre site] may be accepted for a house and the like, provided it is endowed with prominent qualities. Thus it is said.
Examination by means of omens is as follows, according to the *Ajita*:
"Having reached that place and having bowed to Maheśvara,
one should observe the celestial, atmospheric, and terrestrial omens."
"Having observed that [ground] as auspicious or inauspicious, one should examine the site for the auspicious;

indeed, in the case of inauspicious signs, one should offer a hundred oblations with the Aghora mantra. Thus, the method for extracting the "stake" (śalyoddhāra) during the preparatory rites has been described.
At the conclusion of the fire sacrifice, the preceptor should extract the splinters;
having observed the patron, the Guru should speak of the splinters according to their respective qualities.
When the performer touches a particular limb on the body of the site, the wise man should indicate that there is a *śalya* (impurity) in that very limb; this applies if he touches the head.
There, at a depth of eight tālas below, one should indicate a golden arrow;
at the touch of the nose, however, there is sandalwood at seven tālas.
If there is a touch on the throat, there will be a bone-thorn located here beneath the *paṭṭāla*;
and upon touching the chest, there is silver at a distance of five *tālas*.
When the navel is touched, one should indicate a bronze pin located four *tālas* below;
when the private parts are touched, they know it to be copper situated three *tālas* below.
If there is contact with the thighs or the knees, one should indicate an iron [object] the size of a hand;
when there is contact with the ankles, one should specify tin or lead.
Upon touching the arm, one should indicate that there is a naga-bone at the level of the arm;
having thus understood this and removed it, one should then sprinkle it with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
Make [the ground] level and very firm with earth over the sand;
[compact it] below by striking with pestles and by the trampling of elephants' feet,
using eight kinds of earth, stones, gravel, and elephant-footprints, and so forth.
Now, the author states the time for the laying out of the site (vāstu-vinyāsa): Root Text:
[The asterisms] beginning with Mūla, Hasta, Svāti, Anurādhā, Śravaṇa, Dhaniṣṭhā, Citrā, Mṛgaśīrṣa, Revatī, and Uttarā...
On the days of Śroṇa, Āditya, Ghaṭi, Niṣṭhā, Maitra, and during the northern transit (uttarāyaṇa),

having avoided the month of Māgha as well as the months of Āṣāḍha, Kārttika, and Nabhas, and having left aside the movable zodiac signs and the days of Mars and Saturn, the preceptor should lay the foundation on an auspicious lunar day.

Regarding "piercing" (vedha): therein, he first states the lunar mansions (nakṣatras). Vedhas is Rohiṇī; Hasta is Sāvitrī; Marut is Svātī; Maghā and Aśvinī are well-known; Varuṇa is Śatabhiṣak; Tvāṣṭra is Citrā; Indu is Mṛgaśirā; Pauṣṇa is Revatī; and Uttarā—

The three *uttara* constellations—Uttaraphalgunī, Uttarāṣāḍhā, and Uttaraproṣṭhapadā; Śroṇā (Pūrvabhādrapadā); Śravaṇa; Āditya (Punarvasu); Dhaniṣṭhā; Śraviṣṭhā; and Maitra (Anurādhā)—in these sixteen lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*).
Thus it is stated in the *Kāmika-tantra*, in the chapter on the rules of time (*kālavidhānapaṭala*):
Rohiṇī, the three Uttarās, Hasta, Citrā, Punarvasu,
Anurādhā, Aśvinī, Mṛgaśīrṣa, Śatabhiṣaj, Śravaṇa, and Maghā.
"Citrā, Śraviṣṭhā, and Pauṣṇa—these others are not praised among [the nakṣatras]. Thus [it is said].

Having excluded the month of Māgha during the northern transit (uttarāyaṇa), one should also perform [the rite] during the months of Īṣa, Kārtika, and Nabhas in the southern transit (dakṣiṇāyana); here, Īṣa refers to Āśvayuja, Kārtika is well known, and Nabhas refers to Śrāvaṇa; in these months as well, the task should be done.
And it is said in that very same place:
"Except for the month of Māgha, the northern transit (uttarāyaṇa) of the sun is auspicious;
as are the months of Kārttika and Āśvayuja during the southern transit (dakṣiṇāyana)."
"And hearing [the teachings] is prescribed; others besides those are considered censured. Thus [it is said].

Now, he states the rule for the zodiac signs by way of prohibition: one should perform [the rite] having avoided the mobile signs—Aries, Cancer, Libra, and Capricorn—as well as the days of Mars and Saturn (Tuesday and Saturday). This too has been stated in that very same work:
"That which resides in an excellent fixed sign is best, while that which is of a dual nature is middling."
A movable sign (cararāśi) is to be avoided, yet it is considered auspicious when occupied by Jupiter (Jīva).

Regarding the days of the week, having excluded Tuesday (Kuja) and Saturday (Ārkaja), the remaining days are proclaimed [as favorable]. For human [births], one should avoid Sunday; thus have others declared. So it is said.
Regarding "on auspicious lunar days" (*sutithau*): those too are specified in that very same [text]:

"The bright fortnight is auspicious; the dark fortnight is considered auspicious up to the seventh day. In the bright fortnight, one should avoid the first third [of the day]; in the dark fortnight, one should avoid the last [third]."
The two middle portions are considered middling, while the other two are proclaimed to be excellent. (p.
18) One should avoid the ninth and fifteenth lunar days, as well as any odd-numbered tithi;
however, among the even-numbered tithis, one may take the second and likewise the tenth.
"The sixth day in the dark fortnight, and all those [lunar days] which remain—these are all censured here."
At these times, the preceptor should lay out the site. In the *Kāmika*, even the unfavorable planetary positions to be avoided have been stated, as follows:
"The rising of Jupiter, Venus, and the Moon is highly commended."
The rising of Jupiter brings prosperity to Brahmins, while the rising of Venus brings it to kings.
The rising of Mercury is most excellent for Vaiśyas, and it is likewise prescribed for Śūdras;
moreover, malefic planets situated in the third, sixth, or eleventh house from the domicile (vāstu) are auspicious.
Excluding the Vyaya, all auspicious [planets] are considered to bestow auspicious results everywhere;
however, O best of the twice-born, the malefic planets situated in the Caturasra houses must be avoided.
The wise preceptor, established in the fivefold sphere of practice, should avoid the Moon situated between both [the Sun and Venus] and Venus occupying the sixth or seventh house.
The best of teachers should avoid taking up a staff that is thorny, made of *brahmadaṇḍa* wood, thick, loose, joined with a handle, or one that is desired by another.
Vaidhṛta, Tārakṣa, Vyatīpāta, Vajra, and likewise Śūla,
Viṣkambha, Parigha, Gaṇḍa, and Harṣaṇa.
Likewise, [one should avoid] Atigaṇḍa, a weak asterism, the six Aśītimukhas,
a month devoid of planets, and similarly a burnt day (Dagdhavāra).

One should avoid [performing rites] at the end of a lunar day (tithi), a lunar mansion (nakṣatra), or a month, as well as at the end of a year. A wise preceptor, in particular, should avoid the intercalary month (adhimāsa).
In a lunar mansion favorable to the sacrificer, which has few defects and many virtues,
at a lagna endowed with the strength of the planets, either in the forenoon or at midday.
One should have this work on the two doors performed for the sake of the increase of all prosperity. Thus it is said.
Now, since the consecration (pratiṣṭhā) is preceded by the gathering of stone and wood, he states the time for gathering that stone and wood— the root text:

Likewise, during the six months of the northern solstice, one should proceed when the asterisms are those of Tvaṣṭṛ, Soma, Anila, Viṣṇu, the three following [Viṣṇu], Pauṣṇa, Maitra, Maghā, Sāvitra, and Brāhma;
and when the signs are Pisces, Aquarius, Jar, Yama, or Capricorn, provided the omens are auspicious.
Having carefully examined it by its color and other qualities, let a stone or a piece of wood be selected.
Regarding "in six months": during the six months of the northern course, beginning with the month of Capricorn; and likewise in the *Santānasaṃhitā*:
"Having resorted to a mountain cave as one's place, the taking up of the stone is supreme."
In Aries, Taurus, Gemini, Capricorn, Aquarius, and Pisces.
"When these zodiac signs have arrived, they should be accepted; in others, one should avoid them. Thus it is said.
And as for the cause:
during the months of Madhu, Mādhava, Śukla, Sahasya,
and Tapasya— specifically in the bright fortnight of these months on an auspicious day.
"In all other months, one should not cause the commencement of the stone-work;
if it is done, there will be the destruction of the builder, the ruin of the site, and the loss of wealth. Thus [it is said].

Now he mentions the lunar mansions: Tvāṣṭra is Citrā; Saumya is Mṛgaśiras; Anila is Svātī; Viṣṇu is Śravaṇa; the three Uttarās are Uttarāphalgunī, Uttarāṣāḍhā, and Uttaraproṣṭhapadā; Pauṣṇa is Revatī; Maitrabha is Anurādhā; and Madhā is well known.
One should perform the collection of the stone under these twelve lunar mansions: Sāvitra (Anurādhā), Hasta, Brāhma (Rohiṇī), and so forth. Thus it is stated in the Kāraṇa:
"Under Prajāpatya (Rohiṇī), Maghā, Tvāṣṭra (Citrā), Vaiṣṇava (Śravaṇa), and Mṛgaśīrṣaka."
And also under the asterisms of Sāvitra, Revatī, Anila, and the three Uttarās.
"In this same way, one should perform the taking of the stone only during auspicious times. Thus it is said.
Now he states the zodiac signs:

*gauḥ* is Taurus (*vṛṣabha*), *mīnaḥ* is Pisces (well-known), *ajaḥ* is Aries (*meṣa*), *ghaṭaḥ* is Aquarius (*kumbha*), *yame* is Gemini (*mithuna*), and *makaraḥ* is Capricorn (*makara*). In these six signs, the stone should be taken.
As it is stated in the Dīptatantra: "In Aries, Taurus, Gemini, Capricorn, Aquarius, and Pisces— in these zodiac signs, the characteristics for the selection of the stone are to be observed."
Now, regarding the time of departure for the purpose of collecting the stone, it is said that one should go after examining auspicious omens:
"One should go when the omen is auspicious."
And so it has been stated in the *Santānasaṃhitā*:
"The preceptor, together with the artisans, should proceed toward the northeast," beginning thus, and continuing:
"He should examine the omens pertaining to the celestial, atmospheric, and terrestrial realms. (p. 21)

A cow, a maiden, a kettle-drum, a conch, curd, fruit, flowers, a full pitcher, a banner, grain, a pair of Brahmins, a horse, an elephant, a bull, a white umbrella, and a flower; having seen these, or a water-pot filled with drink, a pair of aquatic creatures, or cooked food—one whose life has reached its end— [Note: This fragment appears to be part of a larger text concerning omens (nimitta) regarding the death of a person.]
A courtesan woman [carries] a load of flesh, yet she utters pleasant words intended for auspiciousness.
Cotton, medicinal herbs, black grain, salt, eunuchs, oil-seed carriers, mud, charcoal, molasses, silk-cotton trees, dung, hair, the diseased,
those intoxicated by wind (epilepsy), matted-hair ascetics, wealth, stones, chaff, those emaciated by hunger, the naked, and so forth—
"Women who are shaven-headed, smeared with unguents, with disheveled hair, or wearing saffron robes are inauspicious. Thus it is said.
O Ajita,
hereafter I shall describe the taking up of the stone and other materials, O Hari.
When the preceptor arrives at the site of the stone together with the artisan:
At that time, for a short while, one should observe the auspicious signs:
curd-rice, honey, clarified butter, and likewise a full water-pot.
Gold and silver, all kinds of gems and pearls,
and all ornaments together with weapons, O Lotus-born One.
Along with unbroken rice grains and fruits, as well as yellow pigment (rocanā) and red ochre (gairika),
and likewise a blessed seat (bhadrapīṭha), a conch shell, and white flowers.
White garments, fish, and likewise meat;
a preeminent bull and an elephant; and auspicious brahmins and vaiśyas.
A maiden, a horse, a fish, a peacock,
a blue jay, a tiger, and a mongoose— these indeed are one's friends.
Upon seeing or hearing songs, auspicious musical instruments, the chanting of the Vedas, and so forth, as well as the sound of a whispering voice, the wise man should depart.
All cotton, medicinal herbs, black grains,
as well as salt, oil, honey, and likewise milk;
Mud, charcoal, molasses, leather,
as well as dung, fuel, stones, husks, and hair indeed.
One should likewise avoid a madman, one with matted hair, one with a shaven head, one who is naked, one wearing saffron robes,
one emaciated by hunger, one who is deformed, and even a man carrying a sacrificial offering.
One who is anointed with oil, one with disheveled hair, and likewise one afflicted by disease;
as well as a snake, a monitor lizard, a śarabha, a boar, and a mongoose.
He heard crying, shouting, quarreling, and the sounds of funeral rites,
as well as voices saying, "Come," "Enter," and "Stay."

Having remembered such words as "For what purpose are you going?", one should not go upon merely seeing or hearing them; rather, having stayed for three days with a distracted mind, one should depart.
Having honored the initiated Brahmins who are devoted to Śiva and his attendants,
he should offer a hundred oblations with the *aghora* mantra for the sake of removing defects.
Having smeared [the vessel] and made it shine, one should remain diligent for a day and night;
then, having washed it thoroughly once more, one should examine it for defects.
After examining it in many ways, one should subsequently perform that rite;
at that very moment the mandala should be prepared, and one should designate her as being "with the embryo" (sagarbhā).
In a mañjiṣṭha-colored mandala there is a frog; in a yellow-colored one, a lizard; in a white one, a snake is indicated; and in a tawny-colored one, there would be a mouse.
A lizard appears when the color is red, and a clod of earth when it is yellowish-brown;
a female owl when the color is dove-grey, and likewise a scorpion when it is variegated.
Water in a sword-like [cloud], fireflies in one resembling honey,
and sprinkled ash in one of that color— now hear the fruit of these.
A lizard portends the destruction of the king; a scorpion, the loss of cattle;
a snake brings fever and pestilence; and a frog causes fear from enemies.
The falling of an embryo is said to result from water; a firefly omen portends danger from fire;
a shower of stones results from stone; and consumption disease results from sand.
A chameleon is said to bring disease, while a mouse causes the destruction of grain;
a female ant should be known as a bringer of sorrow—therefore, one should avoid a pregnant female.
If there are signs present here, one should observe the true signs:
resembling a lotus, a svastika, the moon, the sun, a wheel, a womb, or a banner.
(24) It resembles a beautiful body, an umbrella, a lion, a tree, a bow, and a fish;
it is also like an elephant, the Goddess Śrī, a cow, a sacrificial ladle (sruk), matted hair, and an eye.
Indeed, such auspicious signs as these appear,
resembling vultures and herons, and like crows, serpents, and headless trunks.
A line resembling a hawk or an owl, one like a boar’s tusk or a crab, one like a jackal or a camel, and a jagged line like a sword-stroke are all condemned.
O Hari, listen as I describe the marks consisting of color and form which bestow auspicious or inauspicious results when they appear upon the lingas.
Among the vowels, however, ṛ, ṝ, ḷ, ḹ, e, ai, and o are also auspicious;
among the consonant classes (vargas), the first letter is to be known as auspicious, while the second is censurable.
The third is to be known as bestowing auspiciousness, while the fourth is of a dual nature;
furthermore, the first syllable, the *prāsāda*, shall be exceedingly auspicious.
The nasalized letters and the two groups [of sibilants] should be abandoned by the wise;
the *kūṭa* and the *visarga* should be avoided, but that [visarga] with the bindu is most auspicious.
Furthermore, the letters *ma* and *au* also bestow auspicious results;
one should accept [a woman] endowed with auspicious marks and reject any other who is inauspicious. Thus it is said.
Regarding the characteristics of wood in the Ajita [Tantra]:
Then, the wise preceptor should go to a forest or a mountain that is well-guarded,
to a most delightful place suitable for the stage of life of a forest-dweller (vānaprastha).
(25) It was joined by rivers and ponds, beautified by fruits and sprouts,
and adorned with trees bent low under the weight of their blossoms.
When the one wishing to kill has been released, the teacher and the artisan should enter;
for the purpose of seizing the tree, they should take refuge in that tree which was previously indicated.
One should select an excellent tree that is straight, symmetrical in its growth, free from knots and cavities, possessing its bark intact, and abundant with flowers and leaves.

"A knower of mantras should likewise avoid a tree that has been broken by elephants and the like, scorched by lightning and the like, crooked, wounded, or one that has withered of its own accord. Thus it is said.
Now, he states the time for the worship of Vāstu:
In a sacrificial session (*sattra*), in an assembly of the ignorant, at the site of a sacrifice, and during the ritual sprinkling (*samprokṣaṇa*);
in the installation of a *liṅga*, in the rite for a jeweled pavilion (*ratnamaṇḍapa*), and in the laying of the foundation (*garbha*);
in every rite of consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) and for the purpose of dance on the stage—[the following should be performed].
That Vāstupūjā, which is the abode for all deities and brings joy to them, is described in the Āgama.

"In the sacrificial session" means in a sacrifice such as the *sattra*; "in the foundation of a child" means in the ritual for establishing a child; "in the assembly hall" means in the establishment of the pavilion for the formal reception; "on the first brick" means on the initial *iṣṭakā*;

"in the place of the sacrifice" means in the sacrificial shed (*yāgaśālā*); and "in the sprinkling" refers to the repeated sprinkling and other rites performed when there has been contact with impurities and the like.
In the specific ritual action, in the installation of the *liṅga*, in the procedure for the jeweled pavilion— namely, the consecration of the jeweled pavilion—

in the establishment of the womb-chamber (*garbha*)— that is, the procedure for the deposition of the womb-chamber being constructed for the temple, the gate-tower (*gopura*), and so forth— and in the complete rite of consecration— the procedure for the consecration of the twenty-five forms, such as the dancing image (*nṛttamūrti*) and others.

On the occasion of a dance performance, on a stage, and in a theater— during these times, that worship of the site (vāstupūjā) prescribed in the Śaiva Āgamas must be performed for the delight of all the deities residing there. Thus it is stated in the Kāraṇāgama:
Now I shall explain in detail the sequence of the ritual for the Vāstu-homa,
whether at the site of a child’s birth, in an assembly hall, at a sacrificial session, or in a sacrificial pavilion.
Likewise, at the initial laying of the foundation bricks, at the installation of the *liṅga*,
at the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), at the placement of the womb (*garbhanyāsa*), and at the installation of the complete form (*sakalasthāpana*).
One should perform [the ritual] when establishing a pavilion, especially on a dance floor,
in a temple, or when establishing any other structure.
"The Vāstuhoma should be performed, provided with all necessary materials. Thus it is said.
In order to demonstrate the fault that arises in the absence of the Vāstu-pūjā, the nature of Vāstu was described by Ajita as follows:
"In ancient times, there was a certain person who was terrifying to the three worlds."
Covering the worlds with his body, he strode across the earth.
Seeing him, the gods were terrified on all sides;
having deliberated together, they seized him and held him face downwards.
Pressing down upon all his limbs, they cast him onto the surface of the earth;
he alone is called Vāstu, and his limbs were occupied by the gods and asuras.
Wherever and by whomsoever [the mantras] have been mastered, there one should offer them an oblation (*bali*).
Having received the oblation, all those gods remain gratified for a very long time.
If worship of those gods is not performed by them,
then the gods certainly depart, leaving behind their very limbs.
When they have departed, that site will perish; of this there is no doubt.
The cause of its destruction here will be the dispersal of its constituent parts.
Therefore, the wise person should worship the deities residing in that site;
the head of the dwelling is in the northeast (Īśāna), while the feet are in the domain of Nirṛti.
The belly should be known as Brahmā, and one should likewise arrange the limbs;
those deities who reside in the other limbs are to be worshipped as dependent upon them.
"Wherever faith or something else is produced, there [the rite should be performed] by the teachers. Thus [it is said].
Now, in the *Kāmika*:
"I shall now describe specifically the sequence of offerings to the deities of the site (*vāstudeva*).
A wise person should perform the offering at night for villages and other such sites during the day."
Whether by night or by day, in houses, temples, and so forth.
Having thus described the manner of worshipping the *vāstu* deity and so forth, at the end of the chapter [it says]:
"In all auspicious rites, as well as in the purification of the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) and other structures,
one should perform the *vāstu*-worship and fire-oblation (*homa*), accompanied by the ritual of circumambulation with fire (*paryagnikaraṇa*)."
A Śiva-brahmin should especially perform the bali offering;
for if the worship of Vāstu is omitted, the site (vāstu) itself perishes.
"The preceptor should perform [this rite] every year in villages and the like, in the houses of the planets, or in a temple, for the removal of all defects. Thus it is said.
Now, he states the time for the offering of the sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa): Root Text:
One should perform the bathing and consecration according to the ritual procedure for the festival of Śiva.
Sprinkling and all other Śiva-rites are preceded by that [purification];
however, this rite of germinating seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa) may be performed immediately at night or during the day, provided it is done on the ninth, seventh, fifth, third, or first lunar day.

"One should perform" means that one should perform the offering of sprouts (*aṅkurārpaṇa*) during festivals of Śiva and the like. Here, by the word "festival" (*utsava*), the festival of Śiva is intended, which is divided into categories such as those lasting one day, three days, five days, seven days, nine days, twelve days, fifteen days, or seventeen days. By the word "bath" (*snapana*), that which is distinct from the daily bath is meant.

The three intermediate and the three highest categories concerning occasional (*naimittika*) and optional (*kāmya*) rites are intended here. By the word "installation" (*pratiṣṭhā*), the installation of the *sakala* and *sakala-niṣkala* forms of the Śiva-liṅga and so forth is intended. By the word "sprinkling" (*samprokṣaṇa*), the propitiatory rites (*śānti*) such as the *āvartana*, *anāvarta*, and others, as well as the *śānti-homa*, *diśā-homa*, and *mūrti-homa* in the form of expiation (*prāyaścitta*), are intended.

The *saṃhitā-homas* are intended [here]. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the monthly worship (*māsapūjā*) and other rites are also included. In all these rituals, one should perform the offering of sprouts (*aṅkurārpaṇa*) during the night on the ninth, seventh, fifth, third, or first day prior [to the main rite]; if it is to be done immediately (*sadyas*), one may do so even during the day.
As it is stated in the *Suprabheda*:
"Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the sequence of the ritual for the sprout (aṅkura);
at the beginning of all auspicious rites, the auspicious sprout must be prepared."
During the installation, the sprinkling, the bathing, and likewise the festival—
whether during the nine nights, the seven nights, or again the five nights— [one should perform these rites].
In all rites, the preceptor should perform the sowing of sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa) either during three nights or one night; beginning the day at sunset, he should complete it at sunset.
"The Moon is the presiding deity of seeds; therefore, one should sow them at night. Thus it is said.
Likewise, regarding the cause: "During a festival, a ritual bath, a sprinkling, or an installation,
as well as on other auspicious occasions, it is called the 'Auspicious Sprout' (maṅgalāṅkura)."
In all rites preceded by sacrifice, one should worship Śiva on the ninth, seventh,
or fifth day prior and perform the offering of germinating seeds (aṅkurārpaṇa).
Or one may have the offering of sprouts performed immediately;
since the Moon is the lord of seeds, one should therefore perform the scattering at night.
If the offering of the sprouts is to be made immediately, one should perform the oblation by day or by night. Thus it is said.
Likewise, in the Kāmika:
"At the beginning of all auspicious rites and so forth, the 'germ of auspiciousness' (maṅgalāṅkura) must be performed.
It is proclaimed to be of three kinds: superior, middling, and inferior. (p. 30)
"On the ninth day, or the seventh, the fifth, or even the third day, or else immediately, one should perform the rite of offering the sprouts after having fully worshipped Śiva. Thus it is said.
O Ajita, regarding whatever rite is performed on a specific day while aiming for auspiciousness,
one should perform it on the ninth or even the seventh day prior to that.
And on the fifth day, or even after three days, one should perform the sowing of those seeds;
on the night preceding the aforementioned days, one should employ the preliminary rites.
"Or, having worshipped Śiva on a single day, or even immediately upon [seeing] a sprout," so it is said.
Likewise, in the Siddhatantra: "Whatever action lacks its [proper] seed-syllable (aṅkura), that action shall be fruitless. Thus it is said.
Now, he states the time for the depositing of the embryo (garbhanyāsa):
Root Text:
It is said that among the years from one up to nine, the first is excellent; then, the middle and inferior [years] are for consecration (pratiṣṭhā).
When the sun is in its northern course, on an auspicious lunar day and a favorable day, in a month excluding the month of Maghā, and when the hour (horā), decan (drēkkāṇa),

and ninth-part (navāṃśa) are all fixed (sthira) and conjoined with a Karaṇa, the preceptor should perform the consecration of the womb (garbhādhāna) in a temple of Śiva or similar sacred site, specifically at a time endowed with the qualities of an unbroken asterism.

Regarding the time prior to the consecration: among the years preceding the consecration, the placement of the embryo (*garbhasthāpana*) performed before the consecration, at the conclusion of the consecration, or in the single year immediately following it, is respectively considered superior, middling, and inferior.
As it is said in the Kāmaika:
"The installation prior to the installation of the deity is the most excellent;
the installation at the conclusion of the installation of the deity is middling."

"Starting from the layout of the village and occurring at a time later than one year, the installation of the village and its surroundings is declared to be the 'lesser' (kanyasa) rite. Thus it is remembered.
He speaks again of the specific time: when the sun has moved north (during the northern transit), and even therein, in a month excluding Māgha,
on an auspicious lunar day and a favorable day— endowed with a beautiful lunar date and an auspicious weekday— and during stable *karaṇas*, as well as in the *horās*, *drekkāṇas*, and *navāṃśas*.
And so it is said in the *Kāraṇa*:
"During the period of the northern solstice, excluding the month of Māgha,
on an auspicious day in the bright fortnight, with a favorable weekday and a favorable lunar date."

"In a stable portion, in a stable lunar mansion, likewise in a stable hour and planetary period, in a stable decan, on a stable day of the week, and when the planets are in stable signs. Thus it is said.
"Under an unbroken asterism" means under an asterism that is whole and endowed with [auspicious] qualities; as it is stated in the *Kāraṇa*:
"Especially at a firm ascendant under an unbroken asterism and at an auspicious moment."

At such a moment, the preceptor, possessing the characteristics previously described, should deposit the *garbha*—that is, perform the *garbhanyāsa*—in the temple of Śiva or, by the word "etcetera," in the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*), the gateway (*gopura*), and so forth. Thus it is said in the *Ajita*:
"Now I shall explain to you correctly the sequence of the procedure for the *garbhanyāsa*. (p. 32)
In a palace, or in a pavilion, or at a city gate, or in assembly halls and the like.
"The wise one should duly place the womb-vessel for the sake of accomplishment," so it is said.
In that regard, the specific location is also established in that very same place:
"In all cases, the placement of the *garbha* (foundation) is declared to be above the first brick;
however, in a temple (*prāsāda*), one should install it upon the *paṭṭikā* (fillet) above the *pādaka* (pedestal)."
On the right side of the door, or again at the base of a pillar,
and in all pavilions, at the base of the pillar on the right.
One should fix it at the base of the wall on the southern side of the gopura door,
or even at the base of that same pillar within the assembly hall.
When correctly endowed with the inner essence, it brings about various forms of prosperity for human beings. Thus [it is said].
A specific distinction is stated in the *Suprabheda*:
"In the *ālaya* and the pavilion (*maṇṭapa*), [the door] is on the right of the exit;
and for all the gate-towers (*gopura*), it is on the right of the entrance."
One should construct [the temple] starting from the foundation in a palace, or likewise on a terrace or within an enclosure;
for those of the Śūdra caste it should be set upon the ground, while for kings and Vaiśyas it should be on a terrace.
The womb-chamber for the Brahmins is prescribed above the enclosure wall;
however, for all [the other castes], it is recommended that it be made either within the enclosure or underground.
If an eastern gate is to be constructed, it should be placed between the directions of Indra (East) and Agni (Southeast);
if it is a western gate, one should place it on the southern wall.
The wise practitioner should place the vessel containing the embryo either at the junction of the door and its bolt,
or at the base of a pillar in the pavilion during the first enclosure.
"When the gopuras are to be constructed, one should install [the image] on the right side. Thus it is said.
Regarding the causes: for villages and the like, [the time is] at night; but for houses, it is during the day. Thus it is said.
In the *Kāmika*:

"In the case of vimānas with foot-bases, one should place the sanctum (*garbha*) atop the palace structure (*harmya*); but in the case of vimānas with continuous bases, one should place it above the enclosure wall (*vṛti*)."
Above the mat for Brahmins, above the lily for kings,
above the ground for Vaiśyas, and above the sandals for Śūdras.
The work pertaining to the earth is for all [beings], and it brings about the accomplishment of all goals;
it concerns the construction of step-wells, wells, tanks, large ponds, and embankments.
If it is the fetus, one should place it in the northern part or the eastern part;
for villages and the like, this may be done at night, but for a house, even during the day.
In the *nāgayoga*, one may place [the ritual] within the interior of a village even during the day;
for human beings one should perform the placement at night, but for the gods it may be done even by day.
"If the wife of the perpetrator is pregnant, she shall not cause the fetus to be aborted. Thus it is said.

Regarding the fruit obtained when the laying of the foundation (garbhanyāsa) is performed, and the fault that arises in its absence, it is stated in the *Kāmika*: "I shall describe the procedure for the laying of the foundation for villages and other dwellings.
That [foundation] brings about all prosperity, whereas a structure without a foundation leads to destruction."
Therefore, with every effort, a wise person should ensure that the embryo is properly established. Thus it is said.
Now he states the procedure for the Bālā-ālaya: Root Text:
"When the [Liṅga] called Bālā has been described according to the sequence of being preceded by two and interspersed with one..."

In this context, they speak of that [worship] as being of two kinds; it is tenfold: the image, the water-pot, the cloth, the painting, the mirror, the auspicious brush, the mandala, the ground, the sandals, and the first [the root-mantra].
The wise know that in worship, the primary rule applies to the former, while for the others, it depends on their relative degree of excellence.
Regarding the two types of marks designated as "marks of the ignorant" (*bālaliṅga*), which are explained according to the sequence of "the first" and "the intermediate":
the first is that which is performed in full from the root-mark; the second, however, is that which is cut, broken, or worn out.
That which is being performed with respect to objects such as palaces and the like.
And so it is said in the Ajitāgama:
"I shall explain briefly the consecration of the *bāla-liṅga*;
it is declared to be of two kinds: the first being the *antarita* (intermediate) and so forth."
Having thus explained consecration (pratiṣṭhā) in detail, the first [type] has been described; now the second shall be stated.
That, indeed, is to be employed by the teachers (deśikas) when the lingas have become worn out. Thus [it is said].
Likewise, in the *Suprabheda*: "The first and likewise the second are the two types of *varuṇālaya*.
