That which is prior to the primary site (*mūlasthāna*) is the first *taruṇālaya*."

Furthermore, when a temple is built, or when it is broken, cut, or renovated, that which is performed is called the second [type], the excellent *taruṇālaya* (rejuvenation of the abode). Thus it is said.

Among these, there is no division in the first case; however, in the second case, he speaks of tenfoldness. The *bimba*s are the forms such as Umā-Maheśvara and others; the *asi* is a sword; the *kumbha*s are those endowed with the characteristics described in the section on consecration (*snapana*); the *paṭa* is a painting on cloth; and the *citra* is a painting [on a wall] and so forth.

The mirror is a looking-glass; the fine-bristled brush is one endowed with the characteristics described in the section on implements; the mandala refers to the various types of mandalas such as Anantavijaya and others; the ground is a sacrificial mound smeared with cow dung; and the sandals are those characterized by the specific marks of their respective types—all these ten items are intended for the second category of neophyte (bāla-liṅga).
Thus it is said in the *Aṃśumat-tantra*:
"The second [division] therein should be known; its sub-divisions are understood to be tenfold."
In a sword, in a tuft of grass, in an image, in a mirror, and in a reflection.
"One should worship for the sake of the child-liṅga in a water-pot, on a sacrificial mound, in a mandala, or in sandals, or on a cloth, or in wall-paintings. Thus it is said.

In that regard, concerning the initial primary signs (*mūlaliṅga*)— that is, the subject matter of the earlier "child-like" signs— and concerning worship (*arcana*), the rule is exactly as stated in the root text. However, regarding the other— that is, the second [category]— they say it depends on their relative gradation (*tattāratamyāt*),
meaning the gradation in the duration of their persistence, whether for a long time or a short time.
And so it is stated in the *Aṃśumat-tantra*: "The wise know that the installation of the jar (*kumbha*) must not be performed after a month has passed;
one should perform the heating of the jar (*kalaśa*) according to the prescribed method alone."
One should perform the worship of that image specifically upon a mandala, a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), or even on the ground, for up to seven days.
"The most excellent preceptor should cause [the worship] to be performed by way of the mandala-arcana;
he should worship the remaining other images until the age of twelve," and so forth.

Now, demonstrating the time for the installation of the Śiva-liṅga with two verses, the author states in the first verse the forbidden solstices, months, lunar days, and unfavorable yogas and so forth: Root Text:
Likewise, it should be performed during the northern solstice as well, avoiding the month of Māgha, the new moon, the eighth day, the first day, the lunar festivals (parvan),
the days when malefic planets aspect the ascendant or its degrees, and the days of the blind and the one-eyed [planets].
The installation of Śiva begins with the offering of water for the feet, the arghya, and the immortal nectar. || 10 ||

Regarding what must be done: first, he states the determination of the month and the season—during the northern solstice (uttarāyaṇa), excluding the month of Māgha, the installation of Śiva (śivapratiṣṭhā) should be performed. Thus it is stated in the Ajitāgama, following a praise of the installation of the Śiva-liṅga, that it is the locus for the manifestation of Śiva.
After this description (p. 37), I shall explain the installation of the *liṅga*, which bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon men;
[the Lord] who is free from beginning, middle, and end, and whose nature is pure.
In the Śiva-āgama, Śiva is to be known as omniscient and perfect;
he is unconditioned by space, time, and the like, and his domain transcends speech and mind.
He is partless and actionless, the eternal seer and omnipresent;
liberation comes only through knowledge of Him, or through devotion to Him, O Janārdana.
Even worship of him bestows fruits such as the station of Indra;
when the Lord of the Gods of gods is worshipped, he grants devotion and knowledge.
Liberation is not attained anywhere except through knowledge and the yoga of devotion, nor by millions of other ritual acts; therefore, the worship of the Liṅga is supreme.
There is no dharma equal to the worship of the Liṅga in these three worlds;
and that worship is performed toward the three types of Liṅgas: the manifest, the unmanifest, and those consisting of both.
When [the image] has been installed, one becomes liberated; installation is of two kinds:
installation (*sthāpana*) and consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*). Installation is that which is performed by means of an artisan.
If it were devoid of that, the consecration would be ineffective;
for Mahādeva Śiva, the supreme cause, is the very embodiment of the mantra.
The mantra is supreme knowledge, and Sadāśiva is that which is expressed by the mantra;
the relationship between the signifier and the signified is thus observed in this mantra.
O Janārdana, the *liṅga*, the *cihna*, and the *śarīra* of the God of gods, who bestows grace upon the worlds, are described here.
The body itself should be the mantra, designated as Śabdabrahman;
having first established the body as consisting of both the manifest and the unmanifest.
O best of gods, that threefold [rite] is for the purpose of his constant worship;
the mantra established within each individual liṅga is proclaimed as *pratiṣṭhā*.
"Now, I shall describe the time for the ritual of consecration:
it should be during the period of the sun's northern course (uttarāyaṇa), excluding the month of Māgha. Thus [it is said].
Now, he states the rules for the lunar days (*tithi*) by way of those to be avoided:
the *rikta* days, the eighth, and the first; the *rikta* days are the fourth, ninth, and fourteenth;
the eighth and the first are the middle and beginning of the fortnight; and the *parvan* consists of the full moon and new moon days—these [are to be avoided].
The meaning is that others, having been excluded, are to be grasped.
Thus it is stated in the *Kāraṇa*:
"The southern transit (ayana) is not desired; the northern transit is praised.
Also, the fourth, eighth, and fourteenth days of the bright fortnight [are auspicious]."
The ninth, the first, and the fifteenth days are remembered as inauspicious. Thus it is said.
O Ajitā, in the bright fortnight, the second, third, fifth,
as well as the sixth, seventh, tenth, and thirteenth [are auspicious].
The lunar days (tithis) occurring in the first half of the day are declared to be auspicious;
among them, the days of Jupiter, Mercury, Venus, and the Moon are proclaimed to be the most excellent.
"One should also avoid the waning days of the fortnight and those that are empty on the lunar nodes. Thus it is said.
A specific distinction is stated in the *Bhīmasaṃhitā*, as follows:
"The southern solstice (*dakṣiṇāyana*) is not desired, while the northern solstice (*uttarāyaṇa*) is praised;
that [practice] is considered best during the northern solstice, but inferior during the southern."
Even among all those months, Caitra and Vaiśākha are best;
Puṣya, Phālguna, and Jyeṣṭha are declared to be middling.
"In Śrāvaṇa or Pūrvabhādrapada, or in Āśvayuja and Kārttika, it is inferior;
one should avoid the months of Mārgaśīrṣa, Āṣāḍha, and Māgha. Thus [it is said].
In the Mohasūrottara, the avoidance of the intercalary month (adhikamāsa) is stated:

"O Śatakratu, if one desires one's own welfare, one should perform initiations and the like, as well as the installation [of deities], the Pavitraka rite, and so forth, avoiding the intercalary month."

In the *Jyotiṣa*, however, the fruit of establishing [an image] by Jupiter during the twelve months has been stated as follows: "In the month of Puṣya there shall be an increase in sovereignty; in the month of Māgha, one becomes exceedingly generous;
in Phālguna there shall be the acquisition of wealth; and in the month of Caitra, it brings prosperity."
The month of Vaiśākha brings great happiness, while the month of Jyeṣṭha brings prosperity; the month of Kumbha (Māgha) is highly auspicious, provided one does not behold a water-pot [in its sign].
If one observes the Jīva [constellation] when the Sun has entered Pratiṣṭhā,
and the deity is installed in Āṣāḍha, it brings about the destruction of the patron.
By the solar month, it should be known that [the asterism] Śravaṇa brings ruin to the king and the kingdom;
Bhādrapada causes great destruction; and Āśvayujī also destroys the king.
In Kārttika there may be enmity toward enemies, and likewise in Mārgaśīrṣa. Thus it is said.

And so it is stated in the astronomical treatise known as the *Ratnakośa*: "One should perform the rite for establishing a *liṅga* during the bright fortnight, under an auspicious lunar day (*tithi*), in a favorable conjunction, and under a propitious asterism (*nakṣatra*), when the moon is situated in a benefic sign."
And Agastya said:
"The installation of Rudra is most excellent when the sun is in its northern course (uttarāyaṇa);
if one should perform it while the sun is in its southern course (dakṣiṇāyana), it will bring about the destruction of the performer."

Thus, by means of numerous scriptural authorities (*āgama*) and astrological treatises (*jyotiṣa*), it is established that only the northern solstice (*uttarāyaṇa*) is the proper time for consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*). Now, one must avoid evil aspects (*pāpekṣaṇa*), evil divisions (*pāpāṃśaka*), and evil days (*pāpadina*).
As it has been said in the *Ajita*:
That which is joined with a malefic planet, as well as that which is afflicted by a malefic, pierced, or desired [by one],
and likewise that which possesses a vyatīpāta yoga, should be avoided with great effort.
As it is stated in the Bhīmasaṃhitā: "The days of Mercury, Venus, Jupiter, and the Moon are remembered as the most excellent;
the Sun, Saturn, and Mars are inauspicious, yet they bestow auspicious results when in conjunction with benefic planets."
And in the Ajita [treatise] it is said:
"One should also completely avoid the days of Śani, Aṅgāra, and Īśa. Thus.
p. 41) Regarding the cause:
Mars, the Sun, and Saturn yield auspicious results when conjoined with benefic planets;
moreover, a Saturday conjoined with the Rohiṇī asterism and the Anila (Svātī) nakṣatra is auspicious.
A Sunday joined with the asterism Pūṣā (Revatī) and the deity Savitṛ is considered excellent;
a Tuesday joined with the Viśvedevas (Uttarāṣāḍhā) and the Aśvins (Aśvinī) is considered excellent. Thus it is said.
When the [planets] are combust,
the days of Jupiter, Venus, and Mercury are auspicious; likewise,
the decans, horās, and the aspect of their degrees are favorable.
The rising of these very [planets] is auspicious, but likewise, the rising of the Moon is to be avoided. Thus it is said.
Likewise, the Andhaka, Kāṇa, Pāta, Ayoga, Mṛta, and so forth— namely, the Andha-nakṣatra, Kāṇa-nakṣatra, and Mṛta-nakṣatra— are to be avoided.
As it is stated in the Dīptatantra:
A blind asterism and a one-eyed asterism are to be avoided in the rite of consecration. Thus it is said.
Regarding the characteristics of the blind, the one-eyed, and those with the marks of the constellations, as stated in the *Jyotiṣa*:
"One should place the days of the week starting from Sunday three times over the constellations starting from Aśvinī in sequence.
For the remaining [positions], there are nine, seven, six, two eyes, and two eyes for the blind. Thus it is said.
By the word *pāta*, *vyatīpāta* and *mahāpāta* are meant. Thus it has been said in the *Ajita*:
"One should carefully avoid [the yoga] together with *vyatīpāta* and *bha*."
In the *Jyotiṣa*:
"One should avoid that day on which a great eclipse occurs. Thus it is said.

By the word *avayoga*, the causes are stated; these include the burnt (*dagdha*), the barren (*vārā*), and so forth: "The twelfth, the eleventh, the fifth, the second, the sixth, the eighth, and the ninth are respectively associated with the Sun and the other [planets]."
They should be known as "burnt" (dagdhavāra); one should avoid them for rites such as the installation of images. Thus it is said.
In the Bhīmasaṃhitā: An Ekādaśī conjoined with the Sun on a Monday;
a Pañcamī conjoined with Mars; and a Dvitīyā conjoined with Mercury.
The sixth lunar day conjoined with Saturday, the eighth conjoined with Friday,
and the ninth conjoined with Saturday are remembered as the "burned" days (dagdhavāra).
"These [inauspicious signs] must be avoided during the installation and other rites; otherwise, they would bring about the destruction of the kingdom. Thus it is said.
In the *kāraṇa* [section]:
Puṣya is conjoined with the seventh lunar mansion (Aśleṣā), and Aśvinī with the second (Kṛttikā);
Puṣya is indeed joined with the asterism of Viṣṇu (Śravaṇā) under a white weekday (Monday) and the Uttarā [nakṣatras].
A Thursday conjoined with the Uttarāṣāḍhā constellation is auspicious;
a Monday with Hasta, and a Wednesday with Aśvinī.
These should be known as "burnt" (dagdhavāra) and one should avoid them for rites such as installation;
these are said to be inauspicious defects, as follows: "A desired planet that is conjoined with a malefic planet, or a planet that is isolated..."
A thorn, a pillar, a vyatīpāta yoga, poison, one-eyedness, and a bridge.
The thorn, the staff of Brahmā, the falling meteor, the pierced [constellation],
the planet that pierces a lunar mansion, the trident, and the earthquake.
And one should especially avoid a banner with great effort. Thus it is said.
The meaning of *arsya* is as follows: a planet (*graha*) conjoined with malefic planets—meaning joined with the Sun, Mars, Saturn, Rāhu, or Ketu;
"sought" (*kāṅkṣita*), meaning sought by these [planets]; and "released" (*mukta*), meaning being released from these. This refers to the ascendant (*lagna*).
As it is stated in the *Kālavidhāna*:
A lunar mansion (bha) conjoined with or aspected by malefic planets, joined with the junctions of day and night (sandhyā), or a "burnt" house (dagdha-gṛha) is void;
likewise, a mansion termed "blind," "mute," or "deaf" is so designated.
"In auspicious matters, one should avoid [the asterism] and that which is downward-facing. Thus it is said.
The placement of malefic planets even in positions such as the kendras (quadrants) and trikoṇas (trines) should be avoided.
Thus it was stated by Bharadvāja: "If the ascendant, the second house, the seventh house, or the eighth house is conjoined with a malefic planet..."
"They say that a cruel [planet] occupying the ascendant is inauspicious, whereas otherwise it would be auspicious. Thus [it is said].

The defect known as *kaṇṭaka* (thorn) is as stated by Bṛhaspati: "From the Sun to the southwest, and from the asterism of Nairṛta [Pūrvabhādrapadā] for that same distance, there is the great defect called *kaṇṭhaka*, which destroys all undertakings. Thus it is said.

The *sthūṇa* is the defect known as *sthūṇā*. As Bṛhaspati has said: "From the root up to the end of Aṅgāraka (Mūla), the asterisms in that interval are *viṣa*; this is called *sthūṇā*, and it is forbidden for all undertakings by both gods and men. Thus [it is stated].
In this context, by the word *sthūṇa*, *raktasthūṇa* is also included. On this point, Bṛhaspati says:
"From the asterism of Mars, one should subtract the portion of the *dhṛti* yoga;
the remainder, calculated from the asterism of Mars, is called *raktasthūṇa*."
"Whatever auspicious act is performed under the asterism of Raktasthūṇa leads to the opposite;
it quickly brings about the destruction of both the doer and the speaker, as has been declared."
And Bharadvāja said:
"One should clearly abandon from the actual number of parts those that are counted;
having fully understood the remaining parts, one should discard the 'red pillar'."
Here, by the term "pillar-throat" (*kaṇṭhasthūṇa*), the defect known as *kaṇṭhasthūṇā* is intended.
Regarding this, Bṛhaspati states:
"As long as the aspect [of the planets] is like gold or the sun, until the [asterism] of Nairṛta for those two [the Sun and Moon]."
"Endowed with two numbers from the root, it is designated as 'thorn-pillar' (kaṇṭakasthūṇa). Thus [it is said].

Regarding *vyatīpāta*, this has already been stated. As for *viṣa* (poison), here by the word "poison" the *tithi-viṣas* (lunar-day poisons), *nakṣatra-viṣas* (asterism poisons), *vāra-viṣas* (day-of-the-week poisons), and *rāśi-viṣas* (zodiacal-sign poisons) are included. Among these, the *tithi-viṣa* has been described by Agastya as follows:
The lunar days (tithis) corresponding to five, eight, seven, eight, eleven,
four, eight, seven, ten, three, thirteen, seven, eight, nine, and twelve are like the venom of a serpent.
Auspicious actions yield death on the first and subsequent lunar days. Thus it is said.

p. 45) Regarding the poison of the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra-viṣa*), it consists of four *nāḍikās*. On this point, Nārada says: "Thirty, forty, thirty-two, thirty, twenty-six, thirty-two, thirty, and twenty, as well as twenty."
There are twenty-two and twenty Indras, as well as Manus and quarters;
there are twenty, twenty-four, twenty, and the series of the quarters.
In the same way, according to the Purāṇas, there will be thirty or fifty kings associated with the Sun, as well as Jinas, in the asterisms beginning with Kṛttikā.
Beyond the [usual] channels, four further channels are to be known;
they are called "poisons" (viṣa), and for auspicious rites, they are always like drinking poison.
"Brahmā, the preceptor of the preceptor of the gods, declared that whatever auspicious act one performs oneself during the times known as *viṣanāḍī* perishes. Thus it is said.
In the *Kāladīpa*:
"Blue is neither jar nor cloth; mountain, man, plow, mountain, not by rat; lamp, Rudra, man, we, jar, lead; may there be man with water."
"Nārī, nṛtya, nṛpā, jaṭā, kṣaya, virāṭ, nāga, niśā, and vajra"—these are the [names] in the Āgneya and other directions; beyond these, the four channels are the poison. Thus it is said.
Regarding the poison of the days of the week, Agastya says here: on Sunday, four [units] beginning with *vipā* are beyond twenty;
on Monday, four [units] known as *vipā* are equal in number to the Vedas (four).
On Saturday, the four *nāḍikās* following the twelfth [hour] are called *viṣa*;
on Wednesday, the four [hours] following the tenth are called *gara*.
Likewise, on the day of Jupiter, the period after seven nāḍīs is inauspicious;
and on the day of Venus, it is likewise the four nāḍīs after five nāḍīs.
"There are twenty-five poisonous nāḍīs on Saturday; one should avoid all auspicious activities during the poisonous nāḍīs of the weekdays. Thus it is said.
The poison of the zodiac signs lasts for only half a *ghaṭikā*: in Aries, Taurus, Sagittarius, and Virgo, it is the serpent; in Libra, Gemini, Aquarius, and Leo, it is the vulture.
The crocodile [is the sign] at Capricorn, Cancer, and the end of Scorpio; the boar [is the sign] at the end of Scorpio. Thus it is said.
Regarding this, Bharadvāja says:
"In Aries, Taurus, Virgo,
and Sagittarius, three parts in particular— namely the first— are designated as 'poison'."
They know poison to be in Libra, Gemini, Aquarius, Leo, and Aries;
they know poison to be in Pisces, Cancer, Capricorn, and at the end of Scorpio. Thus it is said.
Now, regarding the *kaṇṭaka*—the defect known as *kaṇṭaka*, as well as those called *mahākaṇṭaka* and *yamakaṇṭaka*:
the defect of *mahākaṇṭaka* is as follows, according to Bṛhaspati: "When the Moon is in the eighth house from a lunar mansion conjoined with Mercury..."
"In that which is named Mahākaṇṭaka, the three defects are present. Thus [it is said].
From the lunar mansion [occupied by] Cāndrī, the eighth asterism is Ghṛtibha,
and likewise the twenty-fourth is known as Mahākaṇṭaka.
"Whatever auspicious deed has been performed perishes amidst faults perceived as great thorns, unless the Moon is not situated in its setting. Thus it is said.
Regarding Yamakaṇṭaka, Bṛhaspati says:
"The sixth, tenth, and eleventh [houses] from the sign occupied by Saturn and so forth are called Yamakaṇṭaka."
The "Brahma-staff" (brahmadaṇḍa), which is the fault known as Brahma-staff, and the fault known as the "falling meteor" (ulkāpāta), as Vṛddhagarga has said:
"As many degrees as the sun remains [in the zodiac], for that many degrees [of the same] the moon [remains]."
One should avoid [these] during the defects of the sun, but one may have the remaining rites performed.
In the forenoon there shall be the Brahmadaṇḍa; in the afternoon, however, the Modhaka;
at midnight, the Ulkā; and in the latter part of the day and night, the Kampa.
"The seasons are ninefold for those whose staffs are unfailing and whose lamps are shaking;
among them, the solar *ghaṭikās* should be subtracted by the wise. Thus it is said.
"Viddhaka" refers to a zodiac sign pierced by a malefic planet. "Grahaṇa" refers to the eclipses of the moon and the sun.
Regarding the "pierced asterism" (vedhanakṣatra), its characteristics are stated in the Vṛddhabhāradvājīya: "Ten signs and nine degrees [are pierced] by the movements of twice as many planets."
Having cleared away the remainder, [one should observe] the piercing of the planets by means of the suddenly arisen star. Thus [it is said].
Bṛhaspati has also said:
"In Capricorn, one should discard ten degrees for all planets situated therein;
the remainder shall be the piercing (*vedha*) by that planet, starting from the asterism of that planet."

If there is a piercing by benefic planets at the asterism of the work, the work is destroyed; if there is a piercing by malefic planets at the asterism of the work, the performer of the work is destroyed. A piercing by the Sun constitutes the "Night of Time" (Kālarātri), while a piercing by Mars is the "Night of Destruction" (Tarātraka).
An affliction by Mercury shall last for three nights; an affliction by Jupiter lasts for two nights.
"A Śani-vedha is an 'arātri' (non-night), while a Rāhu-vedha is called 'viṣa' (poison);
a Ketu-vedha is a 'garātri' (terrible night), and they say that all [these] are indeed 'asat' (inauspicious) nights."
"Śūla" refers to the defect known as *śūla* and the defect known as *mahāśūla*.
As stated by Bṛhaspati:
"One should place seven rays from the east and seven from the north above [the central point]."
At its end, there should be the letter *a* (Anala-bha) and so forth, or they may be situated within the houses of the Tārā.
Likewise, a star facing that line is possessed of great defects;
it brings great pain and suffering through the influence of malefic and benefic planets respectively.
"In the Mahāśūla yoga, the action performed perishes along with its doer;
likewise, in the Śūla yoga, [the action] perishes if the Moon is situated therein. Thus it is said.
The two defects known as "earthquake" (bhūmikampa) and "flag" (dhvaja), as well as the "dead asterism" (mṛtabha)— that is, the dead lunar mansion (mṛtanakṣatra).
For instance, an asterism is of three kinds,
according to the division into full-living, half-living, and dead asterisms.
As it is stated in the *Jyotiṣa*: "The stars situated in the rays of the Sun— three are dead, seven have half-life,
one is dead, and then eight have full life."
And one [of them] died; seven remained, and from that point on, they lived for half [the duration]. Thus it is said.
It is established in the *Jyotiṣa* that some of these *avayogas* are also considered defects.
Furthermore, it is taught in the *Ajitāgama* that even defects such as the *ṣaḍaśītimukha* and others are to be avoided.
As follows:
"The six *ṣaḍaśītimukha*s, the malefics (*pāpa*), and the very degrees pierced by them,
when situated in the ascendant, cause a threat to the life of the sacrificer."
The characteristics of the *ṣaḍaśītimukha* are stated in the *Niśvāsakārikā*: "Gemini and Virgo, as well as Sagittarius and Pisces—
these are proclaimed as the other *ṣaḍaśītimukhas*."
Bṛhaspati has also said: "If the Sun is in the ninth degree of a movable, fixed, or dual sign,
there occurs the defect known as Ṣaḍaśītimukha, which bestows death."

In the Ajitāgama, it is stated that even specific times characterized by portents and the like are censured. As it is said: "On a day of a portent, or on a cloudy day, or during a thunderclap, or when an ascetic has died, or when the lord of a region has died—the day is declared to be censured."
"In such times as these, one should not perform the installation of the liṅga. Thus [it is said].
In the Bhīmasaṃhitā (p. 50):
[One should avoid] a lunar mansion conjoined with or released by malefic planets, as well as the Kaṅkāla, Kāṅkṣita, Andha, Bha, Kaṇṭha, Sthūṇa, Vyatīpāta, Viṣṭi, Kāṇa, and Saṅkrama.
The Kaṇṭaka, the Brahmadaṇḍa, the fall of a meteor,
the Viddhaka, the eclipse, the piercing asterism, the Śūla, and the trembling of the earth.
"One should especially avoid the *dhvaja* [day] with great effort;
the wise man should also avoid the *pratiṣṭhā* [day] and the setting of Venus. Thus it is said.
And when there is a blazing rain of dust and blood, when clouds thunder,
during the falling of meteors, the burning of the quarters, and during the eclipses of the moon and sun.
"And one should not perform the installation ceremony at the commencement of the sixty-fourth or the sixty-eighth year. Thus it is said.

Thus, having set aside [the methods of] *avayoga* and so forth, the examination must also be performed according to the pure methods of the sixfold and tenfold groups mentioned in the installation of the Śiva-liṅga and other [icons]. And so it is said in the *Liṅgasthāpanapaṭala* of the *Santānasaṃhitā*:
One should always consider the income and expenditure, the lunar mansion (nakṣatra), the birth sign, the day of the week, and the division (aṃśaka);
the installation of that linga should be performed in conjunction with its specific lunar mansion.
"A wise person should perform the installation during an auspicious time and avoid it during an inauspicious one. Thus [it is said].

This definition of the six groups (*ṣaḍvarga*) is correctly stated in the *Kāmika*: "Nāga, mandaguṇa, nāga, nanda, dṛg, bhānu, nāḍī, vasu, bha, muni, and nava; [these constitute] the birth, the other, the asterism, the day, the division (*aṃśaka*), and the sequence of the decrease of qualities. Thus it is said.
The characteristics of the ten-fold group (*daśavarga*) are stated in the *Mānasāra* on architecture (p.

51): "Income, expenditure, the day of the week, the lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*), the sun, the *aṃśaka*, the fortnight (*pakṣa*), the *yoni*, the zodiac sign (*rāśi*), and age—these are considered the ten [factors]."
Vasu, Bhānu, and likewise Pañca, Nanda, and Āḍī constitute the Vyaya;
Guṇa and Nāga shall be the Yoni, and Vasubha is indeed the Nakṣatra.
Nanda multiplied by seven would be the *vāra* (weekday), and by Nanda-veda (49) it would be the *aṃśaka* (degree).
By Nanda-veda (49) again, the *jāti* (birth-class) is obtained, and by nine times thirty (270) it becomes the lunar day (*tithi*).
"One should calculate the zodiacal sign with thirty-six [units], and the asterism with two hundred and twenty. Thus it is said.
In that very context, the eight wombs (yoni) are set forth:
"The banner, the smoke, the lion, the dog, the bull, the monkey, the elephant, and the crow—these eight wombs are to be known everywhere. Thus it is said.

The characteristics of the *aṃśakas* are as follows: "A thief, one with devotion, one with power, a fortunate man, a king, two eunuchs, one fearless, and one without wealth—these are the nine *aṃśakas* to be observed. Thus it is said.
Now, the examination of the five [periods] beginning with "childhood" (bāla) must also be performed. As follows:
one should divide the number five by the days increased by eight;
the remainder indicates the five stages, beginning with childhood and ending with death.
"A child, a youth, and an old man shall die in due order;
they know that in every case, good fortune follows from good, and misfortune from evil. Thus it is said.

And this examination of the sixfold and tenfold groups (ṣaḍvarga and daśavarga) should be performed by taking the width of the temple, gate-towers, and so forth, while taking the height of the *liṅga*.
Thus it has been stated in the *Aśumatkāśyapa*:
Now I shall describe the specific characteristics of the Ayas and other [elements]. One should divide the number of cubits of the width of the palace by eight, and so forth.
Furthermore, the examination of the linga must also be performed according to five rules,
as follows:
the width of the pedestal should be equal to the circumference of the linga, and the distance between the two *gomukha* openings should be half that width.
The height of the pinnacle should be one-third of the width, and its neck-diameter should be equal to half of that width. Thus it is said.

Regarding the phrase "having a neck equal to its expanded width" (*vistṛtārthasamakaṇṭhanāhaka*): the meaning is that its neck has a name [of such length] such that it is both expanded (*vistṛta*) and equal to half [the total height], being of that same measure.
Having thus examined the characteristics such as the *avayoga* and so forth, he now states the auspicious moment for the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*).
The root text:

On a day joined with the asterisms of Puṣya and others, Śaśin (Mṛgaśiras) and Śiva (Ārdrā), Tiṣya (Puṣya), Mitra (Anurādhā), Aśvin (Aśvinī), Viṣṇu (Śravaṇa), Svātī, Hasta, and the three Uttaras, the installation of a Śiva-liṅga should be performed.

Having abandoned the bow and the deer-sign [Capricorn], one should perform the calculation for the ascendant and the aspect of the Drekkāṇa belonging to Mercury, Jupiter, the Moon, or Venus within their own Navāṃśas and Horās. || 11 ||

Vedhas is Rohiṇī; Pauṣṇa is Revatī; Aditi is Punarvasu; Śaśin is Mṛgaśiras; Śiva is Ārdrā; Tiṣya is Puṣya; Mitra is Anurādhā; Aśvin is Aśvinī; Viṣṇu is Śravaṇa; Svātī is well known; Hasta is Sāvitra; [and] Uttarā—
The three [nakṣatras] Uttaraphalgunī, Uttarāṣāḍhā, and Uttaraproṣṭhapadā— among these fourteen nakṣatras,
the installation of the Śiva-liṅga should be performed. Thus it is stated in the Majjitāgama:
The asterisms of Rohiṇī (Prājāpatya), Mṛgaśiras (Aindava), Puṣya, Ārdrā, Svātī, Punarvasu,
Aśvinī, Revatī, Hasta, and likewise the three Uttaras;
"The lunar mansion conjoined with Maitra (Anurādhā) and Vaiṣṇava (Śravaṇa) is remembered as bestowing auspiciousness. Thus it is said.
In the *Brahmīya-śivāgama*:
"The asterisms Rīhiṇī, Revatī, Tiṣya, Maitra, Āditya, and Maghā,
as well as the Uttarās, Aśvayuj, and Saumya— these days are likewise most excellent."
"Vāyu, Hasta, and Harīśa are proclaimed as the middle [categories];
a wise person should avoid the remaining ones, especially during the sequence of installation. Thus it is said.

In the *Svāyaṃbhuva*: "The lunar mansions presided over by Prajāpati, Aśvinī, Saumya (Mṛgaśiras), Tiṣya (Puṣya), Pauṣṇa (Revatī), the three Uttarās, Maitra (Anurādhā), Āditya (Punarvasu), Maghā, Ārdrā, Hasta, and Śravaṇā are auspicious."
In the Dīpta [state], there are Prājāpatya, Saumya, Śaiva, Āditya, Mitraka,
Pauṣṇa, Bṛhaspati, Citrabha, and likewise Vaiṣṇava.
"In the constellations of Nairṛta, Aśvinī, Vāyavya, Paitṛka, and the triad of the north (Uttaraphalgunī, Uttarāṣāḍhā, and Uttarabhādrapadā), one should perform the consecration. Thus it is said.
In the *Brāhmīya* and *Svāyambhuva*, there are fifteen lunar mansions (*nakṣatras*). In the *Dīpta*, there are sixteen lunar mansions. In the *Cintyāgama*, however, it is said:
"The three beginning with Tiṣya, Āditya, Indu, Paṣṇārka, Vidhi, Vāta, and Uttara."
The best [results] are obtained in Āśleṣā, Maghā, Maitra (Anurādhā), Śravaṇa, and also in Mūla. Thus it is said.
In the *Santānasaṃhitā*:
"Punarvasu, Puṣya, Mṛgaśīrṣa, Rohiṇī,
and the three Uttarās are specifically prescribed for consecration."
"Even if there is a piercing by Raudra in Vaiṣṇava, or by Vāyavya in Maitra, one should especially perform the consecration during the Siddha-yoga. Thus it is said.
The constellations to be avoided are stated in the Kāmika:
"One should avoid Yama, Āśleṣā, Agni, Śūrpa, Śraviṣṭhā, Vāruṇa, Jyeṣṭhā, and the three Pūrvās for rites such as installation. Thus it is said.
Regarding the causes [of failure]: one should avoid the asterisms of Āgneya (Kṛttikā), Śūrpāṇi (Śravaṇa), Sārpa (Āśleṣā), Vāruṇa (Śatabhiṣaj), Jyeṣṭhā, the three Pūrvās, and Nairṛta (Mūla).
In the Bhīmasaṃhitā: One should especially avoid the asterisms of Yama (Bharaṇī), Āśleṣā, Agni (Kṛttikā), Śūrpa (Śatabhiṣaj), Śrāviṣṭhā (Śravaṇa), Vāruṇa (Śatabhiṣaj), Jyeṣṭhā, and the three Pūrvas.
The remaining lunar days and yogas are recommended for the rite of consecration. Thus it is said.
In the *Jyotiṣa* treatise known as the *Suprabheda*: "The asterism of Bhujaṅgendra, then Avāruṇa, Vasu, Bhāgya, Indrāgni, Pūrvaproṣṭhapada joined with Vāruṇa, and both Āgneya and Yāmya."
The asterism of Tvāṣṭra (Citrā) is the root; the cluster of stars beginning with Ārdrā are the enemies in the middle;
and Svātī, Śravaṇa, and Hasta are the remaining ones, which are the most excellent for consecration. Thus it is said.
Now, twelve lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) are prohibited; four are middling;
and eleven are excellent. And so it is stated in the *Vidhiratna*:
"The three *uttarās*, Aśvinī, and Anurādhā..."
Maghā, Tiṣya (Puṣya), and Mṛgaśīrṣa; Pūṣan (Punarvasu), Āditya (Pūrvaphalgunī), Brāhma (Rohiṇī), and Ati (Uttaraphalgunī) are highly praised;
while Raudra (Ārdrā), Anila (Svātī), Arka (Hasta), Śravaṇā, and Samā (Viśākhā) are middling.

Now, he states the rule for the ascendant by means of the ascendants to be avoided, beginning with "having abandoned the five signs starting with Sagittarius": having abandoned (tyaktvā) the five signs beginning with Aries (ra-rabha)— namely Aries, Cancer, Libra, Scorpio, and Capricorn— as well as Sagittarius (cāpam api), other signs are to be accepted.
And thus it is said in the Kāmika:
"The signs [of the zodiac], excluding the mobile ones, are declared as before."

"Even among the causal signs (kāraṇa-rāśis), the bow (dhanus) and the four movable signs (cara-rāśis) are known as inauspicious; the remaining ones, however, are considered to bestow auspiciousness. Thus it is said.
And in the *Ajita*:
"One should avoid the stars of the two feet (Aśleṣā and Maghā); Dhanus is considered to be inauspicious.
Thus, regarding the *dīpta* [nakṣatras]:
"One should avoid Aries, Cancer, Libra, and Capricorn;
one should install the liṅga in the remaining signs, while avoiding the sign of Sagittarius. Thus it is said.
In the *Santānasaṃhitā*:
"It should be performed when the sign is stable, and likewise when it is dual."

Now, he states that for the benefic planets, the decans (drekkāṇa), aspects, ascendants, and so forth, as well as the horās and degrees, are to be taken—excluding the rising of the moon—in the verse beginning with "saumya," etc.
Here, *saumya* is Mercury, *guru* is Jupiter, *indu* is the Moon, and *kāvya* is Venus; [one should take] their decans, aspects, ascendants, horās, and degrees, excluding the rising of the moon.
These are to be accepted.
And so it has been stated in the *Kāraṇa*:
"The portions of diamonds and the aspect of the decan (drekkāṇa) are auspicious for virtuous [planets]."
"The rising of auspicious [planets] is praised there, except for the rising of Saturn. Thus it is said.
In the Ajita [system],
the Drekkāṇas, Navāṃśas, and Horās always grant auspicious results when they are aspected [by benefics],
except for the rising of the Moon; these are used in the rite of the installation of a deity.
In the *Bhīmasaṃhitā*:

"The portions of the diamond (*horaka*) among auspicious [planets], the aspect of the decan (*drekkāṇa*), and the degrees of their own ascension (*svodayāṃśaka*) on the days of Mercury, Moon, Venus, and Jupiter [are auspicious]. (p. 57)
On a day when Jupiter, Venus, or Mercury is combust, their weekdays are auspicious in all matters;
likewise, their decans (drekkāṇas), horās, and their aspect upon their own degrees are auspicious.
The rising of these very planets is auspicious, as is the rising of the Moon; however, the Sun, Mars, and Saturn are inauspicious when situated in the third, sixth, or eleventh houses.
All planets should be avoided, especially those situated in the eighth house;
however, having excluded the sixth, seventh, and tenth houses, Venus is auspicious elsewhere. Thus it is said.
O Ajita, malefic planets situated in the eighth house are censured, while benefic planets are likewise condemned;
furthermore, Venus situated in the sixth, seventh, or tenth house is declared to be avoidable.
Excluding the second and fifth [houses], the Moon is auspicious in the remaining ones;
likewise, excluding the seventh, sixth, and ninth, Jupiter is auspicious in the others.
Venus, when situated in the ascendant, likewise brings about an abundance of auspiciousness. Thus it is said.
Henceforth, another statement is cited to demonstrate specific times:
"When the sun has entered Gemini, which is like a pond filled with the crocodiles of mental activity and the fish of [worldly] actions..."
When the crescent moon shines with great brilliance, it reveals the white teacher.
And for the king and the architect, on days favorable to their respective birth-stars (janmarkṣa). Thus it is said.
In the *Kāmika*, in the chapter on the rules of time (*kālavidhānapaṭala*), it is said:
"Wise men should not perform auspicious rites when Jupiter has set;
nor should they undertake consecrations and the like during the setting of Venus."
A specific rule is stated in the *Kāmika*:
"In the forenoon or at midday, when the lagna is endowed with the strength of the planets;
however, in the afternoon, rites such as consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) and attraction (*karṣaṇa*) must never be performed."
A wise person should perform divine rites either by day or by night.
— — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — — one should perform [the rite] even during the day.
The first part of the night is considered inferior; the middle part is known as middling;
indeed, the latter part is to be known as superior for rites such as consecrations.
In the Makuṭa [Tantra] it is said: "One should not perform the consecration and other rites during the day, in the evening, or in the first part of the night;
rather, they should be performed at night, even if the strength of the planetary conjunctions has declined during the day."
Having reflected thus with diligence, [the image] should be installed by the wise. Thus it is said.
O Ajita, a specific time has been prescribed; however,

in the case of a spacious celestial mansion (*vimāna*), the installation may take place according to one's own preference, either prior to the rite of closing the door or even prior to the rite of laying the crown-brick (*mūrdheṣṭakā*).
"The Bāṇaliṅga produced from that [substance], as well as any other [liṅgas] made of gems and so forth—all these should be installed by the wise once the Dhāman has been completed. Thus it is said.
(p. 59) Now, he states the installation of mobile lingas—the root text:
In the asterisms of Savitṛ, Āditya, Candra, Uttara, Pavana, Surācārya, Vaidhātṛ, and Pauṣṇa...

In the eighth pure station among the fixed signs of the zodiac—those houses which are most stable by their dual nature—the preceptors of pure intellect should install a liṅga made of precious gems such as pearls, rubies, and sapphires, or fashioned from minerals, as well as the forms representing the stages of creation, maintenance, and dissolution. Thus [it is said]. (12)

Sāvitra is Hasta; Āditya is Punarvasu; Candra is Mṛgaśirā; the three Uttarās are Uttaraphalgunī, Uttarāṣāḍhā, and Uttaraproṣṭhapadā; Pavana is Svātī; Surācārya is Puṣya; Vaidhātṛ is Rohiṇī; and Pauṣṇa is Revatī—in these ten lunar mansions (nakṣatras).

Having observed that the houses are very stable in their nature— that is, when both [the lord of the sign and the lord of the navāṃśa] are fixed signs— and when the eighth house is pure and devoid of planets, they should perform the installation of a mobile liṅga. Thus it is said in the Vīra-tantra, in the chapter on the installation of mobile liṅgas:
Rohiṇī, Punarvasu, Puṣya, Mṛgaśiras,
as well as Hasta, Revatī, Svātī, and the three Uttarās;
"It should be performed during fixed signs, or likewise during dual signs. Thus it is said.

Now, he describes the movable lingas themselves: those fashioned from pearls, rubies, sapphires, and other gems—meaning constructed from specific jewels such as pearls and the like; the *bāṇaliṅga*, which arises from minerals such as lead (*bāṇa*);
and those fashioned from metals such as gold (*hiraṇya*). As it is said in the *Vīratantra*:
Crystal, emerald, ruby, and padmarāga;
likewise pearl, sapphire, lapis lazuli, and coral.
"One should likewise have [images] made of sapphire, topaz, and diamond. Thus it is said.
Regarding the characteristics of the *bāṇaliṅga* and others, it is stated in the *Vātula*:
"Having abandoned the bow [on the day] when the sun has entered Capricorn,
one should install the *bāṇa* in the middle [of the confluence] at the union of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā."
In that regard, the Bāṇaliṅga is said to be one from which the stone has been extracted;
it may be made of gold, silver, copper, bell-metal, or brass.
It may be made of iron, lead, tin, or derived from other minerals. Thus it is said.
Their respective fruits are also stated in that very same place: "One should know that [the rosary] made of *bāṇa* wood bestows liberation; one should especially worship it.
One should know that the *māṇikya* (ruby) bestows prosperity, and coral (*pravāla*) is the cause of victory."
For attraction, lapis lazuli is used; crystal grants the attainment of a son. Emerald is for inciting enmity; topaz is for immobilization.
Copper is for the sake of the prosperity of sons; bell-metal is a cause for inciting enmity.
Brass, copper, and iron are causes of depletion.
Lead causes disease, while tin increases longevity. Thus it is said.

Regarding even the forms of creation, maintenance, and destruction—the nature of the forms of creation, maintenance, and withdrawal is described in the *Vīra-tantra*, in the chapter on the installation of the form of creation (p.
61): "Accompanied by Umā and Skanda, and likewise seated comfortably."
Kalyāṇasundara and Candraśekhara as well.
Gaṅgādhara—these five are said here to be the forms of creation;
likewise the form of the Bull-vehicled One and Ardhanārīśvara.
Kirāta, Vīreśa, and likewise Bhikṣāṭana—
these five forms are declared to be the forms of persistence (sthitimūrti).
Nṛtteśa, Kāmari, and likewise Kāladāha;
Gajaghna, Tripuraghna, and likewise Jalandharahara.
"The installation of the six forms of withdrawal is now described here. Thus [it is said].

These very same lunar mansions and ascendants are also mentioned in various places within this very tantra in the chapters on installation (*pratiṣṭhā*). Regarding the dimensions for the linga for one's own benefit and for the benefit of others, it is stated in the *Vātula*: "For one's own benefit, she should worship [the linga] starting from two finger-breadths and ending at five."
"But above that, by one finger-breadth of the elements, it is proclaimed as being for the sake of others. Thus [it is said].
Now, he states the time for the installation of Vighneśa— the root verse says:
under the asterisms of Rohiṇī, Āditya (Pūrvaphalgunī), Hasta, and Uttarā.
One should perform the installation of Vighneśa under the asterisms of Puṣya, Svātī, or Revatī, within his eighth pure abode, avoiding those signs known as "movable" (cararāśi).
(62) Regarding "prājāpatya": Prājāpatya is Rohiṇī; Āditya is Punarvasu; Hasta is well known;
the "Uttaras" are the three—Uttara-phalgunī, Uttara-āṣāḍhā, and Uttara-proṣṭhapadā; Puṣya, Svātī, and Revatī are well known. Among these nine constellations, in the eighth abode...
When the eighth lunar mansion (Aṣṭamārāśi) is pure and devoid of all planets, one should perform the installation of Vighneśa in fixed or dual signs, excluding those known as movable signs.
Thus it is stated in the Vīratantra, in the chapter on the installation of Vighneśa:
Rohiṇī, Āditya (Pūrvaphalgunī), Puṣya, Hasta, Pauṣṇa (Revatī), the three Uttaras,
and Svātī are declared for installation, as is the asterism Pratiṣṭhā (Uttarāṣāḍhā).
"It should be performed during fixed signs or even during dual signs;
however, all planets situated in the eighth house are indeed undesirable for installations. Thus it is said.
Now, he states the time for the installation of the Subrahmaṇyā:
Root Text: Jyeṣṭhā, the three [asterisms] preceded by it (Mūla), Yama (Bharaṇī), Nairṛta (Kṛttikā), Sārpa (Āśleṣā), and Raudra (Ārdrā).

Having avoided the asterisms of Maitra (Anurādhā), Āgneya (Kṛttikā), Vāruṇa (Śatabhiṣaj), Vasubha (Dhaniṣṭhā), and Āgnibha (Pūrvābhādrapadā), as well as the signs of Sagittarius, Capricorn, and Aries, and the defects beginning with "mandha," one should perform the installation of Guha during the auspicious portions of the lunar mansions.
Regarding "Jyeṣṭhā" and so forth: therein, he states the lunar mansions, zodiac signs, and other factors by way of those to be avoided. Jyeṣṭhā belongs to Indra;
the three "Pūrvas"—Pūrvaphalgunī, Pūrvāṣāḍhā, and Pūrvaproṣṭhapadā—are the three [Pūrvas]; Yama is Bharaṇī; Nairṛta is Mūla; Sārpa is Āśleṣā; Raudra is Ārdrā; Aindrāgni is...

Excluding the twelve lunar mansions— Viśākhā, Vāruṇa (Śatabhiṣaj), Vasubha (Śraviṣṭhā), and Agnibha (Kṛttikā)— as well as Dhanus and Carabha; and having avoided the "blind-faced" defects and other faults pertaining to the blind lunar mansions,
the solstices, months, lunar days, and so forth, [one should observe] the auspicious portions.
Regarding the "mouths of the benefic planets"—that is, at the beginnings of the divisions (aṃśaka) and so forth of Jupiter, Venus, Mercury, and the Moon;

by the word "and so forth" (ādi), one should include the decans (drekkāṇa), the half-signs (horā), aspects, and days of the week, one should perform the installation of Guha. Thus it is said in the Kumāra-tantra:
One should not perform [this] during the period of the sun’s northern course (uttarāyaṇa), nor during its southern course (dakṣiṇāyana);
even within the bright fortnight (śuklapakṣa), one should avoid the empty lunar days (riktā), as well as the first and eighth lunar days (tithi).

The fifteenth lunar day (Pañcadaśī) is to be known as inauspicious; Jupiter, Mercury, and Venus are auspicious; while the Sun, Saturn, and Mars are inauspicious. However, when in conjunction with an auspicious yoga, they bestow auspicious results.

Jyeṣṭhā, the three [asterisms] preceded by it (Pūrvaphalgunī, Pūrvāṣāḍhā, and Pūrvabhādrapadā), Nairṛtya (Śatabhiṣaj), Yamāśleṣāgni (Maghā, Āśleṣā, and Kṛttikā), Vāruṇa (Śatabhiṣaj), Śraviṣṭhā, Ārdrā, and Viśākhā are not desired for the rite of installation.
The four movable signs and Sagittarius are not desired among the signs;
however, the aspecting of the horās, navāṃśas, and decans of benefic planets is auspicious.
One afflicted by malefic planets, one who has been released, one who is longing, Andhaka, Kaṇṭha, Sthūṇa, Vyatīpāta, Viṣṭi, Kāṇa, and Saṅkrama.
The *kaṇṭaka*, the *brahmadaṇḍa*, the *viddha*, the *utpātaka*,
the *grahaṇa*, the *vedhanakṣatra*, the *śūlarkṣa*, and the *bhūmikampa*.
"One should especially avoid the Dhvaja [day] with great effort;
one should always avoid the installation [of an image] during the heliacal settings of Jupiter and Venus. Thus it is said.
The specific details regarding the installation and consecration of the Subrahmaṇya [liṅga] are also set forth in that very same place:
"On a peak or on a mountain, or even near a mountain;
on a riverbank, in a grove, in a sacred field, or at a crossroads."
In a village or indeed in a city, in a town or even a hamlet,
in the capital, in the middle of a street, at the head of a street, and in all directions;
Facing either the east, the west, the south, or the north.
"One should establish the one born of the arrow (Kārttikeya) together with his retinue of immortals. Thus it is said.
Having thus stated the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) for an immovable image (*acalabera*), a specific rule regarding the monthly ritual for the consecration of a movable image (*calabera*) is stated:
"O Kauśika, listen, I shall describe the consecration of a movable image,
which bestows enjoyment and liberation upon men and accomplishes all desires and goals."
What other auspicious thing bestows growth upon children, destroys all enemies,
and grants every desire, except for the installation of Kumāra?
During the six months beginning with Mṛga (Capricorn), it is auspicious when the moon is in the *vikumbha* asterisms;
it is excellent during the northern solstice, but during the southern solstice, it is characterized by haste.
One should carefully avoid the two months of Mārgaśīrṣa and Māgha;
however, when Aquarius (Kumbha) is aspected by or conjoined with Jupiter, the installation of a mobile [image] is excellent.
One should properly perform the installation during an auspicious lunar fortnight and under a favorable constellation. Thus it is said.
Now, he states the time for the installation of Gaurī— the root verse says: "The Hasta, Moon, and Vedha [nakṣatras], Aditi, and the Māruta asterisms..."

The wise declare that the installation of Gaurī should be performed under the asterisms of Tvaṣṭṛ (Citrā), Amara (Śravaṇa), Āryā (Punarvasu), Uttarā (Uttaraphalgunī, Uttarāṣāḍhā, or Uttarabhādrapadā), and Pauṣṇa (Revatī), as well as in a pure eighth lunar day and during the application of a fixed (sthira) yoga. || 15 ||
Regarding "hasta" and so forth: Hasta is Sāvitra; Indu is Mṛgaśiras; Vedha is Rohiṇī; Aditi is Punarvasu; the Marut constellation is Svātī; Tvāṣṭra is Citrā; Amarārya is Puṣya;
the "Uttaras" are the three—Uttara-phalgunī, Uttara-āṣāḍhā, and Uttara-proṣṭhapadā; and the "hot-rayed sign" (Ṣoṣṇabha) is Revatī—in these [constellations].

The virtuous— those who know the scriptures— declare that the installation of Gaurī should take place under eleven asterisms, when the eighth house is pure (i.e., when there is purity in the eighth), and in conjunction with fixed signs (i.e., when fixed signs serve as the ascendant).
And so it has been said in the Vīratantra, in the chapter on the consecration of Gaurī:
"Rohiṇī, Punarvasu, Puṣya, Mṛgaśiras, as well as Hasta, Revatī, Svātī, Citrā, and the three Uttarās."
"And it should be performed during a fixed asterism, in the eighth [house], free from [malefic] planets. Thus [it is said].

(p. 66) Now, as an incidental matter, the times for the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) of other deities mentioned in various works on astrology (*jyotiḥśāstra*) are summarized and presented here. Regarding the consecration of Viṣṇu, it is stated in the *Śrīśāstra* proclaimed by Bhṛgu:
Śravaṇa, Śatabhiṣaj (Vāruṇa), Hasta, Revatī, Punarvasu, the three Uttarās, and Rohiṇī are especially to be accepted [for auspicious purposes].
Likewise, the three Pūrvās, Ārdrā, Maghā, Mūla, and Kṛttikā [are to be avoided].
One should avoid Jyeṣṭhā and Āśleṣā; Saturn and Mars should also be avoided. Thus it is said.
Śrīpati states: "The installation of Viṣṇu is prescribed under Rohiṇī, the three Uttarās, Revatī, Hasta, Āśleṣā, Aśvinī, Dhaniṣṭhā, Anurādhā, Mṛgaśīrṣa, and Puṣya."
The Ratnakośa also states:
"One should install Viṣṇu under Rohiṇī, the three Uttaras, or the Vimala [nakṣatra]; and one should duly install Brahmā and Maheśvara under the Puṣya and other asterisms belonging to Viṣṇu."
One should also establish the Sun in Hasta; Maitreya, the son of Umā, in Mūla; and the host of Mothers, all the Sisters, and the auspicious goddess Āryā.
One should likewise establish the hosts of Rākṣasas and Bhūtas, as well as all the serpents; one should always install Maitra, Dhanapati, Śrī, and Śrīpati.
One should install Sarasvatī, who possesses many virtues, in Rohiṇī; and Raudrī, the Gaṇas, and Nandin.
Or one should perform the installation of Viṣṇu according to the rules, with the [deities] stationed as prescribed.

p. 67) One should duly place the painted images of the ancestors during the sacrifices, the planets under the Puṣya asterism, Jvaraka in the southeast, and likewise Hūyavaha for Jña at the rising of the moon. Thus it is said.
Nṛsiṃha, however, has stated the procedure for installation according to the sequence of lunar mansions (nakṣatras),
as follows: [it applies] to Viṣṇu, Vighneśa, Rudra, Arka, the Mothers, and likewise to Brahmā.
And the installation of the two Aśvins and of Durgā should always take place on a Vājibha day.
The wise have declared that Bharaṇī is impelled for the installation of Yama;
the installation of Kuja, Agni, Durgā, and Skanda is auspicious in the fire [constellation].
Of Kama, the Mothers, the Bhutas, and Vishnu; of the Yakshas and the Rakshasas as well;
and likewise of the Gandharvas, the Pisachas, and the Kinnaras.
The consecration of the Sugata is also considered most auspicious under Rohiṇī;
as are those of the Bhūtas, Indu, Mātṛs, Vighnas, Ārka, Yakṣas, Gandharvas, and Rakṣasas.
For the installation of Brahmā, Rudra, Piśācas, Kinnaras,
as well as Viṣṇu and Durgā, the lunar day (tithi) shall be auspicious.
The wise remember that an installation performed with the Āryā meter for the deities Vighna, Rudra, Agni, Durgā, Arka, and the Mātṛs, as well as for Rudra, is exceedingly auspicious.
The auspicious establishment of the Bhūtas, Śaṅkaras, Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Kinnaras,
Rākṣasas, Kinnaras, and Pitṛs is in the Svāti asterism.
In the *nakṣatra* of Pūrvaphalgunī, there is the *bhaga* (fortune) of the Piśācas;
it is auspicious for the installation of the Mothers, Vighnas, Aryaman, the Sun, Brahmā, Śrī, and the Raudra deities, as well as in the *Sāvitra* constellation.
In the asterism of Citrā, the worship of Jyeṣṭhā, Vighneśa, Rudra, Arka, the Mothers, Viśvakarman, Durgā,
and the Grāmas and Raudras is auspicious.
Of the Bhūtas, Mātṛs, Maruts, Vāyus, Yakṣas, Kinnaras, and Rākṣasas;
likewise of Rudra, the world-protectors, and the Gandharvas.
The installation of Piśācas is auspicious when performed under the constellation Vāyu (Svāti);
that of Agni, Indra, the Mātṛs, and Skanda under Jyeṣṭhā; and that of Gandharvas and Rakṣasas under [the same].
The Aindrāgna [oblation] is considered auspicious for Kinnaras and Piśācas;
likewise, it is for Rudras, Mātṛs, Piśācas, Yakṣas, and Kinnaras.
The wise declare that the *Pratiṣṭhā* constellation bestows auspiciousness upon friends when situated in a friend's sign;
it is the mother of the Vighnas, Indras, and Bhūtas, and the elder sister of the Gandharvas and Rākṣasas.
It was auspicious for the Piśācas, Kinnaras, and Yakṣas,
as well as for the Bhūtas, Gandharvas, Mātṛs, Nāgas, Kinnaras, and Rākṣasas, O Indra-like one.
Pūrvāṣāḍhā is auspicious for the Siddhas, Nairṛtas, Yakṣas, Piśācas, water, and those belonging to the Piśāca class, when it is the Mūla nakṣatra.
The Uttarāṣāḍhā nakṣatra is auspicious for the propitiation of Rudra, the group of Mothers, Īśāna, Durgā, Brahmā, Ravi (the Sun), Śrī, Buddha, Viśva, and Viṣṇu.
[Salutation] to the glories of the three forms, of the Sugatas, of the suns, of the Mothers, Gandharvas, and Rakshasas;
of the Bhutas, Kinnaras, and Vighnas; and likewise of the Rudras.
Durgā is auspicious for Piśācas, Yakṣas, and fierce beings; she is auspicious for lions.
She is auspicious for Durgā, the Mothers, Gaṇeśa, the Sun, Rudra, Brahmā, and Śrī.
Likewise, the constellation Dhaniṣṭhā is especially preeminent for Viṣṇu and Vāsudeva;
it belongs to Rudra, the Sun, the Mothers, Viṣṇu, the Bhūtas, Gandharvas, and Rākṣasas.
The auspicious Vāruṇa [mantra] is for Piśācas, Yakṣas, and Vighnas; that of Brahmā is for the Raudras and all the gods, while that of Durgā is especially so.
For the Ajaikapād [deity] and the Piśācas, the Pūrvaproṣṭhapadā [nakṣatra] is auspicious.
Of Durga, the group of Mothers, Ganesha, the Sun, Rudra, Brahma, and Shri.
On the auspicious Ahibudhnya constellation, there is always [the worship] of Ahibudhnya and Viṣṇu,
as well as of Viṣṇu, Vighneśa, the Mothers, Durgā, and Brahmā.
And for the Rudras, for Sarasvatī, for the asterism of Pūṣan, and for its lord, it is auspicious. Thus [it is said].
Now, regarding the general matter of the lunar days for installation, Vasiṣṭha has stated:
"Odd-numbered lunar days are auspicious, and even-numbered ones are highly praised, with the exception of the ninth;
among the even ones, the tenth, the sixth, and the second are especially honored."
Bṛhaspati has stated the distinction according to the sequence of the fortnights: "The bright fortnight (pūrvapakṣa) is declared auspicious, while the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇapakṣa) is censured;
however, within the dark fortnight, [the period] up to the fifth or even the tenth day is honored."
Among those [lines] divided into three parts, both the first parts are auspicious for Brāhmaṇas; furthermore, the second and the third parts are also auspicious.
"For Kṣatriyas, the fifth is auspicious; for Vaiśyas, the seventh is said to bestow prosperity; for Vaiśyas, the tenth is proclaimed [auspicious]; and for Śūdras, the thirteenth. Thus it is said.
And Vasiṣṭha says: "The first, the eleventh, the twelfth,
and likewise the sixth lunar days are recommended for Brahmins and the other castes respectively, in case of an emergency."
"The second, third, fifth, seventh, and likewise the thirteenth [lunar days] bestow auspiciousness upon all during a beautiful lunar mansion. Thus it is said.
But Nṛsiṃha says:
"The fourteenth and the fourth [lunar days] bestow auspiciousness upon Vighneśa;
the ninth is excellent for Durgā, and the full moon is excellent for Viṣṇu."
Bṛhaspati says:
One should avoid the Karaṇas beginning with Śakuna as well as Viṣṭi;
for the twice-born, [the first] two starting from Vava are auspicious, and for Kṣatriyas, the next two.
For Vaiśyas, agriculture is declared [the best livelihood], while for Śūdras, trade is prescribed.
In an auspicious conjunction, it is said to bring good fortune; however, in an inauspicious one, it leads to ruin. Thus it is said.

Now, having thus described the section on consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*), [the author] states the time for the obligatory rites (*nityakarman*), because the daily, occasional, and optional rites performed after consecration are preceded by the obligatory rites.
(p. 71) Root Text:
During the five *ghaṭikās* known as the *brāhma-muhūrta* immediately following dawn,
having abandoned sleep with a pure heart and meditated upon the lotus feet of the Deity,
and having performed purification, the cleansing of teeth and mouth, the ritual bath, and the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyā*).
Then, one should cause the sound of the Atharva-veda, which brings security to the world, to be made with five musical instruments.

Regarding the phrase "from the time of dawn" (*prātaḥkālāt*): from the time of dawn—that is, in comparison with the time of dawn—during the five *ghaṭikās* designated as the *brāhma-muhūrta*, which is so named; and thus, the definition of the *brāhma-muhūrta* has been stated according to the characteristics of subtle time.
Likewise,
starting from sunrise, the period of two nāḍīs until twelve o'clock is to be known as the forenoon; now hear about the midday from that point onward.
Starting from the end of the morning time until that same number of nāḍīs [afternoon], it should be known as midday; now listen to [the description of] the afternoon.
Beginning from the end of midday for ten nāḍikās, it is called the evening time (sāyaṅkāla);
now the pre-dawn period (pradoṣa) will also be described.
Starting from sunset, seven and a half nāḍikās are known as *pradoṣa*; and three nāḍikās, by a third part [of that], are [known as] *triyāma*.
"Half-watch" (ardhayāma) is said to consist of two nāḍīs;
"midnight" (madhyarātra) is said to consist of three nāḍīs by means of a third part.
That which is called the end of night lasts until the *nāḍikā* of *ābhūta*; that which is called the morning time has been declared—having understood this, one should perform the ritual action.
"Brahma-like, even at that time, as well as the requisites for worship," and so forth.
And so it has been stated by the eminent teacher Aghoraśivācārya in the *Kriyākramadyotikā*:
"Then, having risen before the morning time, within the interval of five nāḍīs..."

Having abandoned sleep—having cast off the lethargy of slumber—and having become one of pure heart (vimalahṛdaya), that is, one whose internal organ is stainless; with the lotus-feet of the meditated Deity reflected in his most purified inner self—that is, having contemplated the lotus-feet of the venerable Supreme Lord (Śrīparameśvara)—the Teacher (deśika) [should act]. (The word "Teacher" is to be supplied as the subject.)
In the *Suprabheda*, a specific distinction is stated: "Three *ghaṭikās* [constitute] three quarters [of the night] at the end of the night day by day;
this is declared to be the *brāhma* *muhūrta*, and it is called 'the resonance' (*saṅghoṣa*)."
"In the *brāhma* hour, the wise man should indeed contemplate Śiva with his mind. Thus it is said.
Purity (*śauca*) consists of cleansing the teeth and mouth, including brushing the teeth and gargling;
bathing refers to two or three of the eight types of baths beginning with the *vāruṇa* bath as available; and *sandhyā* refers to the two forms of *sandhyā*, namely the Vedic and the Śaiva.
Having performed [the rite] according to the method taught in the *Kāmika* and other Āgamas, it is stated here in the *Jñānaratnāvalī*:

"The morning twilight is remembered as being of three kinds: the best is when the constellations are visible; the middling is when the stars have disappeared; and the lowest is when accompanied by the sun."
(p. 73) Now, one should cause the sound of the five musical instruments to be made for that which brings peace to the world and confers auspiciousness upon the universe.
As it is stated in the *Kāmika*:
"Prior to sunrise, within the duration of half a watch (prahara),..."
One should produce the five great sounds, which cause the death of all living beings.
In the Vātulāgama:
"If three nāḍīs of three quarters [of a muhūrta] elapse before sunrise,
one should perform the five great sounds (pañcamahāśabda) at that time for the removal of inauspiciousness."
The wooden staff, the leather shield, the bronze gong, the *nyak* drum, and likewise the hollow-sounding instrument— these five great sounds one should offer to Śiva.
Sound, which is a modification of the great elements, is traditionally held to be fivefold.
That which is produced from wood is born of earth, and that which comes from a conch is said to be born of water.
That which is born of fire is made of iron; that born of wind is bamboo;
that born of space is to be sung; therefore, it is a transformation of the elements.
"Sound produced from wood, from a conch, from metal, and that which is hollow, as well as vocal song combined with all these—the sound is traditionally held to be fivefold. Thus it is said.
Having thus performed the rites of the twilight prayers and so forth, the Guru should commence the worship.
Then, he first states the time for worship: Root Text:
This [time] known as day and night, which is established even by the sequence of inhalation and exhalation, is the occasion for this [practice].

There are these eight junctions (saṃdhyās) declared in the Śiva doctrine; in all of them, worship of Śambhu is proclaimed as being of nine kinds—namely, the well-known, the excellent, the superior, the lower, and the worm-like—or even fivefold:
the daily, the occasional, that performed at the proper time, that performed according to one's own will, and the desireless worship.

"By the sequence of exhalation and so forth" means: by the sequence of exhalation, inhalation (*prāṇa*), and so on, time is "endowed with conditions," that is, time joined with limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). Since, in reality, time is one and therefore undivided, it is [only] through its association with the distinctions of limiting adjuncts such as exhalation and inhalation that it [appears divided].
This time-period is designated as day and night in sequence.
Thus it is stated in the Kāmika: "Sixty breaths constitute one *prāṇa*; six *prāṇas* constitute one *ghaṭikā*."
Sixty ghaṭikās constitute a day and night (ahorātra), and that is said to have eight junctions (sandhyā). Thus it is said.
The junctions of that time designated as day and night are eight in number—eight being the count of what are also termed *yāmas*. This is also stated in the *Kāmika*:
"Beginning from the rising of the sun until the [next] rising of the sun."
"A watch (yāma) measuring three and a half ghaṭikās is called a junction (sandhi). Thus [it is said].

Among all those, worship is the best, the most excellent—the meaning being the highest of the high. Furthermore, that worship is "traversed from below," meaning it is endowed with a downward progression. And it is ninefold; by being performed according to the sequence of junctions—eight, seven, six, five, four, three, two, one, and a half—it becomes ninefold.
And so it is said in the *Kāmika*:
"The worship performed during the eight junctions (*sandhyā*) is the most excellent of the excellent;
[the worship] at the seven, six, five, four, three, two, and one watch (*prahara*) of the day is likewise [superior]."
Thus, worship performed at the time of half a watch (yāmārdha) shall be of nine kinds.
For in the *Ajita*, the eightfold nature of worship has indeed been set forth as follows:
"By means of the three superior [types], then by the three middling,
and also by the two inferior, this worship is remembered as being eightfold."
If worship is performed during each of the four watches of the day, and especially during each of the four watches of the night,
according to the prescribed rule, that worship shall be the most excellent of the excellent.
And they should especially perform worship at the crossroads during the day.
That [observance] performed during the three watches of the night is considered superior or middling;
however, it is most excellent when performed during four daytime watches, as well as during the two twilights and the night.
That worship performed at the six junctions of the day becomes superior or inferior [according to the time]:
at dawn, midday, evening, and during the second watch of the night.
If worship is performed during the fourth watch, it shall be middling-superior;
if it lacks worship for half a watch, it shall be middling-middling.
That worship performed at dawn, midday, and evening is middling-inferior;
while that worship performed at dawn and evening is inferior-superior.
But when worship is performed in a single manner, it shall be considered inferior or mediocre; an inferior-inferior form of worship is never seen in the case of the *liṅgas*.
Therefore, it is determined in that very context that this [compassion] is of eight types;
here it is described as being threefold: pure, mixed, and blended.
Among those worships, the pure (śuddhā) ends with the offering of oblations (haviḥpradāna), the mixed (miśrā) ends with the daily festival (nityotsava),
and the impure (saṅkīrṇā) always ends with pure dance (śuddhanṛtta).
The worship that is performed by people in the morning, at midday, and in the evening—
one should perform that as mixed, or especially as combined.

O Janārdana, even when all the [astrological] conjunctions are present along with their transitional periods (upasaṃdhyā), the attainment of the mixed (miśra) and confused (saṅkīrṇa) states is never accepted here.
The firm conclusion of the scripture is that among these, only the pure worship is valid;
whatever is performed beginning from sunrise until the time of sunset.
That is declared to be the morning twilight (pūrvasandhyā), and it becomes the great twilight (mahāsandhyā); and whatever worship is offered during the half-yāma following that, [it is likewise so].

It should be known as "with the twilight" when performed at midday from the [first] watch; that midday twilight is also known by the name "Great Twilight. And the worship which is offered after that for half a watch [is likewise included].
That [period] should also be known as the *upasandhyā* during each of the four watches of the day;
thus, two *mahāsandhyās* and two *upasandhyās* are proclaimed.
But when worship is performed in a single manner, it is considered inferior or mediocre for him; a worship more inferior than the inferior is never seen among the *liṅgas*.
Therefore, it is determined in that very context that this [devotion] is of eight kinds;
here it is described as being of three types: pure, mixed, and contaminated.
Among those worships, the pure [pūjā] ends with the offering of oblations (havir-pradāna), the mixed [pūjā] ends with the daily festival (nityotsava),
and the impure [pūjā] always ends with pure dance (śuddha-nṛtta).
The worship that is performed by people in the morning, at midday, and in the evening—
one should perform that as mixed, or especially as combined.
O Janārdana, even when all attainments are present along with their transitional phases at all times, the occurrence of mixed or confused states is not accepted here.
Among these, worship performed while pure is indeed valid; such is the certainty of the scripture.
Whatever [worship] is performed starting from sunrise until the end of the night, that is accepted.
That is declared to be the morning twilight (pūrvasandhyā), and it shall be the great twilight (mahāsandhyā);
and the worship that is offered during the half-yāma following that [is also included].

It should be known as "with the twilight" when performed at midday during the watch; that midday twilight is also known by the name "Great Twilight. Furthermore, the worship that is offered in the half-watch following that [is also included].
That [period] should also be known as the *upasandhyā* during each of the four watches of the day;
furthermore, the two *mahāsandhyās* and the two *usandhyās* have been declared.
The worship offered at night, beginning from sunset until the end of the first watch, is also the great junction (mahāsandhyā); after that, it becomes the half-watch.
Then, after half a watch has passed, one should determine the third;
thereafter, by means of five nāḍīs, one should determine the fourth.
Indeed, five *nāḍikās* are said to precede sunrise;
during the great twilight of the night, one [period] occurs thereafter, O Hari.
There are also three minor twilights (*upasandhyā*); such is the sequence of worship.
"When wealth exists, this sequence for worship has been declared.
Thus, among these eight kinds of sacrifices, one should resort to one. So it is said.
The detailed division of the seven and a half *ghaṭikās* of the great *saṃdhyās* has been demonstrated in the *Kāraṇa*:
"Two *ghaṭikās* should be for bathing; one *ghaṭikā* should be for worship."
The offering of food (naivedya) lasts for half a ghaṭikā, while the offering of the sacrificial oblation (balidāna) is equal to that.
"The daily fire-ritual lasts for half [a period], and the daily festival for two nāḍīs;
however, in the case of the Tāṇḍava dance, it shall last for one nāḍī; these should be performed at the transitions. Thus it is said.
In the subtle middle worship, fivefold nature is established. As it is said:
"Time is declared to be twofold, divided into two as gross and subtle;
the gross is known by worldly designations, while the subtle is considered internal (ādhyātmika)."
(p. 78) Worship of Śiva and other rites should always be performed during gross time;
for yogins, however, a portion of the Veda is said to be a *truṭi* within *nimeṣas*.
That [lava] multiplied by its own number [sixty] is a *tad-vaya*; that [multiplied] again is a *nimiṣa*.
A *nimiṣa* multiplied by the number of lunar days (fifteen) is proclaimed as a *kāṣṭhā*.
The *kāṣṭhā* is proclaimed as the number of lunar days (*tithi*), and the *kalā* is likewise;
a *muhūrta* is a portion of that *kalā*, and it is equal to two *ghaṭikās*.

Half of the number of breaths of a sage (7,200) is called a *yāma* by the wise; eight such *yāmas*, including their junctions (*sandhyā*), constitute a day and night, during which worship is performed at every *yāma*.
Sacrifice performed at all eight junctions of time (saṃdhyās) is proclaimed as the most excellent;
sacrifice performed at four junctions of time is proclaimed as middling.
One should perform worship at the three junctions of the day; this is proclaimed as the lowest [grade].
In worship, there may be eight junctions, four great junctions (*mahāsandhi*), and four intermediate junctions (*upasandhyā*). Perform the festival at the three junctions.
One should perform worship at the four junctions of the day, and also at one intermediate junction.
One should perform constant festivals during the twilight hours, especially at the three junctions of the day;
or, joined with a single twilight, one may offer the bali-oblation at two twilights.
Alternatively, one may perform the sequence of offerings during a single junction (sandhyā);
however, one should especially avoid giving offerings at the intermediate junctions.
And at the junction of that [time], one should especially perform the rites beginning with the bath and ending with the food offering (*naivedya*),
or else perform those ending with the offering of lamps, up until the secondary junction (*upasandhyaka*).
Thus it is declared: one should always perform the occasional festival in this manner.

O Ajita, an expiation has been prescribed for the deficiency in the sequence of worship that occurs at a previous time. As it is said: "In whatever manner worship was previously performed according to the rule upon a particular linga, when a deficiency arises in that regard, an expiation is ordained."
And in the *Kāmika*:
"Even if [the initiation] was previously established by scripture, an increase [in the number of mantras] thereafter bestows happiness;
therefore, with every effort, one should perform [the initiation] in greater measure than before. Thus it is said.
The *nimittikā* [worship] is that which is performed when a specific occasion arises, such as the worship of the month of *Grahaṇa* and so forth.

The *kāmyā* [worship] is that which is performed with the aim of desiring a son or other benefits, such as the *viśeṣa-yajña* and so forth. For this *kāmyā* worship, there is no fixed rule regarding the time.
And so it is said in the Sūkṣma-tantra:
"One should perform the occasional (naimittika) rite conjoined with the daily twilight worship (nitya-sandhyā);
one should perform the optional (kāmya) rite conjoined with the daily worship (nitya-pūjā), or even unjoined [with it]."
Now, it may be argued that when obligatory (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), and optional (*kāmya*) rites coincide,
they must be performed by a single preceptor located within a single temple;
for according to the *Kāmika* scripture, rites in a single temple must be performed by one and the same preceptor alone.
For example:
"The kingdom and its people perish precisely through the corruption of the teacher. Thus it is said.

If it is asked: "Since it is established in that very same [text] that having multiple teachers brings about faults, and since it is difficult for a single teacher to perform multiple rites at one time, how is this resolved?"—it is true; exactly so has the Lord settled the matter in the *Kāmika* following a question from the sages.
As the sages said:
Fetching water and so forth, the preparation of perfumes, flowers, incense, and the like;
the lighting of lamps, the offering of food, the performance of circumambulation, and the daily worship of the deity.
Whatever constitutes complete worship— including the adoration of the retinue and so forth,
the daily festival, singing and other such acts, the ritual bathing, and the arrangement of the ancillary rites— [is all included therein].
Or else, the arrangement of the components for the festival and so forth, the mounting of the deity’s vehicle and such,
the worship of the primary *mūla-liṅga* and other icons at that time, and the daily fire-oblation (*nityahoma*).
"Aha! How can one person accomplish that which cannot be achieved by many men?
The Lord said: "Those sages are truly wise; I shall explain *samādhi* to you."
Whatever karma resides in the constant, occasional, and optional rites, as well as in the Ekādaśī vow;
It has been well said by me that [the rite] must be performed by a single preceptor;
or else, the son, the grandson, or the kinsmen of this preceptor [may perform it].
Those men who have been initiated by him, who are permeated by his command,
and who are born into the lineage of the primordial Śaivas— whether they be Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, or Vaiśyas— [are likewise empowered].
Even Śūdras, those born in the direct order (ānuloma), Gandharvas, dancers, and the like,
as well as the daughters of Rudra, are my servants if they obey my command.
The ritual performed by them as well would be considered performed by the preceptor,
just as [an act] performed by vassal chiefs and others appointed by a king.
Whatever royal business has been performed is likewise approved here;
otherwise, if what ought to be done is neglected, the ruin of the king is proclaimed.
In the Aṃśumat-tantra, however, it has been explained in detail.

O best of suns, listen as I describe the daily (nitya) and occasional (naimittika) rites: one should perform the daily rite at its prescribed time, and likewise perform the occasional rite when its specific cause arises.
At the conclusion of the daily worship, one should commence the occasional (naimittika) rite;
the end of the twilight worship is of three kinds, specifically by means of each [of the three] twilights.
Whether ending with the food offering (naivedya), the garland (vali), or the lamp (dīpa)— these being the three-fold abodes—
at the conclusion of whichever ritual action has been commenced, that very action [is completed].
Having performed the daily rite remaining from the twilight worship, the best of preceptors,
as well as the teachers and the officiating priests— those who are proclaimed to be of two kinds— [should proceed].
The occasional rites (naimittika-kriyā) and worship must be performed by the preceptor (ācārya) himself;
the daily worship (nitya-pūjā), especially, must be performed by the officiating priest (arcaka).
The *naimittika* rite is said to have four divisions, followed by the *sākalya*, the *pāvana*, the *śāntika*,
and the *māṅgalya*, each of which is likewise declared to have four divisions.

That which begins with the doors and ends with the offering (nivedya), along with the ritual manual (kalpa), is proclaimed as the "entirety" (sākalya). That which begins with the fire-oblation (huta) and ends with the presentation of the bali-offering is proclaimed as the "purification" (pāvana).
That which concludes with incense and dance is here called *śāntika*;
that which begins with the doors and ends with the *tāṇḍava* dance is prescribed as *māṅgalya*.

One should perform the occasional rite according to its specific injunctions; likewise, the occasional rite should continue until the conclusion of that occasion, at which point the regular rite resumes.
The occasional worship must be performed by the preceptor alone;
that which concludes with the daily twilight ritual should be completed by the officiating priest.
