It is proclaimed to be threefold: the obligatory (nitya), the occasional (naimittika), and the optional (kāmya). The obligatory is further declared to be of two kinds: the constant (āgantuka) and the perpetual (nitya).
Daily worship is performed every day, and sacrifice is performed month after month;
that which is the special sacrifice is called the "constant" (nitya) rite.
The propitiation on the eighth day, as well as the sacrifice at twilight,
the propitiation on the new moon day, and the worship at the equinoxes and solstices.
(p. 83) This incidental [worship] should always be performed by the priest alone.
Occasional worship is said to be of two kinds: the occasional and the incidental.

The rites beginning with the plowing [of the site] and ending with the consecration (pratiṣṭhā) are declared to be occasional (naimittika). All other ritual acts are remembered as adventitious occasions (nimittikāgantuka).
That desirable [action] is said to be of two kinds: external and internal.
External action bestows worldly success, while [internal action] pertains to the self among the various types of effortful deeds.
One should indeed have the optional (kāmya) and occasional (naimittika) rites performed by one who is worthy of the office;
it is proclaimed that these consist of three types: the primary limbs (aṅga), the secondary limbs (upāṅga), and the minor limbs (pratyaṅga).
The ritual bath, the offering, the oblation, and the daily festival—
along with the incense, lamps, and so forth— all these are called the "limbs" by the wise.
Clothing, ornaments and the like, as well as perfumes, garlands, and other decorations, along with the fly-whisk,
the parasol, and the mirror, should be known as the secondary attributes (upāṅga).
The remaining services are proclaimed as being for each individual limb;
therefore, a wise person should not perform the bathing and other such ancillary rites again.
One should properly perform the subsidiary parts (pratyaṅga) that constitute the ancillaries (upāṅga). Therefore, with every effort, one should perform the specific sacrifice.
In the occasional worship, as well as in the great ablution and sprinkling,
one should perform the protective consecration through meditative visualization.
One should again perform all the ritual services in their proper manner;
one should carry out the daily and occasional rites at their respective times.
At the time of bathing, the bath must be performed; at the time of the food offering, the offering must be presented;
at the time of the fire-oblation, the oblation must indeed be offered; and at the time of the ritual bali-offering, the distribution of the bali must be carried out.

At that time, one should indeed perform the incense offering and the lamp offering in this very manner; likewise, whatever regular (nitya) or occasional (naimittika) rites are mixed together at that time, they should be performed accordingly.
At that time, both types of ritual action should be performed by the preceptor alone;
the remaining daily rites should be completed by the worshipper.
A worship performed during the non-sandhyā period becomes one that brings about malevolent magic;
likewise, at the commencement of a rite, the preceptor is especially incapable [if he performs it then].
Then his son or his disciple may undertake all the rites;
likewise the preceptor, the worshipper, and the practitioner, being duly adorned.
The reciter and those born of noble families are proclaimed as the five types of preceptors;
the preceptor, having learned from the scriptures and the world, should perform the occasional rites.
Thus should be the duty of the preceptor; perform the worship with a worshipper who is adorned, for the practitioner is one who accomplishes the ritual substances.
The reciter (vācaka), however, is the performer of the *śruti*; they know the sequence of the five teachers (*pañcācārya*).
Among these, the four beginning with the worshipper (*arcaka*) possess the qualification for the daily rites (*nityakarman*).
Thus, having worshipped in this sequence, one should perform the daily and occasional rites. Thus it is said.
(p. 85) At the time of the daily rites (*nitya-kāla*), one should perform all [the duties], such as subtle expiations (*prāyaścitta*) and so forth;
at a time other than the *saṃdhyā*, the wise man should perform that which arises from malevolent magic (*ābhicāra*).
One should likewise perform the obligatory (nitya), occasional (naimittika), and expiatory (prāyaścitta) rites,
joined with the daily twilight devotions (nitya-sandhyā), which bestow all perfections.
"If there is a transgression of the twilight [prayer], it is a fault; however, if it is deficient, one does not incur the fault.
For him, the transgression of the scripture incurs all the fault. Thus [it is said].

In the *Sūkṣmāgama*, having first described the offering of the fourfold services known as *sāvaśya*, *saubhāgya*, *saukhya*, and *saucaka*, the specific times for the water for the feet (*pādya*), the water for sipping (*ācamanīya*), and so forth, are established as follows:
At the beginning of the *sanāna* (bathing) and at its conclusion, at the beginning of the food offering (*naivedya*) and at its end,
and especially at the beginning of the incense offering (*dhūpa*), one should offer water for the feet (*pādya*) and water for sipping (*ācamana*).

At the five times, the wise one should perform the offering of water for the feet and the sipping of water; especially at the beginning of worship, at the end of the consecration, and at the conclusion of the worship.
"One should offer the arghya at the three times of day; one should employ fragrances at the three times of day. Thus it is said.
In the *Suprabheda*:
"One should employ fragrant substances in three instances: in the water-offering (*arghya*), in the unguent (*vilepana*), and in the bath (*snāna*). Thus it is said.
In the subtle [form of worship],
[the rites are performed] at the time of invocation, at the time of offering the arghya water, at the conclusion of the bath, at the time of incense,
during the application of unguents, during the food offering, and especially at the conclusion of the festival.
And one should perform worship; one should employ eight flowers. Thus it is said.
In the *Suprabheda*: "In the rites of invocation, the water-offering (*arghya*), the foot-washing (*pādya*), bathing, incense, anointing,
the food offering (*naivedya*), and the dismissal (*visarga*), one should properly employ eight flowers."
One may properly perform [the offering] at seven times even without an invocation;
in the subtle [practice],
there should be two times for the food offering— at the conclusion of the bath and at the conclusion of the worship.
At the time of worship, however, it should be done prior to that, at the conclusion of the bath, and at the end of the ritual adoration.
One should offer incense and lamps prepared with ghee from a tawny cow;
the wise person should present incense and lamps to the Lord at the four times of the day.
At the beginning of the bath and likewise at its conclusion, at the end of the worship,
at the beginning of the food offering, at the beginning of the festival, at its conclusion, and at the end of the dance.
At such times as these, one should strike the great bell:
at the time of bathing, when the offering is presented, at the time of the circumambulation with the bali-offering,
at the time for incense, lamps, and so forth, and likewise at the time of the *uṣas* (dawn).
One should especially cause the sound of musical instruments to be made at the five times,
particularly during the night vigil, the time of worship, and at the conclusion of the ritual.
And at the time of the circumambulation of the sacrificial offering (balibhramaṇa), accompanied by its specific characteristics,
the courtesan and my maidservant should perform a dance during the three periods [of the day].

At the beginning of bathing and so forth, at the end of those acts, and especially at the conclusion of worship; likewise at the time of offering the food oblation and at the time of offering flowers.
Especially at the five times, one should perform the sounding of the conch;
at the time of bathing, during the offering, and at its conclusion, one should offer incense and a lamp.
The wise person should recite the Rigveda and other scriptures at the three times of day,
especially during the bath, when offering oblations, when burning incense, and at the conclusion of worship.
One should perform [the worship] four times a day with offerings such as food, hymns of praise, and commentaries;
likewise at the time of bathing, when making offerings, during festivals, and at the time of incense.
One should perform the descent of the cloth (paṭāvaroha) and practice it at the four times of day;
in this manner, one should perform it according to the rules during each junction of time (saṃdhyā).
The *tripāda* consists of three *nāḍīs* and is remembered as "necessary";
*saubhāgya* consists of five *nāḍīs*, as does *saukhyaka* and *yāma*.
"The teacher, having thus worshipped the *sauca* [vessel] which consists of ten channels, incurs no fault if there is a deficiency, whereas a fault arises from the lapse of time. Thus it is said.
Regarding the cause:
I shall describe the ritual for protecting the ocean, which dispels the darkness of all living beings,
serves to eliminate all diseases, and increases all substances.
"At the time of Pradoṣa, for the sake of removing the impurity remaining from the Lord's gaze,
the evening protection rite (sāyarakṣā) should be performed, concluding with incense and lamps."
In the Kāmika [Tantra]:
"I shall describe the ritual of lustration (nīrājana); it is performed at night, either beginning at the onset of dusk or concluding with the offering of incense."
"It should be performed at festivals and other auspicious occasions as well.
Thus [ends the section]. Now, O Dispeller of Darkness, listen as I describe the procedure for protection against subtle [spirits].
At the time when the sun was half-set, in the presence of the Lord Sambhu, before the Lord of Dancers (Naṭeśvara).
One who knows the rhythmic measures (*tāla*) should play these twelve [instruments] in sequence according to the *tāla*.
This is for the purpose of averting what remains impure from the sight of the Deity.
Protective rites (*sāyarakṣā*) should be performed as is appropriate for all the deities. Thus it is said.
In the Kāmika [Tantra]:
"The food-liṅga is prescribed for the sake of occasional rites and for the sake of daily rites;
or the food-liṅga may be offered at the three times of day, or at the morning and midday."
"At midday or in the forenoon, the Puṣpaliṅga is prescribed; at dusk, it should be the Akṣataliṅga, wherein one should worship Paśupati. Thus it is said.
In the *Suprabheda*: "During the morning twilights, there shall be the Gandha and Ṣāḍava [melodies], and after that;
at midday, there shall be the Nāṭṭarāga, and after that, the Kauśika."
At evening, however, the Cendala is proclaimed; at midnight, the fifth [is performed]. One should properly perform Bharata’s *uṣka* dance during the juncture (*sandhi*).
Thus the dance was performed there, where there was abundance of food and peace for the world. Thus it is said.
In the *Kāmika*:

"At the conclusion of rites such as consecration and festivals, as well as at the end of daily festivals, the rite for prosperity (*saukhyakarma*) should be performed according to rule; listen, O twice-born ones!"
Having performed his ablutions and being adorned with ornaments and white garlands and the like,
Raṅgeśa, accompanied by the five preceptors, is surrounded as before.

Having worshipped [the deity] before it, one should perform pure dance (*śuddhanṛtta*) accompanied by the nine dramatic sentiments (*navanāṭyarasa*) and imbued with the contemplation of the meaning of the verses.
Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra are remembered as the presiding deities of the three junctions (sandhyās).
One should recite three verses in succession at dawn, midday, and evening— namely,
the three verses beginning with "mandārapuṣpa," "bhāvānubandha," and "santānakādi.
[These are to be used] during the installation, the sprinkling, other occasions, expiatory rites, burnt offerings, and so forth.
During festivals, ritual ablutions, monthly worship, and the performance of fire oblations;
It is especially distinguished at times such as the hoisting of the banner, and during the month of Māgha and so forth. Thus it is said.

Now, in order to determine the time for the *pavitraka* rite, [the author] first establishes the obligatory (*nitya*) nature of the *pavitra*, since it is subject to numerous alternatives such as being obligatory, occasional (*naimittika*), and so forth.
Root-text:
[Prāyaścitta] is constant, optional, and some say occasional; it is the fulfillment of that injunction.
Thus the teachers and the learned have declared: "Because it is an eternal constituent part, this is eternally pure."

Regarding the word *nityam* (constant): according to the *Amara-kośa*, "pavi" refers to the thunderbolt (*vajra*), the mace (*kuliśa*), or the cleaver (*bhidura*). Because it protects one from the hell named Vajra—which arises from the fault of performing worship only occasionally—it is called *pavitram*. This has been stated in the *Siddhānta-śekhara*:
Because it protects a person from hell and from that which is called "vajra," it is therefore pure.

Regarding this purificatory rite (*pavitra*), some learned teachers say it is "constant" (*nitya*). Some say it is "occasional" (*kāmya*) when performed according to one's desire. Others, however, say it is "contingent" (*naimittika*) when performed upon the occurrence of a specific occasion. Still others call it "expiation" (*prāyaścitta*) because it removes defects. Yet others—

Regarding the phrase "for the sake of filling every gap in the ritual procedure for each sacrifice," this refers to the completion of the rite in accordance with the meaning of the mantra. Thus it has been stated by the teacher Aghoraśivācārya in his *Pavitrārohanirṇaya* according to two characteristics:
In determining the essential nature of the qualification (*adhikāra*), the teachers state various alternatives:

some say it is obligatory (*nitya*); some say it is occasional (*naimittika*); some say it is contingent (*kāmya*); some say it is an expiation (*prāyaścitta*); and some say it is the fulfillment of an injunction (*vidhi-pūraṇa*).
Having thus presented the alternative views, he states the established conclusion:
"Because it is an eternal limb [of the ritual], this is eternal and pure.
Like the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifice, the Cāturmāsya is also characterized by an eternal injunction.

Because of the hearing of an injunction (*vidhi*), it is indeed obligatory (*nitya*). For instance: first of all, this is not optional (*kāmya*), because it is not to be performed out of desire (*kāmanā*). If it is argued that "desire" here refers merely to filling a gap in the injunction (*vidhi-chidra-pūraṇa*), this is like covering one's head while grasping the nose; [it is so] by virtue of its being a supplement to the obligatory injunction.
Because it is an obligatory constituent part, it must be stated that it is indeed obligatory, just like the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*).
Thus it has been said by Aghoraśivācārya:
"Just as for one who performs the daily *agnihotra* oblation following the Soma sacrifice, there is an injunction..."

Just as the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifice is performed as a constant subsidiary (nityāṅga) for the purpose of filling a deficiency, so too should this be understood. In the *Ṣaṭsahasrakālottara* it is also said:
"Therefore, they say that the Pavitrārohaṇa is indeed a constant subsidiary."
Nor is it occasional (*naimittika*), because it is prescribed that only initiation (*dīkṣā*) and consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) are occasional.
As it is said in the *Kālottara* in six thousand verses:
"Bathing, worship, recitation, fire-oblation, and meditation as the fifth."
One should perform this constantly and always; it is further called the "constant limb" (nityāṅga).
On the eighth and fourteenth days of both fortnights,
on the fifteenth day, during a vyatīpāta yoga, at the sun’s transit (saṅkrānti), and during the northern course of the sun;
During the increase of a month, at the end of a day, during the six *aśītimukha* periods,
and likewise during solar and lunar eclipses, worship, recitation, and other rites should be performed twice as much.
In the Antyeṣṭyaṅga-āgama it is said: "Now the occasional rites (naimittika) are described;
initiation (dīkṣā) and consecration (pratiṣṭhā)—this occasional rite is twofold."
And likewise, in the *Mohaśūrottara*:

"Thus the [pavitraka] has been eternally explained as threefold; now hear the occasional [pavitraka]," and so forth. By these words, Aghoraśivācārya has provided a resolution for the occasional nature (*naimittikatva*) of the *pavitraka*, stating: "True."
This is because Viṣṇu’s sleep must be performed every day, and it is also suitable to be performed merely as a *nimitta* (occasion).
Alternatively, the word *naimittika* is formed with the suffix *kap* in its own sense (*svārthika*), such that the word for the occasion itself (*nimitta*) is [the meaning of] *naimittika*.
Now, one might object: "In the case of not performing it, just as with bathing during an eclipse and so forth—"

If it is argued that [the rite] is purely occasional (naimittika) because of the scriptural mention of a transgression (pratyavāya)—as stated in the *Kiraṇa*: "Since it is invariably an auxiliary to the ritual action, otherwise a fault must be incurred"—then alas! By the very phrase "because it is an auxiliary to the ritual action," its status as an obligatory auxiliary (nityāṅgatva) is established.
Nor is there any need for expiation (prāyaścitta); for expiation applies only when there is a deficiency in the performance of the ritual action.

It must be performed at the door; for in the absence of a door, there is an absence of a doorkeeper, and because it is stated that this [rite] must necessarily be performed at the times previously mentioned. For this very reason, the fifth position—that it is for the completion of the injunction—is also not tenable. Since that is included within the category of constant auxiliary elements (*nityāṅga*), it does not constitute a separate position. Thus...
(p. 93) Since the positions regarding optional rites (*kāmya*) and others have been refuted, the position of the obligatory rite (*nitya*) alone remains well-established.
The nature of this *pavitra* has, however, been demonstrated in the *Siddhāntaśekhara*:
"Who else is the *pavitraka* other than the one named Vāsuki?"
Having worshipped the two serpents, who were brothers born of the same womb,
with ascetic fervor for fifty divine years,
they granted a boon to Ambikeśa.
Then Hara, seizing the two serpents by the neck and the head, spoke to that snake regarding the sacred thread:
"One performs this thread [ceremony] every year."
May that fruit which belongs to his worship be yours.
Thus they declare this well-known purifier; some say it is occasional (naimittika), but this is indeed obligatory (nitya).
Now he states the rule for its timing— the root text:
"The three-month periods beginning with Āṣāḍha, as declared in the Śiva doctrine, shall be excellent, middling, and inferior [respectively]."

In both the bright and dark fortnights, the eighth lunar day (Aṣṭamī) is the Śiva-tithi for the purposes of worldly enjoyment and liberation. These two are to be accepted if they occur at sunrise and sunset respectively, and they constitute the sacred time (Pavitra) in due order,
provided they are joined with the rules of observance beginning with the sixty [units of time] and preceded by the Āvāsa, while excluding the intercalary month.

"From Āṣāḍha," etc.: the three months beginning with Āṣāḍha—namely Āṣāḍha, Śrāvaṇa, and Bhādrapada—are, in order, excellent, middling, and inferior. If these are unavailable, Āśvayuja and Kārtika may be taken instead.
Thus it is stated in the Kāmika:
"The three months beginning with Āṣāḍha are proclaimed as the superior, middling, and inferior [periods],
or else the two months of Aśvinī and Kṛttikā."
"In the three months beginning with Āṣāḍha, as well as in Libra and Scorpio—
perform the offering of the sacred thread (pavitrāropaṇa) for the sake of completing any deficiency. Thus it is said.
"In the month of Mṛgaśīrṣa, or in Śrāvaṇa, or at its conclusion, or in Nabhasya, or in the month of Aśvina. Thus it is said.
"O Bird, one should spend the four months of the rainy season in disciplined restraint. Thus it is said.
And so it is stated in the Aṃśumattantra:
"O best of suns, listen as I describe the Pavitrārohaṇa;
whatever deficiency has occurred in actions through mind, deed, or speech."
Because it protects from falling, it is called "purifying" (pavitra) in this context;
both that which is self-established and that which is established by all are praised as the two-fold purifier.

It is said that in a sacrifice performed for one's own sake, one should bring about one's own accomplishment; and it is traditionally taught that when a wise person performs worship for the sake of others, all accomplishments are attained.
(95) I shall now describe, in due order, the worship for the sake of attaining all these accomplishments:
in the month of Āṣāḍha, in the month of Śrāvaṇa, and likewise in the month of Proṣṭhapada.
Perform the rite of offering the sacred thread (pavitrāropaṇa) during the months of Aśvinī and Kṛttikā;
likewise, perform the Pavitraka rite on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Āṣāḍha.
In all other months, during both the bright and dark fortnights,
on the fourteenth and eighth lunar days, perform the Pavitraka rite according to the prescribed rules.
After performing the Kṛttikā-lamp rite,
one should then perform the Pavitraka ceremony when two suns appear during the solar transits from Aries through Gemini.
In that year, when the sun is in Gemini, Viṣṇu must certainly sleep;
or even when two new moons (darśa) occur at the beginning of the period known as Cancer.
At the end of that year, Viṣṇu must necessarily sleep at the end of Karkaṭa;
he sleeps in Āṣāḍha and turns over in Bhādrapada.

In the month of Kārttika, on the day of Hari during the bright fortnight—specifically when it is joined with the Maitra (Anurādhā) and Śravaṇa constellations—he should awaken; these two are proclaimed to be purifying.
If, during the dark fortnights of the month of Āṣāḍha, the asterisms Maitra (Anurādhā), Śravaṇa,
and Revatī should occur at the beginning, middle, and end of the twelfth lunar days respectively;
"O best of suns, those purifying rites (pavitrāṇi) and likewise the yogas are now described.
On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, or on the full moon day,
O Śiva, the offering of the sacred thread (pavitrārohaṇa) should be performed while Hari is asleep."
From the *Siddhāntaśekhara*:
"When the sun has entered the zodiac sign called Cancer,
and Murāri is asleep, the intercalary month (*malamāsa*) is to be avoided."
"In the month of Āṣāḍha, [the observance] is most excellent;
in Śrāvaṇa it is middling; any other time is inferior. Thus it is said.

Now he states the rule for the fortnights and lunar days: "In the bright and dark fortnights"—that is, in both the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*) and the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*). The "Śiva lunar day" is the fourteenth day (*caturdaśī*), and the "eighth" is the middle of the fortnight (*aṣṭamī*); these are to be accepted with respect to enjoyment (*bhukti*) and liberation (*mukti*). The meaning is that regarding enjoyment, the bright fortnight is to be accepted, while regarding liberation, even the dark fortnight is to be accepted. And so it is said:
In the *Siddhāntaśekhara*:
"In the month of Āṣāḍha, the fourteenth day (caturdaśī) occurring under a favorable constellation bestows auspiciousness; it is not desired when it falls on the latter part [of the lunar fortnight]."
"The fourteenth and the eighth lunar days, whether in the bright or the dark fortnight, bestow auspiciousness and are the cause of liberation. Thus it is said.
And in the *Kāmika*: "The Pavitraka [rite] is performed on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Āṣāḍha;
in other months, it is performed during both the bright and dark fortnights."
"On the fourteenth or the eighth day, one should perform the *pavitra* rite according to the prescribed rule. Thus [it is said].

By this [statement], only the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*) of the month of Āṣāḍha is to be taken; elsewhere, both fortnights are to be taken. Thus, for both those who desire worldly enjoyment (*bubhukṣu*) and those who desire liberation (*mumukṣu*), the bright fortnight alone is superior. However, for the seeker of liberation, if it is impossible, even the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*) may be taken. And so it is said in the *Kāmika*:
"For a householder during the bright fortnight, and for a mendicant during both fortnights. Thus [it is said].
In this very way, it has also been established by the teachers of the Aghoraśiva school.
Now, if one asks: "When should [the rite] be performed when the two days are connected to the fourteenth and the eighth [lunar days]?"—to that he says:
"These two are to be taken"—meaning these two, the fourteenth and the eighth, when the sun is at its rising or its setting.
If it were otherwise, it would not be pure in sequence. This is the meaning: in the bright fortnight (śuklapakṣa), that [lunar day] which pervades the time of sunrise is to be taken;
in the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇapakṣa), however, that which pervades the time of sunset is to be taken. In this very manner, the Aghora Śivācāryas have cited the words of Mārkaṇḍeya. As Mārkaṇḍeya said:
That lunar day on which the sun sets constitutes the entire day and night;
one should perform rituals according to that [lunar day], for its decrease or increase is not a cause [for changing the timing].
In the bright fortnight, that lunar day on which the sun rises is to be known as complete; it should be understood to last for three muhūrtas.

Based on this statement, he presents another position—that the determination of the rising and setting [of the lunar day] within the *tithis* is established primarily by that much time—by saying: "The sixtieth and so forth are the previous ones. This means that those [lunar days] joined with the preceding *tithi* are to be taken as the sixtieth and so forth. Thus it is stated in the *Suprabheda*:
Those devoted to the worship of Śiva should perform the rite of the offering of the sacred thread (*pavitrārohaṇa*) either in the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha or especially in that of Śrāvaṇa.
In the month of Proṣṭhapada or again in the month of Aśvayuja, specifically during the dark fortnight on the second,
fourth, or sixth lunar days.
The purifying rite (pavitra) that bestows all accomplishments should be performed ending on the eighth day;
alternatively, it may begin on the eighth, the tenth, or the twelfth day.
The ritual for the offering of the sacred thread (pavitrārohaṇa) should be performed ending on the fourteenth day;
one should have it carried out for seven days, five days, or even three days.
"On the seventh or the thirteenth lunar day, under the asterisms of Revatī, Kṛttikā, Ārdrā, or Rohiṇī, one should have that pavitraka prepared. Thus it is said.
In the Siddhāntaśekhara it is said:
"The sixth, the third, together with the seventh, Nārāyaṇī, and the excellent ones preceded by 'va'."
The twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) is the Nārāyaṇī tithi. Regarding this, the designation of the deities for all fifteen lunar days is stated in that very same source:
"Agni, Ātmabhū, Haimavatī, Bhava, Vaktṛ..."
The serpent, fire, earth, the sun, Śambhu, Durgā, Yama, the moon, Govinda, Manobhava, Īśa, Svadhābhuj, and Vāsārpa are [the lords] in sequence.

(p. 99) And this purifying thread (*pavitra*), having been consecrated (*adhivāsya*) on the preceding day and given as the purifying thread for the invitation of the deity, the pure purifying thread (*śuddhapavitra*) should be offered on the following day at the conclusion of the daily worship (*nityapūjā*).
This very procedure has been set forth by the teachers of Aghoraśiva in their manual (*paddhati*).
Also in the *Suprabheda*:
"Having performed the offering of the sprouts in the east, the consecration (adhivāsana) should be carried out."
In the *Mohasūrottara*:

"On the seventh or the thirteenth day, the hymn (*sūkta*) and the fragrant purifier (*gandhapavitraka*)—or on the eighth or the fourteenth day—that which is designated as 'pure' (*śuddha*) should be performed. Thus it is said.

"With teachers endowed with the rules of discipline"—this is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. The specific time for this rule, which constitutes a limb of the *pavitra* rite, is also established in the *Mṛgendra*: "Having offered praise and prostrated, one should cause the people to hear the declaration of the vow (*niyama*)."
But being unknown, I shall carry out that very same task for the sake of accomplishing my destiny.
For four months, or three months, or two months, or even one month;
or for half a month, or seven nights, or five nights, or three days, or a single day.
Or one should know that eating likewise concludes with the completion of the ritual action. Thus it is said.
Also in the venerable Pauṣkara:
"Even in times of calamity, the Pañcarātra or Trirātra rite must be performed."

Now he states the month that is to be avoided: "having excluded the intercalary month" (*varjayitvādhimāsam*). The definition of the intercalary month (*adhimāsa*) is given in the *Mohaśūrottara* (p. 100):
"Where two new moons occur without the sun's transit (saṅkrānti), that is to be known as an intercalary month (adhimāsa); Viṣṇu sleeps in Cancer. Thus it is said.

Even in the reading "two junctions" (*parvadvayam*), by the word *parva* only the new moon (*amāvāsyā*) is intended. Furthermore, the fact that the intercalary month (*adhimāsa*) is to be avoided is stated in the *Mohaśūrottara*:
"The installation [of deities] and so forth, as well as the *pavitraka* rite and other such acts, O Śatakratu..."
"One who desires his own welfare should not perform [rites] during an intercalary month. Thus it is said.
Likewise, having taken the *gaurī-pavitra* as the subject, the time for the offering of the *pavitra* for other deities is also established in the *Āśumā Tantra*. As it says:
"Now, O Divākara, I shall describe the *pavitra* of Gaurī."
It bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation upon those men who are established in the conduct of the samaya.
If the purificatory rite (*pavitraka*) is to be performed separately from the primary ritual itself, then it should be done by Śiva;
however, if she [the Goddess] is associated with him, she should perform it together with him.
When the sun has entered Aries on the twelfth day of the bright fortnight, Hari lies asleep; therefore, one should perform [the rites] when the sun is in the signs beginning with Aries.
In this context, there are six [months], and here there are two *darśas* in Karkaṭaka;
then Viṣṇu sleeps on the full moon day, and it is considered that his sleep follows immediately after that.
If there is a pair of [Tithis] for viewing in that month of Śrāvaṇa, one should perform it;
and at the setting of Venus and so forth, one should carry out the festival and the Pavitraka rite.
O best of men, neither the consecration (pratiṣṭhā) nor the initiation (dīkṣā) should be performed;
the first is said to belong to Fire, and the second is the station of Brahmā.
The third [tithi] belongs to Ambikā, while the fourth belongs to Gaṇeśa;
the fifth is declared to belong to Śeṣa, and the sixth is celebrated as belonging to Skanda.
The seventh [tithi] belongs to Saptasapti (the Sun), while the eighth is for Aṣṭamūrti (Śiva).
The ninth is for Goddess Durgā, and the tenth lunar day is for Yama.
The eleventh day is said to belong to Indra; the twelfth, to the Lord of Kamalā;
the thirteenth, to Māra; and the fourteenth, to Śaṅkara.
Thus, the fifteenth day of the lunar fortnight is proclaimed as sacred for the ancestors:
for one desiring worldly enjoyment, during the bright fortnight; but for one desiring liberation, during the dark fortnight.
"One should perform these [rites] on these lunar days (tithis) as prescribed for each respective deity. Thus [it is said].
In the Kālottara it is said:
"On the fourteenth and the eighth [lunar days], [the rite] remains common to all;
however, for those of a materialistic nature, it is specifically prescribed during the bright fortnight."

Regarding this subject of the *pavitra*, much has been said; all of that has been expounded by the teacher Aghoraśiva—this is the direction [of the inquiry]. Now, the times for not studying (*anadhyāyakāla*) are written down exactly as stated in the *Kiraṇāgama*.
As Garuḍa said: (p.
102) "O Lord, you have indicated and taught to me the occasions when study is forbidden. In which [circumstances] should study be performed, and in which arms is it not permitted?"
The Blessed One said: On these lunar days— the full moon, the new moon, the eighth day, the fourteenth day, and the first day— one should not perform the hearing or study [of the scriptures].
During the Vyatīpāta yoga, at the sun’s transit (saṅkrānti), on all three Aṣṭakā days, at the twilights, during the roar of thunder, and when there is a conflagration or the glowing of the quarters;
When the ascetic has suddenly attained perfection, when a great king has died,
when a meteor falls like a star, and when the comet is displayed;
When the wind carries away dust, when there is unseasonable rain,
or when a chameleon, a mouse, a frog, or a cat has entered between [the teacher and the student].

O Bird, during an eclipse of the moon or sun, as well as throughout the entire month of Caitra, there shall be a suspension of study for three nights, and no giving of gifts or worship should take place.
Others are also said to be momentary; listen to that with a concentrated mind, even amidst the throngs of ascetics or the trampling of cows, elephants, and horses.
When the sound of funeral drums is heard in battle, when women are weeping nearby,
when a cruel king is seen, or upon seeing artisans;
When a friend has arrived from afar or another kinsman is seen, they say that even a moment's study is not appropriate; rather, conversation regarding other matters should be conducted at the end.
(There shall be a suspension of study for five nights upon the planting of purified [seeds].
All suspension of study is to be understood as being prompted by one's own purposes, such as worship and the like. Thus it is said.
Having thus explained the regular time, he now states the occasional time. Among those, first the time for the monthly worship is shown—
the root text says:

The month called solar is declared to be of two kinds: subtle and gross. The subtle is that which begins with Aries (Meṣa) and so forth; the other is said to begin with the month of Mārgaśīrṣa and so forth, starting from the Puṣya asterism. [One should avoid] the lunar mansion of the month, the asterisms of Śiva (Ārdrā), the solstices, the equinoxes, the festival days (parvan), and the two types of eclipses.
One should worship Śiva with the substances prescribed for those [deities] during the transits of the planets, the lunar mansions, and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "subtle and gross": the month called *saura*—the month primarily defined by the solar transit (*saṅkrānti*)—is declared to be twofold, according to the distinction of subtle and gross. The word "from the Āgama" is to be understood as the ellipsis; since the solar month alone is praised in the Āgamas and other scriptures, it is the solar month that is mentioned here. Thus it is stated in the *Kāmika*:
"The solar [day] is declared here to be the best; the lunar is considered mediocre; the civil (sāvana) is said to be the lowest, and therefore it is not desired for ritual purposes. Thus it is said.
And so it is stated in the Bhāradvājīya:
"The lunar month and the solar month should be understood with particular distinction:
for the purpose of worldly transactions, one uses the lunar; for auspicious rites, the solar."
In astrology as well:
from the conjunction of the Sun with the two zodiac signs beginning with Capricorn (Mṛga),
spring occurs during the first six months of the year for a child.
Summer, the rainy season, and autumn—likewise, that which is called winter is said to be the sixth. Thus it is said.
For this very reason, it has been established even by the masters of the Aghora Śaiva school as follows: "Now,

since it is heard everywhere that the signs beginning with Capricorn (makara) are designated by the names beginning with Māgha according to the solar calendar, and since the seasons occurring during the northern transit (uttarāyaṇa) are heard to begin with the cool season (śiśira), [the calculation] among those..."

Because of Vedic statements such as "The three seasons beginning with Śiśira constitute the northern course (udagayana) of the Sun, while the remaining [three] constitute the southern course (dakṣiṇāyana)," and because of the statement of the author of the *Nighaṇṭu* that "an ayana consists of three seasons," an ayana cannot logically occur within a single season; furthermore, since technical designations (*saṃjñā-śabda*) are established through conventional usage (*rūḍhi*), the designation [of the months] beginning with Māgha corresponds to the zodiacal signs beginning with Capricorn (*makara*).

"It is certain that it is indeed the group of six. Therefore, the solar month alone is the most excellent. Regarding that, he states its twofold nature through the distinction between subtle and gross forms: "Beginning with Aries" refers to the month beginning with the month of Aries, which is called the subtle;
whereas the gross month begins from Mārgaśīrṣa, starting from the month of Puṣya.
Or from the beginning of the month of Puṣya.
As it is stated in the Aṃśumattantra:
"O Divākara, the month is said to be of two kinds: gross and subtle."
Beginning with the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, it is designated as "gross."
"O Sun, the subtle [cycle] is thus proclaimed as beginning with Aries and ending with Pisces; some say it begins with the month of Taiṣya and ends with Mārgaśīrṣa."

Thus, according to the division into subtle and gross, there are two types [of months]; however, within the [lunar] month, all rites such as the monthly worship (*māsapūjā*) and so forth must be performed by means of the gross month alone. As it is stated in the *Aṃśumattantra*:
"Everything should be performed by means of the gross; listen to the rule for the gross time."
And in the *Sūkṣmatantra*:
"Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the supreme procedure for the monthly worship (*māsapūjā*).
The month is declared to be of two kinds; it is traditionally known as gross (*sthūla*) and subtle (*sūkṣma*)."
The gross zodiacal sign is traditionally known to extend from its commencement to its end— for example,
from Aries to Scorpio— and it is that which revolves as a lagna from one rising point to the next.
"That should be known as subtle; O Wind, the subtle month is [the time].
Whether in the gross month or the subtle month, the worship of the month is prescribed. Thus [it is said].

For this very reason, the author of the *Amarakośa*, beginning with "Mārgaśīrṣa is also called Sahāmārga" and ending with "Bāhula and Ūrja are Kārtikika," has established [the names] according to the gross (sthūla) month alone. Within that context as well, he states the specific time:
"in the lunar mansion of the month" (*māsarkṣe*), meaning in the respective lunar mansions of each month. And the lunar mansions of the months are established in the *Candrajñāna*.
Namely: Citrā, Viśākhā, Mūla,
Uttarāṣāḍhā, Śraviṣṭhā, Proṣṭhapadā, Āśvinī, Kṛttikā, Ārdrā, and Punarvasu.
Maghā and the Uttarā [nakṣatras] are present in all twelve signs, beginning with Aries.

(p. 106) The teachers have stated a specific rule regarding the lunar mansions of the months, as follows: The months beginning with Caitra are to be known [as occurring] when the moon reaches the pairs of asterisms beginning with Citrā; likewise, [the months] ending with Kanyā, Tulā, and Jhaṣa (Pisces) are determined by Dhṛti, Bharaṇī, and Kara respectively, in this sequence.

"In the month of Ārka (Kārttika), when the twenty-seven lunar mansions have arisen, that among them which is joined with a parvan is designated as a 'month'; worship performed according to rule therein is declared for the sake of the complete prosperity of all attainments. Thus it is said.

In the asterism of Ārdrā belonging to Śiva; during the solstices—the southern and northern courses; at the equinoxes—the transits into Aries and Libra; or on the five festival days (*parvan*), which are either the full moon and new moon days, as stated in the *Kālādarśa*: "The five festival days..."
"The fourteenth and eighth days of both fortnights, the new moon, the full moon, and the solar transit— these, the great seers have declared, are the five festival days (parvan)."

During the two eclipses— the lunar and solar eclipses— at the *pāta* (the *vyatīpāta* yoga), during the transits (*krānti*) such as the entry into Aries and other signs, during the asterisms of kings' birth (*nṛparkṣaka*),
and by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), including the commencement of war and so forth; at these times, with the substances— clarified butter and the like— as prescribed for each respective month.

One should worship Śiva. This has been stated in the *Aṃśumat*: "One should perform [the rite] under the lunar mansion of that specific month, or under the birth-mansion of the king, or on the birthday of the performer, or under the Ārdrā mansion in his birth-month."

"At the solstices, at the equinoxes, during lunar and solar eclipses, on the two parvan days, at the transit of the sun (saṅkrānti), during the vyatīpāta yoga, O Divākara, and at times such as the solstices,
one should perform sacrifice with the substances appropriate to those months. Thus it is said.
And likewise, in the *Sūkṣma*: "At the beginning or end of a battle, during the solstices or the equinoxes,
or again under a lunar mansion favorable to the birth-star of the performer, or under his monthly star."
"One should especially perform the monthly worship during auspicious times. Thus it is said.
The specific substances for each month are set forth in the *Aṃśumattantra*. As it says:
"In Mārgaśīrṣa, ghee is prescribed; in Puṣya, honey is praised;
in Kumbha, a woolen blanket with ghee; and in Tapasya, curd is extolled."
In the month of Madhu, there is worship with *damanaka*; in Mādhava, worship with fragrances;
in the month of Śukra, worship with fruits; and in Āṣāḍha, worship with milk.
In the month of Nabhas, there is sugar; and in Nabhasya, worship with cakes (*apūpa*).
The offering of food during the month of Tulā and the worship of lamps during Kārttika.

"The sequence of substances has thus been declared; now hear their number. Thus begins the section where the twenty-eight services, beginning with the water for the feet (*pādya*), are prescribed for each month in that very same [text]. As follows:
Water for the feet, water for sipping, the respectful offering (arghya), water for bathing, clothing, sandalwood paste,
ornaments, flowers, incense, lamps, and the food offering (naivedya).
A fan, water, and likewise mouth-perfume;
as well as passion, song, dance, rhythm, and the sequence of instrumental music.

"I shall explain individually all these materials: the mantra, the preparation of the leaf, the mandala, the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), the universal fuel-sticks (viśvadhānī), the oblation (homa), as well as the recitation (japa), and the substances. Thus it is said.
In the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, ghee is prescribed; in Puṣya, honey is commended.
In Māgha, a woolen blanket with ghee is recommended, and in Phālguna, curd is proclaimed.
In the month of Caitra, the offering of *damanaka* is prescribed; in Vaiśākha, worship with fragrances;
in the month of Jyeṣṭha, worship with fruits; and in Āṣāḍha, worship with milk.
In Śrāvaṇa, there is worship with sugar; in Proṣṭhapada, worship with cakes;
in Āśvina, there should be worship with food; and in Kārtika, the offering of lamps.
One should install them in due order and worship them just as one would the primary *liṅga*,
offering water for the feet (*pādya*), water for sipping (*ācamana*), the respectful oblation (*arghya*), the bath (*snāna*), clothing (*vastra*), and unguents (*vilepana*).
Ornaments, flowers, incense, lamps, and the food offering; the sacrificial ground for the fire, the fuel-sticks, the oblations, and the recitation of mantras.
"One should arrange for water, mouth-fresheners, song, dance, instrumental music, betel-leaf, and the ritual application of mantras, each separately. Thus it is said.
Regarding the fruit of offerings such as ghee,
it is stated in the *Sūkṣma*:
"The offering of ghee leads to liberation, while honey increases longevity."
The Ghṛtakambala sacrifice shall bring about security and prosperity.

From the *dradhi* [flower], there shall be an increase of sons; from the *damana*, it brings prosperity. From the fragrance of the *mālākya*, one obtains the fruit that grants the fulfillment of desired aims.
Milk causes the destruction of enemies; molasses bestows the fruit of affection;
cake is for the sake of gaining wealth; and food and other such items grant all desires.
"O Wind, the offering of lamps destroys faults such as the killing of a Brahmin. Thus it is said.
Having thus described the time for the general monthly worship, the root text states the determination regarding the specific cases arising from two lunar days (*tithi*) and so forth: Root Text:

If, at the time of the monthly sacrifice (*māsejyā*), [the moon] has risen twice in one month, it should be performed on two days; if during the day, it is auspicious even beyond what was stated. Alternatively, if the sun's transit (*saṅkrānti*) or an eclipse occurs in conjunction with a meritorious yoga (*puṇyayoga*) in the preceding [period], [it is auspicious].
Having abandoned [the previous procedure] and performed the consecration (adhivāsa) on the preceding day, it should take place after the daily worship (nityārcanā) on the following day. || 21 ||

Regarding "māsejyeti": in one month—that is, in a single month—at the time of the *māsejyā*, which is the monthly worship (*māsapūjā*) during the prescribed period such as the lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) of that month; when it has arisen twice—meaning when it occurs at both the beginning and the end of the month—it should be performed in both instances. Thus it is stated in the *Aṃśumattantra*, in the chapter on monthly worship (*māsapūjāpaṭala*):
"One should worship with the substances appropriate to that month during the times prescribed for the solstices and so forth;
one should worship both when there are two lunar mansions in a single month. Thus it is said.

If it is argued that, since neither [alternative] is the intended meaning of the scripture, one must accept only one of the two positions—just as in the case of the sacrifice with *vrīhi* or *yava* rice—lest there be a contradiction with Mīmāṃsā; we say no, because the statement of both is stronger due to the necessity expressed by Śiva’s own words, "one should worship both. Furthermore, when two days exist, on whichever day it is prescribed for the daytime...

The meaning is that on that day, the auspicious [observance] should be performed even if the time has exceeded [the prescribed limit]. In that regard, according to the principle of the synthesis of qualities (*guṇopasaṃhāranyāya*):

"When the lunar mansion (*ṛkṣa*) is divided into two parts and the day is greater in one part, one should perform the festival at the sacred ford (*tīrthotsava*) during that [day]; when [the day and night] are equal, the former [the day] is distinguished as superior."

The sense is that it should be accepted according to this principle. Now, if on the previous day there is a conjunction with a *puṇya-yoga*, such as being joined with *vyatīpāta*, the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*), or other such yogas, then because of the rarity of such an occasion, the rite should be performed on that very [previous] day. As it is said in the *Kāmika*:
That which is conjoined with the union of a lunar day (tithi) and a lunar mansion (nakṣatra) is said to be difficult to obtain. Thus it is said.
And also: "When the lunar mansion has passed through two watches, or when a conjunction occurs on the lunar day. Thus it is said.

Regarding *saṅkrānti* and *rāhūdaya*: *saṅkrānti* refers to the transit [of the sun] into Aries and the other signs; *rāhūdaya* refers to an eclipse of the moon or the sun. Having excluded these two—meaning, having excluded the day on which these two occur—one should take the subsequent [time] if it occurs before [the exclusion], and the preceding [time] if it occurs after, as stated previously. This is the meaning.

And so it has been said by the Teachers: "If the asterism of the Sun (Aśleṣā), the asterism of the Tīrtha (Punarvasu), and the asterisms of the month (the two Aṣāḍhās) should recur within a single month," [then a calamity follows].
For indeed, in future existences alone, karma must perform its function;
likewise, it is worn away by transmigration and eclipses. Thus it is said.

The intention is that for each of those two as well, it is the time for specific worship (*viśeṣapūjā*). However, the determination regarding their simultaneous occurrence (*samāveśa*) due to their inevitability will be explained later. Now, he describes the method of worship at the aforementioned time itself: "Having performed the rite called *adhivāsana* on the previous day."

On the following day, at the conclusion of the daily worship, it is stated in the *Aṃśumattantra* that the wise preceptor, accompanied by the disciple, having performed his bath and being well-composed,
should clothe himself in a new, unwashed garment.
Having procured the materials prescribed for that particular month according to the rules, the wise one,
on the night preceding the designated day at the conclusion of the lamp-offering, should proceed.
"Then, having entered the sacrificial hall, one should commence the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana)," and so forth.

One should perform the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) immediately for the Apāmārga, sandalwood, fire, flowers, and likewise fruits; for other items, it should be performed during the previous night.
There is a certain distinction in this matter; listen, O best of the Sun-gods:
[it is performed] either at the conclusion of the morning twilight or at the conclusion of the evening twilight.
Then, having performed the food-offering according to the rules, the most excellent preceptor should dismiss the food-liṅga at the time of the midday sacrifice.
"At that time, one should perform the ritual bathing and cast the food-representative into the water;
he who eats it intentionally shall go to the Raurava hell. Thus [it is said].
And at the time of the evening sacrifice, one should dismiss the food-linga. Thus it is said.

p. 112) Thus, having established the time for the monthly worship, the scriptural statements from the respective Āgamas are cited here to determine the timing for the specific offerings, such as the nine types of food-offerings (*naivedya*), during those various months.
In the *Kālottara*:

Now, therefore, I shall fully explain the characteristics of the nine types of food offerings (naivedya); one should avoid them during the months of Virgo, Aquarius, Cancer, and Sagittarius. Thus it is said.
In the Bhīmasaṃhitā:
"One should avoid [the performance of rites] with great effort during the months of Proṣṭhapada, Māgha, Āṣāḍha, and Mārgaśīrṣa; the remaining months are traditionally held to be auspicious."
"The bright fortnight (śuklapakṣa) is praised, whereas the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇapakṣa) is censured. Thus [it is said].
In the *Kālottara*: "On the second, third, and likewise the fifth [day] of the bright fortnight,
as well as the seventh, eleventh, tenth, and thirteenth."
These lunar days (tithis) are auspicious, as are the asterisms Hasta, Śravaṇa, Revatī, Āditya (Punarvasu),
Puṣya, Anurādhā, Aśvinī, Citrā, and the three Uttaras.
Soma (Mṛgaśiras), Prajāpati (Rohiṇī), Mūla, Viśākhā, Vasu (Dhaniṣṭhā), Vāruṇa (Śatabhiṣaj), and those born under the signs of Pisces, Aries, and Cancer— these are declared to be auspicious.
These and all other groups are impossible [to overcome], yet they all bestow auspicious results:
Jupiter is indeed auspicious in the fourth,
as well as in the sixth and tenth houses.
In the eleventh and the tenth houses, benefics are remembered as being auspicious;
likewise, in the sixth, the tenth, the twelfth, and the seventh as well.

The Moon is said to bestow auspiciousness when situated in the ninth, twelfth, sixth, tenth, or seventh house from the ascendant; as for the other planets, they are likewise auspicious in these positions.
Inauspicious [planets] are thus declared, while others are remembered as bestowing auspiciousness;
the days known as those of Mercury, Venus, and the Moon are remembered as the most excellent.
Having deliberated for a short while, one should perform the rite of offering the sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa). Thus it is said.
The time for the offering of fresh food (naivedya) to Ajita may occur even during three months;
however, it is not recommended in the month of Māgha, nor when Jupiter and Venus are in the Hasta constellation.
"O Supreme God, it should also be on an auspicious day during the bright fortnight of Caitra or Phālguna,
under a favorable asterism, a favorable yoga, and in a favorable lagna."
He states the time for Śivarātri as follows in the Kāmika:
"The fourteenth day that occurs in the dark fortnight of the month of Māgha—
that night is Śivarātri, which brings all merit and auspiciousness."
In the *Kumāra-tantra*: "On whichever fourteenth day occurs in the dark fortnight of that month,
that night shall be Śivarātri, which brings all merit and auspiciousness."
(114) One *ghaṭikā* before two watches (*yāma*) at night is the "great midnight" (*mahāniśā*).
If the fourteenth day falls on that [time], that night is Śivarātri.
The thirteenth day mixed with the fourteenth is considered the primary [Śivarātri]; that which is overlapped by the new moon (parvan) is deemed inferior;
and when the fourteenth day lasts for a full day and night, it is the middling Śivarātri.
"In that [city], Mahādeva is to be worshipped by those who desire their own welfare. Thus it is said.
Īśvara said: "O Kauśika, this hundred [of offerings] is true; yet it is fourfold for one worthy of my worship.
Even so, O Senānī with the single tusk, I am pleased by your worship."
In the *Cintyāgama*:
"One should perform the rite of investiture (*vṛta*) during one month or two fortnights;
and it should be at night, for a full day and night, on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight."
O Great Goddess, it would be most excellent for worship if the night were joined with the Trayodaśī during the day and the Caturdaśī during the night.
O Lord, that sacrifice performed at night would be most excellent;
for the thirteenth lunar day (trayodaśī) should first consist of ten nāḍikās at the beginning of the night.
If twenty *nāḍīs* remain after the fourteenth lunar day (*caturdaśī*), that night shall be Śivarātri; this is considered the middling [type], O beloved of Śiva.

"If the fourteenth day occurs first and lasts for twenty nāḍikās during the night, the remainder joined with the full moon (parvan) is the latter; one should perform the vow in this inferior manner. Thus it is said.

Thus, since the Great Liṅga manifested at midnight itself to quell the quarrel between Brahmā and Viṣṇu, the fourteenth day (caturdaśī) that extends through midnight alone is to be accepted. In the absence of such [an overlap] due to the increase or decrease of the lunar days, that which extends through the evening (pradoṣa) is to be accepted; however, the thirteenth day (trayodaśī), even if it has the form of Bhaga or the form of a Liṅga, is not.

"Fourteenth [tithi]," and "Thus, one should avoid that which is pierced by the new moon (darśa)," and so forth—since these and many other scriptural and traditional (smṛti) statements declare that the [fourteenth] pierced by the thirteenth is to be accepted, while that pierced by the new moon is to be avoided, one might ask: "How can this be? It is true; regarding the prohibition of being pierced by the new moon...

This is because the subject matter concerns the pervasion of midnight (*ardharātra*) across two days. Even when there is no pervasion of midnight across both days, just as with midnight, that which pervades the evening (*pradoṣa*)—being the time of the Supreme Lord’s dance—is to be accepted. In this way, there is no contradiction with the *Smṛtis* or the *Āgamas* anywhere. However, some [hold that] on the eleventh day...

Just as they do not tolerate the overlapping of the tenth lunar day (*daśamī-vedha*), they likewise do not tolerate the overlapping of the new moon (*darśa-vedha*) on the fourteenth day (*caturdaśī*). In the *Īśānasaṃhitā* of the *Skanda Purāṇa*, it is said:
"One should perform the breaking of the fast (*pāraṇā*) at the end of the lunar day, together with one's kinsmen, sons, and others."
In this very manner, the observer of the vow should perform the rite every year.
A person should perform the twelve-year rite as well as the twenty-four-year rite; they shall attain all desires. I shall now describe the method.
"One should perform the breaking of the fast at the end of the lunar day, whether by day or by night;
on the preceding day, one should eat once, preceded by the cleansing of the teeth."
(p. 116) He states the time for the spring worship:
"In the month of Phālguna, one should worship with all kinds of perfumes, accompanied by a special ritual bathing and joined with a special sacrifice. Thus it is said.
O Janārdana, I shall describe in brief that which dwells in the month of Ajita (Vaiśākha):
it is traditionally held to be on the full-moon day of the two months of Madhu and Mādhava.
At that auspicious time and favorable moment, one should cause [the rite] to be performed according to the prescribed rules. Thus it is said.
In the *Vātula*: "One should perform [the rite] on the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight during the months of Caitra or Vaiśākha,
under an auspicious lunar mansion, on a favorable day, and at a propitious moment."
"One should perform this annually, which brings happiness to the world. Thus it is said.
In the month of Phālguna, in Caitra, and especially in Vaiśākha—
whether for nine days, seven days, five days, or even three days.
"Alternatively, that festival known as Vasanta should be performed on a single day;
one should perform the Vasanta festival in succession according to the lunar mansion (nakṣatra) of each respective month. Thus it is said.
The ritual procedure for *pūraka* is stated in the *Kālottara*:
"One should perform the *pūraka* rite during the month of Āṣāḍha;
it bestows longevity, prosperity, fame, and accomplishment upon kingdoms, villages, and kings."
Thus, that which is joined with a lunar festival (parvan) is the most excellent; otherwise, it would be middling.
When two [such] days occur within a single fortnight, the wise man should take the later one.
"When both sides have become equal, the preceptor should take the subsequent one;
having thus taken the lunar mansion, he should properly perform the rite for the Goddess. Thus it is said.
The ritual procedure for the Kṛttikā-lamp is stated in the *Kāmika*: "O best of Brahmins, listen as I proclaim the sequence of lamps;
it is performed in the month called Kṛttikā, under the lunar mansion named Kṛttikā."
Or else, at the time of the full moon, for the sake of accomplishing all desires,
one should begin the lighting of lamps at the moment of sunset.
In this context, the examination of the eighth house from the natal ascendant for defects of the ascendant,
as well as the observation of the Viṣṭi yoga, the Vaināśika asterisms, and so forth, is not approved.
The time from before sunset until the end of the first watch (yāma) is intended;
the time thereafter, up to the end of half a watch, is also considered [the period for recitation].
Having thus determined the time, one should perform the offering of the ritual sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa). Thus it is said.
In the *Kāmika-tantra-sāra*:
"O best of the twice-born, whichever lunar day the sun reaches its rising upon, that entire lunar day is complete in the bright fortnight; in the dark fortnight, it is the opposite."
Whichever lunar day (tithi) the sun reaches at its setting, that lunar day is to be known as complete; this is likewise the case with respect to the constellations (nakṣatra).
"When the Lord of Day (the Sun) is situated in Scorpio and the Moon is in the seventh house, and there is conjunction with the Kṛttikā asterism, one should arrange lamps at night. Thus it is said.
"In Raurava, when the moon has entered Scorpio and is conjoined with the fire-constellation [Kṛttikā],
or on a full-moon night, one should perform the Kṛttikā-lamp ritual. Thus it is said.
In the month known as Svāyambhuva and also in the month called Kṛttikā, when conjoined with that lunar mansion and lunar day,
three types are declared to be excellent; listen to their distinctions, O observer of noble vows.
This should be performed throughout that month, especially with disciplined application;
however, one should practice it specifically on the lunar days joined with the junctions (parvan) within a single month or two fortnights.
If, on that very same lunar festival, the moon is conjoined with the Kṛttikā constellation, a lamp should be offered there; for indeed, there is something special about it.

When a lunar mansion or a lunar day occurs twice, or when a conjunction (yoga) arises, one should perform the rite on the day joined with the auspicious occasion (parvan); otherwise, one may observe it on either of the two other days.
That which is conjoined with the lunar mansion of the fortnight is considered excellent and highly praised;
that known to belong to the Vaiśyas is middling, while that in the fourth [position] is inferior.

"In this manner, it should be performed in sequence to bestow the increase of wealth, grain, and so forth; it is declared to be both common and supreme, dispelling the darkness of all living beings. Thus [it is said].
In that very same section on the determination of lunar days (*tithi-nirṇaya*), it is stated:
"The full moon conjoined with Kṛttikā brings happiness to both the king and the kingdom;
conjoined with Bharaṇī, it removes disease; and when joined with Rohiṇī, it likewise does so."
It should be known as the bringer of all happiness, conjoined with the deity Moon;
it is declared to be the cause of abundance, and its fruit is thus proclaimed.
Therefore, when the Moon is joined with a festival day, it shall be the most preeminent of all.
If it is performed on a day lacking the prescribed festival, the Festival of Lights (Dīpotsava) must be observed.
Therefore, for the sake of averting calamities against the king and the kingdom, one should cause [the rite] to be performed on a festival day. Thus it is said.
In the month of Āśvina, on the full moon day when the lunar mansion is Kṛttikā— the deity of fire—
one should perform the Kṛttikā-lamp rite at the time of twilight.
One should perform it exclusively on the full moon day, or at twilight. Thus it is said.
The procedure for the Ārdrāvṛta: as stated in the Kāmika-tantrasāra—“In the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, one should perform the Ārdrāvṛta on the day of Ārdrā;
whether it coincides with a lunar festival (parvan) or not, it is indeed the Ārdrā [that matters].”
It is taught that [the rite] performed specifically under Ārdrā is the most excellent;
one should perform the consecration during the eight nāḍīs of Ārdrā or under the final lunar mansion.
"Except for the eight nāḍīs [of the asterism], one should perform the vrata in the forenoon. Thus it is said.
In the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, during the lunar mansion Ārdrā, worship should be performed within one's continuum;
if it is conjoined with a festival (parvan) and associated with an auspicious yoga, it becomes most excellent.
Before sunset, for one watch or even for half a watch.
That day joined with a lunar festival (parvan) is declared to be "middling," whether it be by means of a constellation ending at sunset or by any [other] festival.
Having thus determined that it is known as the "inferior" [type], one should arrange it accordingly;
when the lunar day is deficient and the full moon occurs on the following day, then it is primarily determined by the asterism (ṛkṣa).
"If a lunar mansion is divided [between two days], it shall belong to the one for which there are more than two nāḍīs;
if they are equal, the latter should be taken, as it is the cause of all auspiciousness. Thus it is said.
In the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, during the Aṃśumatī [fortnight], when the moon is in conjunction with the constellation Ārdrā;
whether at the junction of a lunar phase (parvan) or not, one should perform the rite of consecration (vṛta) under Ārdrā.
Likewise, when the day is exceeded or deficient, one should perform [the rite] under that same lunar mansion;
however, under Ārdrā during eight nāḍīs, one should perform the vow under the final lunar mansion.
"One should perform the rite during the forenoon within the asterism [of the day], excluding the eight nāḍīs;
that asterism which is deficient by eight nāḍīs shall be fruitless. Thus it is said.
In the *Svāyambhuva*:
"In the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, one should perform the vow under the asterism Ārdrā;
if that Ārdrā is joined with a lunar festival (parvan), it is praised as the most excellent."
If, however, it is not joined with a lunar day (parvan), or if it is only the Ārdrā asterism,
or if two asterisms occur in one month, one should perform the selection (vṛta) under the final asterism.
And having obtained two such occasions joined with a festival, which are preeminent,
for one, two, or three *vināḍikās* beginning from sunrise;
Having taken that which is joined with the lunar mansion (parvan), and likewise up to the end of the asterism,
the wise one should perform the eight nāḍīs, grasping its gateway.
If it is devoid of eight nāḍīs, one should perform the previously mentioned rite;
in that previous case, one should perform the excellent offering of sprouts (aṅkurārpaṇa) as before.
"One should begin the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) under the lunar mansion named Mṛgaśiras. Thus it is said.
In the *Sūkṣma*: "Now listen, O destroyer of obstacles, to the worship of Vighneśa;
it should be performed in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, on the sixth lunar day conjoined with the planet Mercury."
"On that day, whether it falls on a Saturday or not, the wise man should perform the rite of investiture;
he should worship Vighneśa with perfumes, flowers, and other offerings. Thus [it is said].
p. 122) Regarding that which is born of yoga:
when the constellation Ārdrā is conjoined with or separated from Vāmbu (the Wind), one should perform the rite in the manner described on the tenth day from that point. Likewise—

"When the sun has reached the sign of Sagittarius (Cāpa), during the ten-day period preceding Raudra [the month of Mārgaśīrṣa], one should properly worship Vighneśa on either the sixth lunar day or when the moon is in the Śatabhiṣaj asterism. Thus it is said.

He states the rule for the time of *pradoṣa*: on whichever day, at the onset of night— the beginning of the night— the thirteenth lunar day (*trayodaśī*) is seen to last for two, one and a half, two, one, or half a watch (*yāma*), or even less than that, for two or one *ghaṭikā*, there [the rite is performed].
During the time known as *pradoṣa*, one should worship Giriśa during both fortnights—the bright and the dark.
However, in the month of Māgha, one should especially worship Giriśa during the bright fortnight. As it is said in the *Aṃśumat*:
"O best of suns, hear now the rule for *pradoṣa*."
This meritorious rite removes all sins and destroys all defects;
it should especially be performed at the time of Pradoṣa,
specifically on the evening of the thirteenth day, [commemorating] that which arose from the churning of the Ocean of Milk.
For the sake of the welfare of the gods, he swiftly mounted his bull and swallowed that terrible poison, which was like the fire of cosmic destruction.
At that time, I drank the poison for the protection of the world;
whoever performs worship of me is liberated from all sins.
Therefore, with every effort, one should commence the worship of Śiva;
that which is performed in the evening on the thirteenth lunar day is remembered as the remover of all defects.
On the thirteenth day of both the bright and dark fortnights, the sacrifice preceded by the bull [should be performed];
from sunrise until sunrise, the thirteenth day shall be most excellent.
Beginning from the rising of the sun until its setting, one should perform the sacrifice on that day; this is proclaimed as the middling [rite].
Sacrifice performed until twenty-seven *nāḍīs* would be inferior;
after midday, the thirteenth [tithi] lasts for two or one watch (*yāma*) of time.
That [period] shall consist of half a watch (one hour and a half), specifically thirteen nāḍīs;
it is certain that at the conclusion of that day, it is called *pradoṣa*.
Therefore, on the eighth part of that day— at its beginning, middle, or end— the wise man should worship Śiva when He is visible on the thirteenth lunar day.
"On the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of Māgha, the most excellent of the excellent [rites] is prescribed;
one should perform the sacrifice on that day and obtain the fruit of all months. Thus it is said.
In the Svāyambhuva [Purāṇa]: "Beginning from the setting of the sun, three nāḍīs and three quarters of a nāḍī constitute what is designated as 'pradoṣa'; during that time, one should worship Śambhu."
"When the thirteenth lunar day extends beyond sunset, the worship at twilight (pradoṣa-pūjā) must be performed on that very [day] for the sake of accomplishing one's desired goals. Thus it is said.
In the *Aṃśumat-tantra*,
it is prescribed that one *ghaṭikā* (twenty-four minutes) is allotted from the bull [procession] up to the ritual bath;
and five *nāḍīs* (twenty-four minutes each) are proclaimed for the period from the food offering (*naivedya*) up to the festival conclusion (*utsava*).
The ritual from incense (dhūpa) up to the bull (vṛṣa) is prescribed to consist of three parts;
at the conclusion of the evening worship, one should perform the evening protection rite.
Thus, the mortal who performs this shall attain a meritorious state. So it is said.
Now, in order to state the timing for the sixteen sacraments beginning with *garbhādhāna*, the author first states the time for *garbhādhāna*: [Root Text]—
The Sāvitra, Vedha, Hari, Varuṇa, Pauṣṇa, Anurādhā, and the two Uttarās (Uttaraphalgunī and Uttarāṣāḍhā) are auspicious for conception when conjoined with Jupiter, the Moon, or Venus.
In the context of storage, the days, degrees, and so forth are commended. || 22 ||

Sāvitra is Hasta; Vedhā is Rohiṇī; Hari is Śravaṇa; Vāruṇa is Śatabhiṣak; Pauṣṇa is Revatī; Anūrādhā is well known; Uttarā refers to the three [asterisms]—Uttaraphalgunī, Uttarāṣāḍhā, and Uttaraproṣṭhapadā; Māruta is Svātī. These are they.

The ten lunar mansions belonging to Jupiter, the Moon, and Venus—namely Bṛhaspati, Candra, Budha, and Śukra—and the portions of their days (dināṃśaka), etc.; by the word "etc.," the decans (drekkāṇa), horās, and so forth are included. These are recommended and should be adopted for the rite of conception (garbhādhāna). Thus it is stated in the Vīratantra, in the chapter on conception:
Rohiṇī, Revatī, Hasta, Śravaṇa, Anurādhā, Svātī, Śatabhiṣaj, and the three Uttaras.
"O gentle one, the drekkāṇas, days, and degrees for Jupiter, Venus, and the Moon [are as follows]."

Since no specific rule for the zodiac signs (*rāśi*) is mentioned there, according to the maxim "what is not stated here should be taken from elsewhere," one should exclude Cancer (*karkaṭaka*), Gemini (*nṛyugma*), and Virgo (*abalā*)— as per the statement "leaving Cancer, Gemini, and Virgo"— and instead take the remaining nine signs. Likewise, among the lunar days (*tithi*), one should exclude the *riktās*.
Others are to be accepted; however, Nṛsiṃha states:
"The [lunar days] with defects are considered suitable for the Puṃsavana rite, excluding the ninth."
Thus he spoke. In that regard, the eightfold purity (aṣṭaśuddhi) must also be required.
As stated by Vasiṣṭha:
"All planets situated in the eighth house are undesirable; among them, both the auspicious and inauspicious [planets] are so."
Having thus examined [the matter] correctly, one should perform the puṃsavana rite. Thus it is said.
Now, he states the time for the *puṃsavana* rite— the root text says:
"When the embryo has become manifest, then in the third month..."
One should perform the *puṃsavana* rite for the deity Hari during the month of Puṣya;
it is auspicious when performed in the eighth [lunar day] of the bright fortnight, under the rising of Venus, Jupiter, or the Moon.

When the embryo has become manifest—that is, when it has become clearly visible—then, in the third month, one should perform the *puṃsavana* rite; one should carry it out. Regarding this, he states the asterisms: under Puṣya, Hari (Śravaṇa), and Śravaṇa. Furthermore, one should perform the *puṃsavana* when the eighth house is pure and during the rising of Venus, Mercury, and the Moon.
And so it is said in the Vīratantra:
"Now I shall explain the rite for ensuring a male child; listen to its true nature, O you whose wealth is asceticism."
At the end of two months, it should be performed, adorned with all ornaments.

A wise man should perform the *puṃsavana* rite under the asterisms of Puṣya or Śravaṇa, or indeed when there is the rising of Jupiter, Venus, Mercury, or the Moon. The planets praise the rising of the Moon, but it is not desired when [the Moon] is in the eighth house. Thus it is said.
[Objection: But surely, since the rising of the moon is prescribed for the *puṃsavana* rite, it would follow that the rite should be performed even at night;

therefore, how can this [prohibition] be said to contradict the practice of the astronomers? [Reply: True—it should indeed be performed at night by the force of the scripture (*āgama*) alone. For this very reason, later in that same section:
Having said, "Surely by which [path]," he should then show Arundhatī and Dhruva;
if these are not seen, O Brahmin, one should see gold together with silver.
And because it has been established in this way, it can indeed be performed even at night.
(127) "Wherever a contradiction is observed between what is stated in the *Jyotiṣa* and what is stated in the *Āgama*,
one should indeed set aside what is stated in the *Jyotiṣa* and practice what is stated in the *Āgama*.
Thus, there is scope for the statement of Bodhāyana.
Now he states the time for the parting of the hair (*sīmantonnayana*):
Root Text:
The piercing [of the fetus] from the asterism of Revatī (*pauṣṇa*)—namely Mṛgaśiras, Hasta, Śravaṇa (*viṣṇu*), and the three Uttaras—is auspicious.
Regarding the *sīmanta* ceremony for a Śaiva woman, it has been declared here by the noble ones to take place under these asterisms;

it should be performed in the fourth or sixth month on an auspicious lunar day, avoiding the signs of Leo and Scorpio, in a pure *lagna* conjoined with the eighth house, and with Jupiter in the eighth house, following the worship of Viṣṇu.

Regarding "piercing" (*vedha*): therein, he first states the asterisms for the *sīmanta* ceremony. Piercing: Rohiṇī; Pauṣṇa: Revatī; Aditi: Punarvasu; Mṛgaśiras; Hasta (well-known); Viṣṇu: Śravaṇa; the three Uttarās: Uttaraphalgunī, Uttarāṣāḍhā, and Uttaraproṣṭhapadā; Ārya: Puṣya—in these [asterisms].

Among the ten lunar mansions (*nakṣatras*), the rite known as *sīmanta* (the parting of the hair) has been declared—stated here—by the noble ones, namely the learned Śaiva teachers (*śaivācāryas*). Thus it is said in the *Vīratantra*:
"In Rohiṇī, in Puṣya, in the [three] Uttaras, and in Punarvasu..."
Likewise, under the asterisms of Hasta, Śravaṇa, Revatī, and Mṛgaśīrṣa.
"One should perform the Sīmantonnayana rite during an auspicious lunar division (aṃśa) and at a favorable astrological moment (lagna). Thus it is said.
(p. 128) Now he states the procedure for the month:
in the fourth, or the sixth month, on an auspicious lunar day—that is, a lunar day other than the *rikta*, the *pakṣacchidra*, and the new moon (*darśa*).
As it is said in the Vīratantra:
"And I shall now describe the parting of the hair (sīmanta); listen, O Lotus-seated One!
When four months have passed, one should perform it in the sixth month. Thus [it is said].
Now he states the rule for the ascendant (*lagna*): "Avoiding Leo and Scorpio"—Leo is well known, and *ali* is Scorpio;
[the ascendant should be] other than these two. "In conjunction with a pure eighth house"—meaning it must be endowed with the purity of the eighth house. As it is said in the *Vīra-tantra*:
"It should be in a sign excluding Leo and Scorpio, and the eighth house should be devoid of planets."
Now, he states the time for the Viṣṇubali as well in this very context: "The worship of Viṣṇu on the eighth [lunar day] in the month of Śrāvaṇa.
This means that in the eighth month, under the asterism of Śravaṇa, the rite named Viṣṇubali is to be performed;
the word "should be done" is understood from the context.
"And I shall describe the bali-offering to Viṣṇu; for one performs that during the Śroṇā [constellation]. Thus [it is said].

Now, since the birth-rite (*jātakarman*) must necessarily be performed at the very moment of birth, and because that specific time is difficult to determine, the author takes that time as a given and states the time for the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*). The root text says:

When a son is born, with a joyful mind, having quickly performed the birth-rite (*jātakarman*), one should have him invested with the sacred thread during the asterisms of Svāti, Śroṇa (Pūrvā-Phalgunī), Āditi (Uttarā-Phalgunī), Śatabhiṣaj, Saumya (Mṛgaśiras), Mūla, the two Uttarās (Uttarā-Phalgunī and Uttarā-Āṣāḍhā),
Ārya (Jyeṣṭhā), Pauṣṇa (Revatī), Ambuja (Śravaṇa), Bhava (Uttarā-Bhādrapadā), and Kara (Hasta)— these being the auspicious times.
Or else, the naming ceremony (nāmakaraṇa) should be performed according to the rules on the eleventh or twelfth day.

"Upon the birth"—that is, when a son is born, as soon as he is born—the father, with a delighted mind, his inner heart rippling with a spontaneous surge of joy, [performs] the *jātakarman* immediately at that very moment, because it effects the liberation of the ancestors from bondage and produces the sprout for the growth of the lineage; such is the meaning. "Quickly" means at that very instant.
The meaning is that immediately after performing that [rite], at the very next moment, due to the impurity of touch;
as it is said in the Vīratantra:
"I shall describe the procedure for the birth-rite (jātakarma), which is the means for accomplishing dharma, kāma, and artha."
