Then, one should show the newborn boy with the heart-mantra;
specifically, having cut the umbilical cord with the Astra-mantra itself, and so forth.
Now he states the asterisms for the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*): *Svātī* is well known; *Śroṇā* is *Śravaṇa*;
*Āditi* is *Punarvasu*; *Śatabhiṣak* is well known; *Saumya* is *Mṛgaśirā*; *Mūla* is well known;
and the three *Uttarās*—namely, *Uttaraphalgunī*, *Uttarāṣāḍhā*, and *Uttaraproṣṭhapadā*—are the *Ārya* [asterisms].

Puṣya, Pauṣṇa (Revatī), Ambujabhava (Śravaṇa), Rohiṇī, and Kara (Hasta)—in these thirteen lunar mansions, it is praiseworthy [to perform rites] according to the rules, accompanied by the practices prescribed in the Āgamas. One should indeed adopt and carry out what is taught in the Āgamas. As it is stated in the Vīra-tantra:
(130) I shall explain the naming ceremony; listen, O Lotus-seated One!
[The asterisms] Uttarā, Revatī, Hasta, Śatabhiṣaj, Mūla, and Puṣya—these are auspicious.
"Punarvasu, Śravaṇa, Svātī, Rohiṇī, and Mṛgaśīrṣaka—these constellations are indeed recommended for the naming ceremony. Thus it is said.
One should perform the naming ceremony for the son with reference to a deity;
first [the name] should be Mahādeva, and secondly Maheśvara.
The third is Śaṅkara, the fourth is Vṛṣabhadhvaja,
the fifth is Kṛttivāsas, and the sixth is indeed Kāmanāśana.
The Lord of the gods of gods is remembered as the seventh, Śrīkaṇṭha as the eighth;
Īśvara is declared the ninth, and the beloved of Pārvatī the tenth.
Rudra is indeed the eleventh, and Śiva is remembered as the twelfth;
a wise person [should know] those twelve names in the [asterisms] beginning with Kṛttikā.
One should recite the names of liberation ending with "Śiva" in the presence of the fire. Thus it is said.
In the Vīra-tantra:
"Having recited 'Svastimūrdhin' followed by a pair of syllables ending in 'Śiva',
it is remembered that [the mantra] is 'Śaṅkara' in Mārgaśīrṣa and 'Śambhu' in Puṣya."
In the month of Māgha he is named Maheśvara; in Phālguna, Mahādeva;
in Caitra, he is named Sthāṇu; and likewise in Vaiśākha, Śiva.
In Jyeṣṭha, he is named Paśupati; in Āṣāḍha, he is named Ugra;
in Śrāvaṇa, his name is Śarva; and in Bhādrapada, he is Triyambaka.
"In the month of Āśvina, one should recite the name 'Īśvara,' and in Kārtika, the name 'Rudra';
or else, one should recite the name of the Guru throughout all the months."
In the *Suprabheda*, a specific rule regarding the naming of girls is stated as follows:
"Having uttered the mantra of Śiva, [one should name] the girl according to the names of his powers (śaktis):
Ambikā, Pārvatī, Gaurī, and Bhavānī, who is worshipped by the gods."
Dākṣāyaṇī, Haimavatī, Mahādevī, Harapriyā, Umā,
and Śivakarī— these are the twelve forms of Girijā.
"One should apply that which is known as the 'power' (śakti) to the Kṛttikās and the other lunar mansions. Thus [it is said].

But surely, since in the *Aṃśumat*, the *Sūkṣmatantra*, and other texts, the months are proclaimed for all rites according to their gross and subtle divisions— beginning with Mārgaśīrṣa and beginning with Caitra— and since in the *Vīratantro* the naming of rites such as name-giving is specified as starting precisely from Mārgaśīrṣa, [how can it be otherwise] than what is stated in the *Suprabheda* regarding Kṛttikā and so forth?

If it is argued that the statement is contradictory, we say no; for in the expression "Kṛttikādi" (beginning with Kṛttikā), by means of an *atadguṇasaṃvijñāna* bahuvrīhi compound—meaning "those for which Kṛttikā is the first"—it is actually Mārgaśīrṣa itself that is indicated. Thus, there is no contradiction whatsoever.
Having thus explained the time for naming according to the lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) method, he states another alternative: "Or else (*athavā*)..."
One should perform the naming ceremony on the eleventh or twelfth day. Accordingly, it is stated in the *Suprabheda* (p.
132): "This rite of rising has been explained; now hear the instruction regarding the naming.
The instruction for the naming should be performed in sequence on the eleventh or twelfth day."
Having thus stated the time for the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*), he speaks of the time for the first outing (*upaniṣkrāmaṇa*). Root Text:
Aśvin, Śroṇa, Āditya, Vasu, Marut, Maitra, Citrā, Uttara, Indu—
The rite of the first exit from the womb should be performed during the asterisms of Rohiṇī,

Revatī, Hasta, Śravaṇa, and Uttarāṣāḍhā; in a pure month, at a proper time, on the tenth lunar day, in a favorable zodiacal sign, and during an auspicious muhūrta— thus is the auspicious ceremony for children prescribed according to rule.

Regarding the first lunar mansions for the rite of the horse's departure (*aśvīti-upaniṣkrāmaka-karman*), he says: *Aśvī* is well-known; *Śroṇā* is Śravaṇa; *Aditi* is Punarvasu; *Vasu* is Śraviṣṭhā; *Marut* is Svāti;
*Maitra* is Anurādhā; *Citrā* is well-known; *Uttarā* refers to the three *Uttarās*; and *Indu* is Mṛgaśiras.

In these sixteen lunar mansions— Brahmā (Rohiṇī), Pauṣṇa (Revatī), Savitṛ (Hasta), Varuṇa (Śatabhiṣaj), and Ārya (Puṣya)— the auspicious rite known as *niṣkramaṇa* (the first outing) for children is prescribed. Thus it is said in the Vīra-tantra:
Aśvinī, Mṛgaśiras, Revatī, Punarvasu,
Śravaṇa, Śraviṣṭhā, Hasta, Svātī, and Anurādhā.
"Citrā, as well as Uttarās, Śatabhiṣaj, Rohiṇī, and the lunar mansion Puṣya—these are praised for the purpose of departure. Thus it is said.
Now he states the procedure for the month: "In the fourth month"—that is, in the fourth month—it is stated in that very same place:
"I shall describe the procedure for the exit; it is performed in the fourth month."

Now he states the determination of the auspicious moment (muhūrta): "In an auspicious moment," meaning free from defects such as uneven planetary positions; "in a good lagna," meaning a lagna free from the transit or aspect of malefic planets; and "the tenth house" being perfectly pure.
This has also been stated in the Vīratantra:
"All planets situated in the tenth house are undesirable with great effort;
however, during an auspicious and propitious moment, one should perform the rite of offering oblations into the fire."
Now he states the time for the first feeding of solid food (annaprāśana): Root Text—
In the sixth month, during an auspicious moment (muhūrta).
One should perform the rite of first feeding (annaprāśana) for an infant under the asterisms of Śaśāṅka, Deverḍita, Vāruṇa, Aśvin, Prajeśa, and the pure tenth [asterism]. || 26 ||
Regarding the word "māsa" (month): therein, he first states the rule for the month—(p.
134)—"But in the sixth month, at the auspicious moment. Thus.
Thus it is stated in the *Suprabheda*:
"The rite of first feeding with solid food (*annaprāśana*) should be performed during the sixth month under an auspicious lunar mansion;
the child must not be touched while still having remnants of food on them, and it should be done at a favorable moment on an auspicious day."

Now he mentions the lunar mansions (nakṣatras): Śaśāṅka (Mṛgaśiras), Deva-ḍita (Puṣya), Vāruṇa (Śatabhiṣaj), Aśvī (Aśvinī), and Prajeśa (Rohiṇī). Under these five lunar mansions, one should perform for the child the rite known as *annaprāśana* (the first feeding with solid food).
And so it is said in the Vīra-tantra:
"When the sixth month has arrived, the first feeding of solid food (annaprāśana) should take place;
[under] Aśvinī, Mṛgaśiras, Śatabhiṣaj, and likewise Rohiṇī."
And the Puṣya constellation is indeed praised for the consumption of food. Thus it is said.
Now he states the point of purification: "When the tenth house is purified. This has been stated in that very same work:
"All planets situated in the tenth house are certainly undesirable with great effort."
Now, he states the time for the tonsure ceremony (caula):
Root-text—
In the third year, under the asterisms of Dhaniṣṭhā, Revatī, or Puṣya...
In Punarvasu, Saumya (Mṛgaśiras), Karā (Ārdrā), and Aśvinī; and in Meṣa (Aries).
In the eighth pure abode of Tvaṣṭṛ, one should perform the *sanāndīmukha* tonsure ceremony (*caulakarma*). (27)
Regarding "in the year"—therein he first states the rule for the year: "In the third year. This is stated in the Vīratantra:
"I shall describe the rite of the tonsure ceremony (caulakarma), which increases longevity and health."
"When the third year has arrived, conjoined with an auspicious lunar mansion," so it is said.
Likewise, in the *Suprabheda*: "In the third year, under an auspicious lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*), on a favorable lunar day (*tithi*), and during the northern course of the sun (*uttarāyaṇa*).
Now, he states the lunar mansions: [the asterisms] Vasu (Dhaniṣṭhā), Śraviṣṭhā, Pauṣṇa (Revatī), Puṣya, and Punarvasu are well-known.

One should perform the *caulakarma* (tonsure ceremony) under these nine asterisms: Saumya (Mṛgaśirā), Kara (Hasta), Aśvibha (Aśvinī), Tvāṣṭra (Citrā), and Hari (Śravaṇa). As it is stated in the *Vīratantra*:
"Citrā, Śraviṣṭhā, Hasta, Aśvinī, Revatī, and Śravaṇa are auspicious."
Puṣya, Punarvasu, and likewise Mṛgaśīrṣa;
"These indeed are declared to be the bestowers of auspiciousness. Thus [it is said].
Now he states the locus of purification: "When the eighth house is pure.
Thus it is said in the *Vīra-tantra*: "In the eighth [house], free from malefic planets.
(p. 136) Regarding the *nāndīmukha-caulakarma*: the *caulakarma* preceded by a *nāndīmukha-śrāddha*.
One should perform it; and that must be performed on the very day prior.
Thus it is stated in the *Suprabheda*:
"Having again performed the *nāndīmukha* rite on the day preceding that day..."
And likewise at the tonsure ceremony, the initiation ceremony, and the return home from studentship.
"And at their marriage ceremony, the Nāndīmukha rite is indeed prescribed for the ancestors. Thus it is said.
Now, he states the time for the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*): Root Text:
For the Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas, respectively, at the proper time beginning from the eighth month of pregnancy, during the [appropriate] season—

One should perform the initiation (upanayana) during the asterisms of Madhu (Punarvasu), Ādya (Puṣya), Vidhi (Rohiṇī), Maitra (Anurādhā), Vāyu (Svātī), Aditi (Uttarā Phalgunī), Bhava (Ārdrā), Tvāṣṭra (Chitrā), Indu (Mṛgaśiras), Sāvitra (Hasta), and the three northern asterisms; and when the Sun is in Taurus, Gemini, Virgo, Cancer, Sagittarius, or Pisces, provided there is purity from the eighth house and the age is sixteen years or more.

Regarding the term *vipra*, it refers to the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas; for them, the time is the eighth month from conception and so forth—the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes the eleventh and twelfth months from conception.
This is stated in the Vīratantra:
I shall now declare the Upanayana ceremony, which increases longevity and health:
for Brahmins it is in the eighth year from conception, and for Kshatriyas in the eleventh thereafter.
Regarding the twelve [years] for Vaiśyas, a specific rule is stated in the *Suprabheda* (p. 137):
"After birth, in the fifth, sixth, or seventh year..."
In the eighth or ninth year, the rite consisting of the nature of knowledge [should be performed].
It bestows spiritual luster, longevity, and especially confers prosperity. Thus it is said.
"And it should be performed according to the narrative in the Suprabheda during the spring and during the northern course of the sun. Thus [it is said].
Now he states the asterisms: Vidhi (the asterism of Prajāpati) is Rohiṇī; Maitra is Anurādhā; Vāyu is Svātī; Āditya-bha is Punarvasu; Svaṣṭra is Citrā; Indu is Mṛgaśiras; Sāvitra-bha is Hasta;
and the three Uttara asterisms are the three Uttarās. In these ten asterisms, one should perform the initiation ceremony (upanayana).
As it is stated in the Vīratantra: "Rohiṇī, Hasta, Citrā, the Uttarās, Anurādhā, Svātī, Mṛgaśiras, and Punarvasu are proclaimed [to be auspicious]."
Now he states the rule for the ascendant (lagna): Taurus (vṛṣa), Gemini (yuga), Virgo (kanyā), Cancer (kulīra), Sagittarius (dhanus), and Pisces (mīna)— in these six signs,
when they possess the purification of the eighth house (aṣṭamaśuddhi), the rite should be performed.
And so it has been said in the Vīra-tantra: "In Taurus, Gemini, Virgo, and Cancer,
as well as during the ascendants of Sagittarius and Pisces, [the rite] is auspicious when the Moon is in the eighth house and free from malefic planets."
(p. 138) Now, raising the doubt as to what should be done if, due to the force of fate or other causes, the [initiation] is not performed at the aforementioned times, he says:
"From the sixteenth year onwards"—this refers to the period up to sixteen years as the time for the *upanayana* of a Brāhmaṇa.
This too has been stated in the *Vīratantra*:
"And for Brahmins, it shall last until the sixteenth year from then. Thus [it is said].

By the mention of "Brāhmaṇas" here, the twenty-first and twenty-second year periods prescribed by Bodhāyana for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas are to be understood. An expiation is established for a Brāhmaṇa upon the passing of sixteen years [of age].
As stated in the *Suprabheda*:
"Alternatively, one should perform the initiation (*aupanāyana*) up until the sixteenth year;
but once the sixteenth year has passed, one should perform the *caulāla* rite."
Having eaten barley gruel for two months, one should drink milk for one month;
then, for half a month, one should consume blameless curdled milk (āmikṣā).
When curd is added to boiled milk, that is known as *āmikṣā*;
here, the ghee from a black or tawny cow is [to be kept] for eight nights.
In the Dvāpara Yuga, [the fast] consists of six nights of eating only what is unasked for, three nights of water, and likewise a fast of one day and night once that period has passed.
O Uddālaka, this one supreme rite must be performed;
O Vināyaka, it is like a bath at the conclusion of an Aśvamedha sacrifice, yet it is inverted for me.
One should perform the rites beginning with *garbhādhāna* (conception) in sequence as before; then, at the conclusion of the vow (*vṛtānta*), the [final] rite should be performed. Thus it is said.
Now, he states the time for marriage— the root verse:
All months except Māgha and Proṣṭhapada [are auspicious], as well as the month of Rohiṇī.
The asterisms of Revatī, the three Uttarās, Maghā, Mṛgaśīrṣa, Svātī, Anurādhā, Hastā, and Śatabhiṣaj;

the pure seventh house; and the signs Leo, Capricorn, Aquarius, Virgo, Libra, and Cancer—these, along with Sagittarius and the Jar (Aquarius), are declared by the wise to be auspicious for marriage when their faces are turned upwards. (29)
Regarding the month: first, he states the rule for the months—Māgha, Proṣṭhapada, and all others; that is, all months except Māgha and Bhādrapada are recommended for marriage.
Thus it is said in the Suprabheda:
A marriage may take place in any month, except for Māgha and Proṣṭhapada. Thus it is said.
Now he speaks of the lunar mansions (*nakṣatras*): Rohiṇī is well known; Pauṣṇa is Revatī;
the three *Uttaras*—namely Uttaraphalgunī, Uttarāṣāḍhā, and Uttaraproṣṭhapadā; Paitra is Maghā; Saumya is Mṛgaśiras; Pavana is Svātī; Anurādhā and Hasta are well known; and Asura is Mūla.
These eleven lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) are to be accepted for marriage.
As it is stated in the *Vīratantra*:
"Śvātī, Mūla, Anurādhā, Maghā, and likewise Mṛgaśiras..."
Revatī, Hasta, Rohiṇī, and the three Uttaras are auspicious. Thus it is said.
Now he states the place of purification: "In the pure seventh abode. This too is stated in the *Vīratantra*:

"In the seventh [house], free from planets. Now he states the rule for the ascendant (*lagna*): Leo is well known; Yama is Gemini; Go is Taurus; Virgo and Libra are well known; Karkaṭa is Cancer; Kodaṇḍa is Sagittarius; Ghaṭa is Aquarius.
These eight zodiac signs—Libra, Virgo, Aquarius, Sagittarius, Taurus, Cancer, and Leo—are auspicious for marriage when facing upwards, that is, with their mouths directed upward.
As it is stated in the *Kālavidhāna*:
"The signs of Libra, Virgo, Aquarius, Sagittarius, Taurus, Cancer, and Leo are excellent [for marriage]."

"In marriage, those in the middle [of the zodiac] joined with Saumya (Mercury) are all 'upward-faced' (*ūrdhvavadana*). Regarding the definition of "upward-faced": "That which begins from the sign occupied by the Sun is upward-faced. Thus it is said.
In this regard, since the zodiacal signs (*rāśi*) are not explicitly mentioned in the [Vedic] *Āgamas*, those described in *Jyotiṣa* alone have been adopted;

for there is no mutual contradiction between them, and because they are necessary, the scriptural maxim "that which is not stated here should be taken from elsewhere" dictates that they must be accepted. Furthermore, the absence of mutual contradiction has already been established in the introduction (*upodghāta*).
It has been established that this is indeed a fault, but not a fault of the scripture.
Now, he states the time for initiation (dīkṣā): [p. 141] Root Text—

Then, having recognized the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) through the signs obtained from the disciple, the Guru should perform the rite of initiation (*dīkṣāvidhi*) here in the prescribed locations— whether it be the highest or the middling— during the month of Magha,
Mārgaśīrṣa, Śrāvaṇa, Kārttika, Māgha, Pauṣa, or during the asterisms of Uttarāphālgunī, Uttarāṣāḍhā, Uttarābhādrapadā, or Uttarāproṣṭhapadā.
In the constellations of Diti, Ārdrā, and Mitra, and in fixed or dual signs, there is no [inauspicious] time for one desiring liberation. || 30 ||

Regarding the phrase "of the power" (*śakteḥ*): thus, the Guru, possessing the aforementioned characteristics, should offer the body, wealth, and life-force of the disciple who has arrived to the true Gurus. Having understood—by means of the signs of one who has arrived according to the sequence of the *Nyāya*, such as the symptoms of perspiration and so forth—the descent of power (*śaktipāta*), that is, the falling of power; for it has been said accordingly:
In the *Siddhāntaśekhara*:
"Thereafter, the characteristics of the various types of the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) will be explained;
when equilibrium between demerit and merit has arisen, that power descends."

When the supreme power (*parāśakti*), whose nature is knowledge, is bestowed upon someone by Śambhu, initiation (*dīkṣā*) is performed for that person alone; he is liberated, of this there is no doubt. I shall now describe the characteristics of falling [into grace] for embodied beings according to their degrees of excellence.
Then there is the falling of the body, trembling, and the thrill of supreme bliss.
"Sweating and horripilation—these are the signs of the descent of power. Thus [it is said].
Furthermore, its fourfold division—based on the distinctions of *tīvratara* (most intense), *manda* (mild), and *mandatara* (very mild)—is set forth in the Āgamas.
The syntactical connection is: "therefore, one should perform initiation (*dīkṣā*). In that regard, he first states the specific location:
"in the prescribed fields" (*proktakṣetreṣu*), meaning in those fields mentioned in the Āgamas and by the teachers (*ācāryas*). Likewise...
In Cintyaviśva, Mahendra, Malaya, Sahya, Pāriyātra, Himālaya,
Vindhya, Mandara, Śrīgiri, and Himaparvata;
On the banks of the Gaṅgā and the Kālindī, on the Narmadā and the Tuṅgabhadrā,
on the Sarasvatī and the Bhīmarathī, and on the banks of the Kāverī and the Kanyakā;
Or likewise in meritorious fields and regions such as Vārāṇasī,
or on the pure bank of a great river flowing to the sea, or at a large lake.
Either in a beautiful flower garden, or near a milk-exuding tree,
or in a palace, or in a monastery, or in the house of one learned in the Vedas.
"In a pure, delightful place, with a level surface abounding in soft earth. Thus it is said.
And so it has been said by the former masters: "In gardens, in temples of Śiva, on the banks of rivers, in lotus-pools, in Kāñcī, in Vyāghrapura, near the ocean, at Jalpeśvara, and on the mountain."
The excellent Guru should likewise perform initiation at Gokarṇa, in the house of his preceptor, in his own home, at the venerable Kālahastīśvara, at Śaktinipātana, and at Sthaleśa.
(p. 143) Now he states the rule for the months:
"In the best or the middling month. This rule regarding the months is stated by way of prohibition in the *Kāraṇa*:
"In Pūrvabhādrapada, Māgha, Āṣāḍha, and Mārgaśīrṣa..."
"The wise one should not perform initiation; he should not perform it in other months. Thus [it is said].
In the *Siddhāntaśekhara*:
"Initiation in the autumn season and in Vaiśākha bestows the most excellent fruit;
initiation in Phālguna, Mārgaśīrṣa, and Jyeṣṭha is middling."
"In the months of Āṣāḍha and Māgha, Kaniṣṭhā is proclaimed;
she is censured in Śrāvaṇa, Caitra, Puṣya, and likewise in Bhādrapada. Thus it is said.
In the *Lakṣmaṇīyapaddhati*:
"Initiation is declared auspicious even during censured months, during eclipses,
at the equinoxes, at the two solstices, and during the festival of *damanaka* in the month of Āṣāḍha."
During the rites of initiation, at the proper times, on the *pavitra* festival,
during the bright fortnight, or even in the dark fortnight up to the fifth day, the initiation is auspicious.
The fourth, ninth, eighth, and likewise the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight are inauspicious lunar days;
the remaining ones are excellent, as are the days of Venus and Jupiter.
"The days of the week grant auspicious results when they are in conjunction with auspicious yogas; otherwise, they are inauspicious. Thus it is said.
144) In the *Vīratantra*: "The second, or even the fifth, and especially the sixth;
or the twelfth should be observed, or it may be the thirteenth."
"These lunar days have indeed been declared; now hear also of the weekdays:
Monday, Friday, Wednesday, and Thursday are considered the most excellent of days."

Now he mentions the lunar mansions (nakṣatras): Vedhāḥ is Rohiṇī; Maghā is well known; Indu is Mṛgaśiras; Śravaṇa is well known; the Uttarās are the three—Uttara-phalgunī, Uttara-āṣāḍhā, and Uttara-proṣṭhapadā; Ārya is Puṣya; and Āditya is [Punarvasu].
Punarvasu, Ārdrā (well-known), Mitra (Anurādhā)—in these fifteen lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*s), one should perform the initiation (*dīkṣā*). Thus it is stated in the *Kāraṇa*:
"Pūṣan (Puṣya), Rohiṇī, then Āditya (Pūrvaphalgunī), Śravaṇa, Aśvinī, and Maghā."
The Sāvitra, the Tvaṣṭra, the Vāyavya, the Nairṛta, and the Mitra [mantras].
"The wise have declared the constellations Tiṣya, the three Uttarās, and Ārdrā to be auspicious for the rite of initiation, as they are the birth-stars of the three disciples."
In the Siddhāntaśekhara:
Rohiṇī, Mṛgaśīrṣa, Maghā, Puṣya, Punarvasu,
Hasta, Svātī, Anurādhā, Śravaṇa, and likewise Revatī.
The three Uttaras, Mūla, and the fourteen asterisms—these are auspicious for initiation; when joined with an auspicious yoga, they bring supreme benefit.
In the *Vīratantra* it is said: "Rohiṇī, Śravaṇa, Ārdrā, Śraviṣṭhā, the three *Uttarās*,
Puṣya, and Śatabhiṣaj are declared to be the lunar mansions for initiation (*dīkṣā*)."
In the Siddhāntaśekhara, the yogas are stated as follows:
"There are eighteen excellent yogas, which bestow auspicious results according to their own names."
Now he states the rule for the ascendant (*lagna*): "In a house joined with a fixed sign" means in a fixed (*sthira*) sign and in a dual (*ubhaya*) sign.
As it is said in the *Vīratantra*:
"Either Taurus, or Leo, Scorpio, or Aquarius."
Or a Gemini, or a Virgo, or a Sagittarius, or indeed a Pisces.
And these zodiacal signs have been declared; one should avoid those that are movable signs. Thus it is said.
And regarding the cause:
"The movable signs are best when stable, while those of a dual nature are middling;
furthermore, all planets are to be avoided when situated in the eighth house (Naidhana) from a movable sign. Thus it is said.
In this matter, the mutual compatibility between the teacher and the disciple must also be taken into account. As it is stated in the *Lakṣmaṇīya*:
"The mutual compatibility of the teacher and the disciple shall bring about auspiciousness."
In the *Siddhāntaśekhara*, it is established that when Venus and Jupiter are situated in a quadrant (*kendrastha*) and are strong, they act as removers of all defects. As it says (p.
146): "When Venus is mature and situated in the ascendant, or when Jupiter is situated in a quadrant..."
"All defects become auspicious; thus it has been declared by Śambhu. So it is said.

Thus, the rule for examining specific times applies only to one who desires enjoyment (vibhukṣu). But for one who desires liberation (mumukṣu), there is no restriction of time; so it is said: "There is no such thing as 'the wrong time' for one who seeks liberation."
And so it has been said in the Siddhāntaśekhara: "Having mastered the astronomical treatises— including the Karaṇas, the ascendants, and the strength of planetary conjunctions—
one should bestow initiation upon those who desire worldly enjoyment."
"For one who desires liberation, initiation is always [possible]; there is indeed no restriction regarding time and so forth."

The various types of initiation (*dīkṣā*) have been thoroughly explained by us in the *Dīkṣāmaṇḍalapaddhati* according to the requirements of their respective qualified recipients. Now, having thus described the occasional (*naimittika*) portion,
he describes the optional (*kāmya*) portion, first stating the time for the festival (*utsava*).

If it is asked: "Since the threefold division of festivals—into the obligatory (*nitya*), the occasional (*naimittika*), and the optional (*kāmya*)—has been established by the root scriptures (*mūlāgama*) and the authors of ritual manuals (*paddhati*), how is it appropriate to provide an analysis specifically for the optional portion?"—it is replied: because the determination of the obligatory and occasional festivals is already accomplished simply by the determination of their respective times.
Since only the optional festival (*kāmyotsava*) is the subject of this investigation, it is appropriate to analyze it right here.
Thus it has been stated in the *Yogaja*:
"The festival is traditionally remembered as being of three kinds: obligatory (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), and optional (*kāmya*)."
One should perform the daily rites constantly, and especially the occasional rites with particular care.
It is said: "According to one's desire, it is called 'kāmya'; thus the festival (utsava) may be of three kinds. (p. 147)
Since the prescription for the festival is preceded by the determination of the sacred site (*tīrtha*), he first states that [determination],
as it has been said in the *Kāmika*:
"Having first determined the sacred site, [the festival should be performed] either on the day preceding it or even three days before."
Or one should begin the hoisting of the flag on that very day, or on the second day. Thus it is said.
Root Text:

If two tithis occur on one day, and the latter is endowed with a good yoga while the former is not, then this very [latter] day is superior when both days have arrived. However, that which occurs on the additional day is indeed superior.

In the case of equality, first [the lunar day] in the ocean (the month of Āṣāḍha), and elsewhere the lunar mansion; thus the Guru, having distinguished the month, the lunar mansion, and so forth, should perform that ninefold festival of Maheśa. || 31 ||

"But not in one month"—that is to say, when two *tīrtha* asterisms occur within the same month, upon the arrival of those two *tīrtha* asterisms, the final one—the last asterism—is to be taken as the *tīrtha* asterism; this is the remainder [of the sense]. This applies provided the former [asterism] is conjoined with the moon, except in the case of a solar transit (*saṅkrānti*) or an eclipse.
If a meritorious time (*puṇyakāla*) and so forth is conjoined with an astrological yoga (*yoga*), then the former must be adopted. As it is stated in the *Kāmika*:
"When two auspicious asterisms (*tīrtha-ṛkṣa*) coincide in a single month, the latter is superior;
yet even in that case, if it is conjoined with a yoga, the former alone should be adopted."
In the *Svāyambhuva*:
"When two lunar mansions associated with a sacred site (*tīrtha*) coincide within a single month,
the latter should be adopted after discarding the former, provided the former is joined with a [planetary] conjunction (*yoga*)."
In that regard, a sacred site (tīrtha) should be established.
Likewise, in the *Jyotiṣa*:
"The asterisms passed through by the natal asterism and the asterism of the sacred site..."

If they arise again within a single month, then indeed there would be a defilement of the sacred ford (*tīrtha-bhaṃ*) in those very rebirths, provided it occurs in the same manner, excluding the transitions of the sun and moon and eclipses.
The sense is that both the transit (*saṅkrānti*) and the eclipse (*uparāga*) are each occasions for occasional festivals (*naimittikotsava*).

Even if there is a coincidence of both due to their inevitability, the necessity of performing them at that time has already been established in the context of the monthly worship (*māsapūjā*). When a holy asterism (*tīrtharkṣa*) occurs during the junction of two days, whatever is additional on that very day—that alone [is to be observed].
It should be grasped. When there is equality [of time], it should be grasped at the earlier [time]. As it is stated in the *Kāmika*:

"Whether in the forenoon or in the afternoon, when endowed with the lunar day (*tithi*) and the asterism (*ṛkṣa*), the rite should be performed at the sea or at a river and so forth; however, midday is best."
"If a lunar mansion or a lunar day exceeds its duration during the day, it should be included;
likewise when a constellation or a lunar day extends across two days, provided that a conjunction occurs. Thus it is said.
And in the *Svāyambhuva*:

"In the same way, when a lunar mansion associated with a sacred site (*tīrtha*) occurs on two days, it should be performed during the day if it is superior; provided, however, that it is joined with a festival (*parvan*)."
That very Balatīrtha is most excellent when visited at midday;
if visited in the forenoon it is middling, but if visited in the afternoon it is inferior.
When a conjunction with a lunar holiday occurs during any of the three periods of the day,
that asterism which pervades the time of sunrise is to be accepted for the fast.
"In all vows and at sacred fords (tīrtha), that which extends through midday is praised. Thus it is said.
And in the *Jyotiṣa*:

"When two lunar days are divided within a single asterism, on whichever day the daytime portion is greater, one should perform the festival at the sacred ford (*tīrtha*); if they are equal, the former [day] is superior."

Now, regarding the subject of the ocean-tirthas, he states that the lunar day (tithi) alone must be accepted as primary: "Now, at the ocean—the lunar day. Therefore, elsewhere than this ocean—in rivers, lakes, and so forth—only the asterism (ṛkṣa), i.e., the lunar mansion (nakṣatra), must be accepted as primary. Thus it is stated in the Kāmika:
"The Sāmudrika [system] has the lunar day (tithi) as its primary factor, while another has the asterism (ṛkṣa) as its primary factor;
that which is joined by the conjunction of both the lunar day and the asterism is said to be difficult to find. Thus it is said.

In this manner, the Guru, having analyzed and determined the lunar month, asterism, and so forth, as well as the asterisms of the sacred sites (*tīrtha*), sets forth the months and asterisms as propounded in the *Candrajñāna*: "Citrā, Viśākhā, Mūla, and Uttarāṣāḍhā likewise... (p. 150).
"Śraviṣṭhā, Proṣṭhapadā, Āśvinī, Kṛttikā, Ārdrā, Punarvasu, Maghā, and the Uttarā nakṣatras—these are [the lords] of the twelve signs beginning with Aries. Thus it is said.

By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "the lunar mansion of the month and so forth," the *ārdrā* constellation, which is the *pratiṣṭhā* (installation) asterism for each respective month, and others are to be understood.
Thus it is said in the *Candrajñāna*: "It should be performed in all months, or else specifically until the *ārdrā* star."
In the Bhīmasaṃhitā:
"Beginning every month under that same lunar mansion (nakṣatra) until the conclusion of the festival—this indeed is the festival of installation;
therefore, one should perform it annually."
The lunar mansion (nakṣatra) of the sacrificer, as well as that of the village and so forth,
the nakṣatra for the installation of the Liṅga, and likewise the two [other] grounds.
One should perform the rite at a sacred ford (tīrtha) on the end of the new moon, or in all months;
whether it coincides with a subtle lunar festival (parvan) or not, the lunar mansion (nakṣatra) of the month is the primary factor.
"On the fourteenth day, on the new moon, and especially on the sixth and eighth days. Thus it is said.
In the *Candrajñāna*:
"The month of Jyeṣṭha should end on the eighth day of the dark fortnight; in Gādhi, it should end on the sixth day;
or on the new moon, the full moon, or on other auspicious days."

"On the birthday of kings, in battle, at the birth of one performing a sacrifice, or on the day of consecration and the like—a sacred ford (tīrtha) is ordained that bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation. (p. 151)
In the Kāmika:
"The birth-star and the death-star of kings, or indeed their consecration-star;
in the month of Māgha, [the rites should be performed] ending on the sixth lunar day, or at the end of a festival (parvan) in every month."

"The period ending with the equinoxes and solstices, as well as the time up to an eclipse, is the auspicious time for pilgrimage; for others, it lasts until the fourteenth day (bhūta) or the eighth day (aṣṭamī), or until the conclusion of their respective lunar days. Thus it is said.
Furthermore, regarding that very matter of festivals, a specific rule is stated: "In whichever month and under whichever asterism a pilgrimage was previously performed,
one should perform it again in that same month and under that same asterism."
Having thus determined the auspicious lunar mansion (tīrthanakṣatra), one should perform the ninefold festival of Maheśa.
And so it is said in the Sūkṣma-tantra:
"The Śaiva, the Gauṇa, the Bhautika, the Bhaumana, and likewise the Daivika..."
That which pertains to the ancestors, that which pertains to youth, that which pertains to Savitṛ, and likewise that which pertains to the moon.
It is said that the Śaiva [initiation] lasts for one day; likewise, the Gauṇa is said to last for three days.
The Bhautika is declared to last for five days, and the Bhauvana is remembered as lasting for seven days.
Nine days are declared for the gods; eleven days are remembered for the ancestors;
thirteen days for the youth (Kumāra), and likewise a fortnight for Sāvitra.
The lunar [initiation] lasts seventeen days; thereafter, the Śaiva, Gauṇa, and Bhautika are called the triad of inferior [initiations] in successive order.
The Bhauvana, Daivika, and Paitṛka constitute the middle triad;
the Kaumāra, Sāvitra, and Cāndra constitute the highest triad.
Thus, O wise one, the ninefold festival has been proclaimed in sequence.
I shall now describe their order; listen to it, O Prabhāñjana.
Prosperity, victory, and happiness—these three types of results are traditionally taught for the Ekāha sacrifice;
one should commence it in the evening, joined with the first part of the night.
At the time of dawn, there should be a sacred bathing place (tīrtha), and on that single day, two offerings (bali) should be made.
Thus, it is declared to be a source of prosperity; now, listen to the account of victory (vijaya).
Then, on that day, one should hold a festival during the night;
having performed a single bali offering, one should perform the rites at the sacred ford (tīrtha) at dawn.
Thus indeed has Vijaya been described; now hear about Saukhya.
On that day, whether in the forenoon, at midday, or in the afternoon—
Having undertaken a single vehicle, one should perform the ritual at the sacred ford at the end;
it may last for one day, beginning with the rite of prosperity—listen further to this triad, O observer of noble vows.
One should begin on the afternoon preceding the appointed day;
one should perform the festival for three days, with offerings (bali) in the number of owls (kauśika).
When the fourth day has arrived, at dawn one should perform the ritual at the sacred ford (tīrtha).
On that same day, the wise practitioner should perform the weapon-sacrifice (astrayāga) in the evening.
Having commenced the festival, one should perform the rites at the sacred ford on the third day, following the four offerings of bali-oblations.
At the conclusion of the daily worship, however, perform a festival for three days;
and during those three days, at the end of each day's procession, one should engage in water sports.
Thus the three-day period has been described; now hear about the five-day period, which begins at evening on the day preceding that [first day].
One should especially construct a vehicle and perform the bali offering ten times;
on the morning of the sixth day, the preceptor should perform the rite at the sacred ford (tīrtha).
On the day specified, one should begin in the evening;
one should offer oblations eight times, and after five days, one should perform the pilgrimage.
This is called the "inferior" [observance]; now hear about the "middling" one:
one should begin it on the night preceding the day specified.
One should perform the *homa* that night and offer the *bali* fourteen times;
on the eighth day, one should perform the powder festival (*cūrṇotsava*), the *kautuka*, and the pilgrimage (*tīrtha*).
On the night of the designated day, one should perform the festival;
the wise person should have the fire-oblation (homa), the offering (bali), and the procession (yāna) conducted during that night.
One should perform the *bali* offering twelve times and observe the sacred ford (*tīrtha*) for seven days;
it should be performed on the specified day during either the forenoon or the afternoon.
One should perform only circumambulation, and at the end, one should visit a sacred site (tīrtha);
this is known as the *bhauvana* [type]. Now hear about the *daivika* [type] from me.
One should begin in the evening prior to the designated day;
one should offer the *smṛtisaṅkhyā* oblation and perform the rite at the sacred ford on the tenth day.
Now listen to what is known as the *daivika* [rite], and after that, the *paitṛka*.
On the day preceding that [main] day, one should perform the *astrayāga*.
One should perform twenty-two offerings at the sacred ford on the twelfth day; it is renowned as "Viddhida" (the Piercer). Now hear about Vijaya.
On the evening of the day specified, one should commence the festival;
on the day of Rudra (the eleventh lunar day), one should perform the tying of the auspicious thread, the ritual bath, and offer the twentyfold oblation.
Simply perform a festival by means of the vehicle-path previously described;
finally, one should practice at the sacred site (tīrtha) renowned as Brāhmika.
The triad of middling [levels] has been declared; now hear the triad of superior [levels].
On the day prior to that, the wise one should perform the weapon-sacrifice (astrayāga).
On the fourteenth day, there should be a sacred bathing (tīrtha), and one should perform the bali offering twenty-six times.
This is indeed declared to bestow prosperity; now listen, O observer of noble vows, to [the rite of] victory.
On that day, there shall be the weapon-sacrifice (*astrayāga*), and one should offer twenty-four oblations (*bali*).

On the thirteenth day, there shall be the pilgrimage site (*tīrtha*), which is proclaimed as "Victory" (*vijaya*). One should perform a simple circumambulation, and at the conclusion, one should perform the rite of the pilgrimage site.
Now listen to that which is renowned as Kaumāra, and after that, the Sāvitra.
Starting from that previous night, one should then perform thirty offerings;
on the sixteenth day, the ritual at the sacred ford (tīrtha) must especially be performed.
On that day, there shall be the weapon-sacrifice (astrayāga), and one should offer twenty-eight bali-offerings.
On the fifteenth day of the fortnight, O Prabhajana, there is the auspicious bathing ceremony for Vijaya.
At the conclusion of the daily worship, one should perform a single ritual procession;
at the end of that, however, the rite pertaining to the sacred ford (tīrtha) is proclaimed as the "Brāhmika" rite.
O Prabhajana, listen to the renowned Sāvitra rite and the Cāndra rite;
on the day preceding that, the wise one should perform the weapon-sacrifice (astrayāga).
One should offer thirty-four oblations at the sacred ford on the eighteenth day; this is declared to bestow prosperity. Now, listen to that which brings victory.
On the evening of that day, one should perform the festival;
and on the seventh day, the offering of thirty-two *bali*s and the pilgrimage to the sacred site (*tīrtha*) should be performed.

"Having attained the single vehicle, one should finally perform the rite of crossing over (tīrtha). This is called the 'Festival of Brahman' (brahmotsava); listen, O observer of good vows, to its beginning and end. Thus it is said.

Thus, by way of the divisions of *uttama* and so forth, there are three types; and likewise, each of those being again threefold, there are nine types of festivals (*utsava*)—namely, the Śaiva and the others.
Since the Śaiva is threefold and the others are each twofold, twenty-one varieties are thus established.

Furthermore, the ninefold nature of the constituent elements of the festival (*utsavāṅga*) through their threefold division, as well as their threefold nature according to the sequence of the banner (*dhvaja*), the drum (*bherī*), and the sprout (*aṅkura*), is established in that very same [text]. As it says:
"The procession (*yāna*), the ritual bath (*avabhṛta*), and the mounting (*āroha*) are recorded as the three types of constituent elements of the festival."
Each one is said to be threefold: beginning, middle, and end.
The festival is said to be threefold, beginning with the flag, the drum, and the ritual sowing of seeds.
First, one should hoist the flag; afterwards, one should beat the drum.
Thereafter, one should offer the sprouts following the hoisting of the banner;
first one should strike the drum, and then one should raise the banner.
One should subsequently offer the sprouts preceded by the beating of the drum;
alternatively, one may offer the sprouts first, and thereafter the sounding of the drum.
The hoisting of the banner is preceded by the offering of the ritual sprouts (aṅkura);
however, in the first three [consecrations], the act of hoisting the flagstaff (dhvaja) does not take place.
One should begin the hoisting of the banner during either the period of the Bhauvana or the Daivika;
it may be done after nine days, or after three periods of nine days, or even after three periods of seven days. Thus it is said.
In the *Kāmika*:
"The festival is considered to be threefold when preceded by the hoisting of the banner;
it is considered twofold on that day if preceded by the beating of the drum."
On that day, the wise one should first perform the rite of planting the sprouts. Thus it is said.
And the sequence of subsidiary ritual actions (*upāṅgakriyākrama*) regarding the subtle [level] has been stated as follows:
first is the sprout of the banner (*ketvaṅkura*), second is the sacrifice to the bull (*vṛṣayāga*),
the third should be the circumambulation (*pradakṣiṇa*), and the fourth is the purification of the staff (*daṇḍaśodhana*).
The fifth is called the rite of the banner; the sixth is the bathing with the water-pot;
the seventh is the worship of the staff, and the eighth is the worship of the weapon.
The ninth is the Bheri sacrifice, and the tenth is called the Devatāhvaya;
the eleventh is the daily worship, and the twelfth is the distribution of the bali offering.
The thirteenth is the purification of the site (vāstuśuddhi), followed by the sprouting for the festival (utsavāṅkura);
then the binding of protection (rakṣābandha) is proclaimed, and the sixteenth is the ritual of sacrifice (yāgakarma).
Know that the seventeenth is the *huta*; after this follows the sequence of the *bali*.
The nineteenth is the vehicle (*yāna*), and beyond that is the server (*pariveṣaka*).
The Nīrājana rite is performed twenty-one times, followed by the viewing of the dance;
thereafter comes the ceremonial bath for the festival procession, and finally, the supreme special sacrifice.
The sprout of the sacred site (*tīrthāṅkura*), the wonder of the twenty-fifth and twenty-sixth sacred sites,
the consecration of the sacred site (*tīrthādhivāsana*), and thereafter the ritual of the sacred site (*tīrthakarma*).
The twenty-ninth is the avabhṛtha bath, then the thirtieth is the pūrṇāhuti;
the thirty-first is the consecration with the sacrificial jar, and the supreme thirty-second is the final ablution.
There is also the worship with the great oblation and other offerings, as well as the giving of sacrificial fees;
after lowering the banner, the supreme bali-offering known as the Paiśāca follows.
Thus, the festival is proclaimed to consist of thirty-six parts;
the wise man should worship Vighneśa at every single ritual action. So it is said.

Thus, from among the many kinds of festivals accompanied by their constituent parts, one should perform whichever festival is appropriate according to the requirements of place, time, and materials. This is the summary.
Now, he states the time for the ritual bathing (snāna): Root Text:
On the fifth lunar day, on the ninth lunar day, on the day of Śiva (the fourteenth), on the two festival days (parvan), and during the transit of the sun (saṅkrānti)—
During solar and lunar eclipses, at the solstices (ayana), and at the equinoxes (viṣuva), the fruit [of the rite] increases in proportion to the number of jars used.

During the ceremonies for initiation (dīkṣā), consecration (sthāpana), festive sacrifices (adhvara), sprinkling (samprokṣaṇa), and for averting portents (utpāta)— as well as on one's birth star (janmanakṣatra) and during rites for human attainment (sādhana) and the like— one should bathe Śaṅkara with jars.
"Regarding 'on the fifth': this refers to the auspicious time on the fourteenth, fifth, ninth, and fourteenth days of both fortnights; on the two parvan days—the full moon and the new moon;
at the transits—during the transits of the sun into Aries and other signs; during solar and lunar eclipses—the occultations of the moon and the sun; and at the solstices."
During the transits of Cancer and Capricorn, as well as the equinoxes of Aries and Libra—at these times—one should bathe Śakra with jars, that is, with water-pots numbering five, nine, and so forth.
The fruit of this, however, occurs through an increase in sequence—namely, an increase by ten. Furthermore, he states a specific time:
Initiation (dīkṣā), specific observances (samaya), [the rites of] Nirvāṇa and so forth; installation (sthāpana)—such as the installation of the Śiva-liṅga and other icons;

festivals (utsava)—the ninefold festivals of the Śaivas and others; the rules for sacrifices (adhvara-vidhi)—such as the Agniṣṭoma and others; consecration by sprinkling (samprokṣaṇa)—such as the Āvartana and Āvarta rites; portents (utpāta)—such as excessive rain, drought, earthquakes, and so forth; and the birth-star (janmarkṣa).

The birth asterism of the patron (*yajamāna*), the means for human accomplishment such as the preliminary recitation (*puraścaraṇa*) of mantras, and so forth— the word "and so forth" including the auspicious rites for the consecration of a king and the like— at these times one should bathe Śaṅkara.
This is stated in the *Suprabheda*:

On the fifth, the ninth, and the fourteenth days, on the two lunar festival days (parvan), at the sun's passage into a new sign (saṅkrānti), at the equinoxes (viṣuva), at the solstices (ayana), and likewise during an eclipse;
From the fifth day up to the end of an eclipse, the fruit increases tenfold;
likewise at the conclusion of initiation, the conclusion of consecration, during sprinkling, and at the end of a festival.
At the conclusion of the sacrifice, under an auspicious asterism such as Kṛttikā and the like, the rite of illumination should be performed;
it should be done under one's birth asterism during an auspicious time for the accomplishment of mantras.
At the time of a king's consecration, at the end of life, or at birth;
during excessive rain, drought, famine, or when there are ill omens.
"When there is an earthquake, the burning of the quarters, affliction by fever, Āryās, and the like;
when all diseases have arisen, and even during affliction by enemies—at such times for expiation and other rites, the Guru should perform the ritual bathing of Śiva. Thus it is said.

In the Bhīmasaṃhitā it is said: "During the solstices, the equinoxes, the eclipses of the moon and sun, at the beginning of the Ṣaḍaśīti period, at every transit of the sun, and at the conclusion of festivals."
During the Ajita-pavitra and other rites, during the consecration (pratiṣṭhā), during the rising of the Kṛttikās and so forth,
at the time of offering the nine-fold food-offering (naivedya), and likewise after the bathing with clarified butter (ghṛtasnāna).
"In all expiations, as well as in the rite for the restoration of what has become worn out," so it is said.
Likewise, in the Siddhāntaśekhara: "I shall declare the procedure for the ritual bathing as taught in the Śiva-siddhānta;
it is declared to be threefold, and each of those is again threefold."
Subtracted by five and nine, there are twenty-five *kumbhakas*;
likewise, fifty minus one and eighty-one constitute a *ghaṭa*.
One hundred and eight is excellent; two hundred and sixteen is also praised;
for the sake of the goal of one thousand and eight, nine thousand is declared.

p. 161) These three are considered, in order, to be the obligatory (nitya), the occasional (naimittika), and the optional (kāmya) [rites], [to be performed] on the eighth, the fourteenth, the fifth, and on Monday.
On the new moon day and the full moon day, at the sun’s passage into a new zodiac sign and likewise during eclipses;
on all auspicious occasions, and during the Pavitra and Damanaka festivals.
On the fourth day of the consecration, when the month is complete and a year has passed,
on the birth-star of the patron king, or during the exertion for battle when victory is at hand.
At the time of the coronation ceremony, during initiation, or at an ablution;
in times of drought, fever, or when afflicted by malevolent planets.
In rites of atonement, as well as in portents, in offerings such as the *ghṛtakambala*,
in all propitiatory ceremonies, in auspicious rites, and in the practice of mantras.
At such times as these, the wise man should perform the ceremonial bathing. Thus it is said.
The specific procedure for the rite of bathing has been correctly set forth by us in the *Snānapaddhati*; it should be understood from that very source.
Now, he states the time for the ritual of the cold-water jar (śītakumbha): Root Text:
In times of famine, during ill omens, when there is fear arising from fever or the mouth [of disease], and when the plague (mārikā) has broken out—

During an earthquake, when the quarters of the sky appear to be ablaze, or for the purpose of a rite for victory, or due to the influence of the year, in the months of Māgha, Caitra, or Vaiśākha; when the birth asterism of the king coincides with the month's asterism; on the new moon day, the fifth lunar day, and so forth; and on Sundays, Wednesdays, or Thursdays—one should perform the ritual of the Cold Jar (śitakumbha). (33)

Regarding "in times of famine": during a famine, such as a period of scarcity and the like; in times of ill omens, such as the sight of birds and other portents that are causes of suffering; in fear arising from fever and so forth—by the word "and so forth," epilepsy, smallpox, and the like are included; and when pestilence has broken out, namely the emergence of the disease known as the Great Plague (mahāmārī).

The phrase "in earthquakes, the burning of the quarters, and so forth" implies [occurrence during] portents (*utpāta*). Regarding the rite for victory—concerning the defeat of enemies—for the sake of rain, one should perform the *śītakumbha* rite at these times. Thus it is stated in the *Sūkṣma*:
I shall describe the ritual of the cold-water jar; listen to it, O Prabhajana!
It is for the sake of rain, for victory, and especially for the destruction of fever.
During a famine, at an ill omen, when a great pestilence breaks out,
during an earthquake, when the quarters of the sky are ablaze, or when a mock sun is seen;
During such times as these, one should perform the cold-water rite (śītakumbha). Thus it is said.
Regarding that which is born of yoga:
now I shall describe specifically the sequence of the ritual for the cold-water jar (*śītakumbha*),
for the destruction of fever and epilepsy, and for the removal of heat and burning sensations during the eighth and twelfth lunar days.
One should prepare it for the purpose of destroying all diseases and for the sake of rain. Thus it is said.

Ajita, I shall describe the ritual for the Cold Jar (śītakumbha); listen, O destroyer of the enemies of the gods! It is the means for the destruction of wonders occurring in the heavens, the atmosphere, and on earth.
It pacifies pestilence and fever, and is supreme for removing drought, and so forth.

Now he states the rule for the months: "In the month of Tapasya (Phālguna), Caitra, and Vaiśākha, there is the birth of kings; [this occurs] in the month of the king's birth-nakṣatra, or in the month-nakṣatra beginning with Citrā."

Now he states the rule for the lunar days (*tithi*): on the new moon (*darśa*), the fifth day (*pañcamī*), and so forth—the word "and so forth" including the fourteenth day (*caturdaśī*). Then he states the days of the week (*vāra*): one should perform the *śītakumbha* rite on the days of the Moon, Venus, and Jupiter—that is, on Monday, Friday, and Thursday. Thus it is said in the *Sūkṣma*:
Especially in the month of Caitra, Vaiśākha, or Phālguna,
or again on the birth asterism of kings, or on the asterism of their [current] month.
One should perform it specifically on the fourteenth day, the new moon day, or the fifth;
or one may practice on Wednesdays, Mondays, or Thursdays. Thus it is said.
Now, he states the time for the worship of the birth asterism (janmanakṣatra): Root Text:
When the sun has moved toward the northern direction, on an auspicious lunar day, and upon the victory over cruel [planets] and untimely death (apamṛtyu)...

The Guru should perform the worship of the birth-star on days joined with auspicious yogas, whether for the destruction of enemies and calamities, during the chanting of mantras for the planets, for the attainment of all desired goals, on the king's birthday, at the time of his consecration, or at the beginning and end of a battle.

(p. 164) Regarding the phrase "when the sun": when the sun is situated in the northern direction—that is, during the northern solstice—and on an auspicious lunar day (tithi), on a propitious day, for the conquest of cruel untimely death (*apamṛtyu*), for the destruction of terrible untimely death, for the removal of the affliction of enemies—that is, for the avoidance of the distress caused by enemies; for the conquest of the planets—that is, for the subjugation of evil spirits such as *bhūtas* and *pretas*; and for the accomplishment of all desired goals.

On the kings' birthday, on their birth asterism, at the time of consecration— specifically the time of the coronation— at the beginning and end of battle— the commencement and conclusion of war— and on days joined with auspicious conjunctions such as Vyatīpāta and other meritorious times; on these occasions, the Guru [performs] the worship of the birth asterism.
One should perform it. As it is stated in the *Aṃśumattantra*:
"Hereafter, I shall proclaim the sequence of rites for one's birth-star (*janmarkṣa*);
one should perform them during the periods of the northern solstice (*uttarāyaṇa*) on an auspicious day."
It causes the destruction of all enemies, the eradication of all calamities,
the pacification of untimely death, and the subduing of malevolent planets;
[it should be performed] at the time of a king's consecration or on his birthday.
"At the beginning or the end of battle, or even on a day joined with yoga, the worship of one's birth-star (janmarkṣa) should be performed for the fulfillment of all desires. Thus it is said.
And the method for performing this should be observed in that very same place.
Now, he states the time for the worship of the day (vārapūjā): Root Text:
Also for the purpose of averting untimely death (apamṛtyu) throughout the year, as well as for the rite of destroying pestilence (mārī).
In the case of affliction by malevolent planets, in rites for victory even over a formidable enemy,
in a king’s conquest of foes, in the pacification of fevers and the like, as well as in the propitiation of villages and so forth,
and for the fulfillment of the practitioner’s desired aims— the worship of the [planetary] days (vārārcana) is prescribed in the Āgama.
Regarding the phrase "for the sake of the year" (*varṣārtha*): the worship of the day (*vārapūjā*) for the purposes of the year and so forth is proclaimed in the *Āgama*.
Thus it is said in the *Aṃśumattantra*:
"I shall declare the procedure for the worship of the day; listen, O best of suns."
For the purpose of destroying untimely death and for the destruction of the great pestilence.
It is declared to bring rain, victory, and the destruction of planetary afflictions and the like;
it brings peace to the village, and kings shall achieve triumph.
The fruit of the practitioner's desire shall be accomplished; this indeed is the fruit of the worship of the gateway.
One should perform it beginning from Sunday and ending on Saturday.
"At the conclusion of the morning twilight worship, however, the worship of the day-lord (vāra) must be performed. Thus [it is said].
The method for performing this is also explained in that very same place.
Now, he states the time for the worship of the lunar mansions (nakṣatras)— the root text says:
At the time of a king's consecration, during the birth asterism of the monarch, on the middle or penultimate lunar day of either fortnight,
or at the conclusion of battle, or when joined with a [favorable] yoga—
The Nakṣatrayāga has been declared for the accomplishment of all goals.

p. 166) On the two fortnights—the bright and the dark—on the eighth day, which is near the end of the lunar month, on the fourteenth day when it is joined with an auspicious conjunction (*yoga*), or at other times endowed with such auspicious conjunctions; for the sake of accomplishing all goals, the *nakṣatrayāga* (star-sacrifice) is prescribed: the worship of the constellations should be performed during these times.
And so it is said in the Aṃśumat-tantra:
"O best of suns, listen as I describe the worship of the lunar mansions (nakṣatra),
which pacifies the great elements and causes the enemy army to flee."
It brings about the destruction of all fevers, grants the accomplishment of all desired goals,
pacifies untimely death, and destroys droughts.
At the time of a king’s consecration, or on his birthday,
or on the fourteenth or eighth day of either fortnight,
or at the conclusion of battles, or on a day endowed with auspicious astrological conjunctions.
The worship of the constellations should be performed for the sake of accomplishing all desired goals.
That specific method has been explained in that very same place.
Now, he states the time for the auspicious worship (*bhadrapūjā*):
"In every month, on the day of the birth of the Lord of the Earth, and during the lunar mansions (*ṛkṣa*) of the month, such as Ārdrā..."
On the day of the Red Bear (Mṛgaśīrṣa),

during the two junctions of the lunar fortnights, when the moon is eclipsed by the sun, at the transits (saṅkrāntis), on the eighth day, on the day preceding a festival, during the two solstices, at the equinoxes, or at other auspicious times, one who is disciplined in the stainless ritual should perform the preliminary consecration before midnight and carry out the worship of Bhadra.
Every month— in all months— on the days of the lords of the earth (the kings), on the birth asterisms of the king,
in the pair of parvas— the full moon and the new moon—
during the eclipses of the moon and the sun, during the transits at the twelve entries [of the sun] into Aries and the other signs, and on the eighth day.
In the middle of the fortnight, on the fourteenth day preceding the full moon;
during the solstices and equinoxes—that is, during the southern and northern solstices; at the transits of Aries and Libra;
at other auspicious times—or even at other auspicious times, the Guru, being disciplined by the pure rule, [should perform the rite] specifically in the first part of the night.
Having performed the ritual of acceptance (adhivāsana), one should carry out the auspicious worship (bhadrapūjā).
And so it is said in the Aṃśumattantra:
"O best of suns, listen as I shall explain the auspicious worship (bhadrapūjā),
which bestows long life, health, and victory, and increases nourishment, prosperity, and fame."
The most auspicious of all auspicious things, the bestower of all desired fruits,
the pacifier of untimely death, and the liberator from epilepsy.
There shall be the destruction of famine in the world, and especially in that village;
it serves for the sake of rain, for victory, and especially for the sake of kings.
It bestows long life upon the performer and brings all prosperity and happiness;
whoever performs the auspicious worship (bhadrapūjā) experiences complete auspiciousness.
This should be performed by kings in every month, or on their own birthday,
or under the lunar mansion (nakṣatra) of that particular month, or under Ārdrā or Śravaṇa.

On both lunar festival days (parvan), at the sun's passage into a new zodiac sign (saṅkrānti), during the eclipses of the moon and the sun, on the eighth or fourteenth lunar day, as well as at the solstices and equinoxes;
"Or even by the desire of the sacrificer, especially at an auspicious time;
having determined [the day], on the previous night at the conclusion of the lamp [offering]," and so forth.
Now, he states the time for secret worship (channapūjā): Root Text:
In every month, the weekdays [beginning with] Monday, Saturday, and Sunday shall be excellent, middling, and inferior [respectively].
The third lunar day (tithi) occurring in the middle or at the end [of a fortnight], as well as the ninth and the new moon (darśa)—these should be avoided.

On a day when the asterism (nakṣatra) is favorable to the performer's birth, from sunrise until three quarters of an hour (tri-pāda) or three nāḍīs have passed, one should perform the secret worship (channapūjā) of the desired Gaṇapati at the conclusion of the daily morning worship. || 38 ||

In all these months, regarding the days of the week—Venus (Sita), Saturn (Śani), and the Sun (Tapana)—they are, respectively, excellent, middling, and inferior; that is, they are best, mediocre, and lowest. Now, he states the rule for the lunar days (tithis) by way of those to be avoided: the middle and the penultimate [days], namely the eighth and the fourteenth.

The third, ninth, and new moon (darśa) days are to be avoided; the meaning is that other days are to be accepted. On a day favorable to the practitioner’s birth star (janmanakṣatra), on days that accomplish prosperity and security—namely, the Maitra and Paramamaitra days—at sunrise (sūryodaya), during the three-quartered period of three nāḍīs in the morning, following the daily morning worship (prātaḥ-nityārcana). In the morning time.
Immediately after the worship, one should perform the secret worship (channapūjā) of one's chosen form among the sixteen Gaṇapatis of the beloved Gaṇapati.
Thus it is said in the *Aṃśumattantra*:
"I shall describe the procedure for secret worship specifically for Vighneśa;
it bestows long life, health, and victory, and increases one's sons and grandsons."
For the sake of accomplishing all desires, it bestows universal sovereignty;
indeed, it brings about the destruction of enemies and grants supreme longevity to the practitioner.
Therefore, with every effort, one should perform secret worship;
it should be carried out in all months in accordance with the desire of the patron.
Friday is the best, Saturday is middling, and Sunday is the lowest; one should avoid all other days.
The ninth, the third, the eighth, and the fourteenth—these lunar days are declared the lowest; one should also avoid the new moon day.
One must determine the time favorable for the birth of the patron, as well as the site for establishing a village and so forth; this is especially necessary when establishing a temple for Śaṅkara.
p. 170) Or else, one may perform the independent worship of the retinue or the supreme worship of Vighneśa;
beginning at sunrise, for three quarters of an hour—that is, three nāḍīs.
At the conclusion of the daily worship, one should perform the secret worship (channapūjā):
Bāla, Bhakta, Vīra, Śakti, Dhvaja, and Piṅgala.
Ucchiṣṭa, Rakta, Kṣipra, Heramba, Lakṣmīpūrvaka,
Vijaya, Nṛtta, Ūrdhva, and those named Mahā and Hāridra.
Thus the names of the sixteen Gaṇeśas have been proclaimed;
the distinction of their forms, beginning with the Brahmins and ending with the Śūdras, is now described.
The form of the pair beginning with the Child (Bāla) is prescribed for the Brahmins;
the others should likewise be so, especially for those beginning with the ornaments.
Now he describes the milk-bath:
at the commencement of war, during the oppression by an enemy, or when drought, heat, or pestilence prevail.
And in the event of illness, the preceptor should perform the milk-bath for Śaṅkara as prescribed in the Āgamas.
One should perform the milk-bath as prescribed in the Āgamas. Regarding this, it is stated in the Vīratantra by Pitāmaha:
"O Śaṅkara, what are the procedures for the milk-bath?
O Lord, you ought to explain all of this to me in brief."
Īśvara said: "O Four-faced One, listen; I shall explain all of that in due order:
[the rites] for times of drought and the like, and when fever and pestilence prevail."
In the event of a great disease, at the commencement of war,
and likewise during times of affliction by enemies, a milk-bath is prescribed;
the milk of a Kapila cow is considered the best, and so forth.
Now, he states the time for the jar-bath (ghaṭasnāna): Root Text:
Even at a time conjoined with the birth asterism of the king’s consecration...
At the beginning and end of battle, as well as at the time of taking up one's weapons,
and on other auspicious days, one should perform the ritual consecration of the jar (ghaṭābhiṣeka) for Paraśiva after having performed the morning twilight worship (pūrvasandhyā). || 39 ||
At a time conjoined with the birth asterism of the king, or conjoined with the asterism of his coronation, or conjoined with his natal asterism; at the beginning and end of a battle;
at the time of undertaking worship of Śiva and other rites preceded by initiation; and on other auspicious days.

On other auspicious occasions as well, having performed the morning twilight rite (*pūrvasandhyā*) following the morning worship, one should perform the ritual for Paraśiva known as the "Vase Consecration" (*ghaṭābhiṣeka*). As it is stated in the *Sūkṣma*:
"I shall explain the Vase Bath; listen to it, O Prabhajana."
For the purpose of destroying all diseases, it is the destroyer of the great pestilence.
For the purpose of destroying untimely death, for the destruction of famine within the kingdom,
for victory, and for the sake of prosperity, this auspicious [rite] brings about all accomplishments.
On the birth asterism of kings, or indeed on their consecration asterism,
at the time of commencing worship, or at the beginning and end of a battle.
On another auspicious occasion that is pleasing to the performer,
having determined the day beforehand, he should then feed the Brahmins.
"It should be performed on that very day at the conclusion of the morning twilight," and so forth.
Now, regarding the time for the stream of clarified butter (*ghṛtadhārā*), the root text says: "It should be performed during the four months beginning with Āśvina."
On the day of one’s birth-star, on the anniversary of one’s birth, and during other auspicious times— even on a most extraordinary or wondrous day in the middle of the dark fortnight—
one should duly offer a stream of ghee to Giriśa.
During the four months beginning with Āśvina—namely the months of Āśvayuja, Kārttika, Mārgaśīrṣa, and Puṣya;

on the day of the month’s asterism (māsanakṣatra) and the day of birth (janmadina)—that is, on the auspicious occasions of both the month’s asterism and the natal asterism; during the solstices, equinoxes, eclipses, and so forth; on days of great wonder (atyadbhuta), of great marvel (mahādbhuta), or of wonder (adbhuta)—that is, on days characterized solely by wonders.

In the middle of the dark fortnight, on the eighth day (kṛṣṇāṣṭamī), during these times, the rite known as Ghṛtadhārā— “the stream of clarified butter”— should be performed toward Giriśa, the Supreme Lord. As it is stated in the Sūkṣma:
I shall describe the rite of the stream of clarified butter; listen to it, O wise one!
It brings prosperity, victory, merit, and increases longevity and health.
For the purpose of destroying untimely death, for warding off all enemies,
for the sake of prosperity throughout the year, for victory, and for the destruction of fever and epilepsy.
For the purpose of destroying all diseases and eliminating great sins,
[one should perform this] during the solstices, the equinoxes, and during the eclipses of the moon and the sun.
In the month of Puṣya, the month of Aśvayuj, the month of Dhanus, and Kārttika;
on the day of the month's asterism, the birth asterism, a day of propitiation, or an auspicious constellation.

"On the Mahādbhuta and Adbhuta days, and especially on the eighth day of the dark fortnight (Kṛṣṇāṣṭamī), one should perform the continuous stream of ghee (ghṛtadhārā) at such times as these. Thus it is said.
Now, he states the time for the worship on the eighth day: Root Text:
If the eighth day of the dark fortnight occurs with either the later [tithi] or the earlier [tithi],...
When there is equality regarding the time of overlap, that [Ekādaśī] pierced by the previous night's watch during the Śiva-yajña must indeed be accepted; likewise,
among the months, [the Ekādaśī] at the beginning of Mārgaśīrṣa and at the conclusion of the Tripurā-victory [festival] should be taken as the one overlapping with the previous day.

Regarding the eighth day of the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇāṣṭamī): if it is pierced by the night of the preceding [seventh] or the following [ninth], or by the preceding [seventh] or the following [eighth], it should be accepted for the worship and sacrifice of Śiva. In the case of equality—where [the tithi] is equal during the first watch of the night on both days—it is indeed the one pierced by the preceding [tithi] that is to be taken.

Only the eighth lunar day (aṣṭamī) pierced by the seventh (saptamī) is to be accepted; the meaning is that in cases where it is either deficient or excessive, the one that is longer (adhika) alone is to be taken.

Furthermore, this worship should be performed in all months; regarding that, he states the rule for the commencement as "starting from Mārga" (mārgamukhataḥ)—that is, beginning from the month of Mārgaśīrṣa—and thereby explains the reason for performing the worship on the eighth day.
Regarding *Tripurā*, it refers to the context of victory (*vijaya*) at the end of the conquest of the three cities (*pura-trayasya jayānte*). Thus it is stated in the *Aṃśumattantra*:
"O best of suns, listen as I describe the worship on the eighth day (*aṣṭamī*), which is beneficial for all the worlds, meritorious, and the bestower of all sovereign powers."
It accomplishes all desired objects and goals, bestows both worldly enjoyment and liberation,
destroys all enemies, and annihilates all sins.
One should know this to be the best among all observances; one should worship Śiva on the eighth lunar day (aṣṭamī) of the dark fortnight in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa.
At the conclusion of the victory over the three cities, for the purpose of pacifying the heat,
he was worshipped by all the gods during the first watch of the night.
One should consecrate [the deity] with the ghee and milk of a tawny cow,
having praised and fully worshipped the Supreme Lord with the twelve names.

Having thus performed worship in sequence, on the great festival of Kṛṣṇāṣṭamī, the eighth lunar day that coincides with the full day and night (ahorātra) is the best; that which is overlapped by the following day is middling.

(175) It is declared that the eighth lunar day (aṣṭamī) joined with the preceding [tithi] is inferior; one should worship Śiva on the eighth day when even a single digit (kalā) of it is present during the evening (pradoṣa).
In a single month, the eighth day of both fortnights is highly praised;
having declared that month to be superior, one should worship Śiva during both fortnights.
If the eighth day is missing from a month, then after that month,
when two of its own lunar dates have arrived, one should perform the sacrifice for half of the omitted month.
One should worship the previous [deity] on the eighth day of the latter fortnight, and the subsequent [deity] on the eighth day of the former fortnight;
beginning at sunset, this lasts for seven and a half nāḍīs.
If the eighth lunar day is seen pierced by the preceding or the following [day],
then on that eighth day, during the first watch of the night, there is indeed a great festival.
"The lunar day of the eighth of the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇāṣṭamī) must be observed by the wise as that which is joined with the previous [lunar day];
especially so when it is conjoined with the evening twilight worship and the ritual bath with ghee," and so forth.
Now, he states the time for the occurrence of a pearl-eclipse (mauktika-grahaṇa):
The root [verse]:

In the months of Caitra, Kārttika, and Māgha, during the waning fortnight, starting from the ninth day; and if it falls in the dark fortnight, starting from the fourth day—excluding the three days beginning with Friday (Bhṛgu).

One should perform the rite of releasing the captive elephant during the asterisms of Puṣya, Maghā, Uttarās, Aśvinī, Savitṛ (Hasta), and Śroṇā (Śravaṇa), under an auspicious conjunction, and when the sun is in Aries, Capricorn, Leo, or Aquarius. (42)

(p. 176) Therein, he first states the rule for the months: *caitre* means in the month of Caitra; *ūrja-tapasyayoḥ* means in the months of Kārttika and Phālguna. Next, he states the lunar days (*tithi*) and weekdays by way of prohibition:
*site pakṣe* means in the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*); *navamyādi ṣaṭ tithīn* refers to the six lunar days beginning with the ninth—namely, the ninth, eighth, fourth, second, and third.

Six lunar days (tithis) known as *parva*—namely, the eighth, ninth, thirteenth, and the new moon (*amāvāsyā*)—if they fall within the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*), as well as the three weekdays beginning with Bhṛgu—that is, the days of Venus, Saturn, and the Sun—should be avoided; the others are to be accepted, such is the meaning. Now he states the asterisms (*nakṣatras*): *Vedha* is Rohiṇī.
Puṣya is well-known; Maghā is well-known; the three [nakṣatras] are Uttaraphalgunī, Uttarāṣāḍhā, and Uttaraproṣṭhapadā; Aśvinī is Aśvi; Hasta is Savitṛ;
Śravaṇa is Śroṇā—in these nine nakṣatras. Now he states the rule for the conjunction (yoga): "In an auspicious conjunction..."

Regarding the auspicious conjunctions mentioned in the scriptures among the eighteen conjunctions beginning with Vajra: he states the ascendants—namely Aries (meṣa), Cancer (karka/karkaṭaka), Scorpio (ali/vṛścika), Leo (siṃha), and Aquarius (ghaṭa/kumbha).
In these five zodiac signs, one should perform the rite known as the "taking of pearls" (muktāgrahaṇa).
And so it has been said in the *Sūkṣma*:
"I shall describe the collection of pearls; listen to that, O Wind-god!
[It should be done] in the month of Phālguna, Caitra, Kārttika, or even others."
Indeed, it is proclaimed that [the fast] is praiseworthy in the bright fortnight (pūrvapakṣa) or even in the other;
and if it is undertaken in the bright fortnight, then on the eighth and likewise the ninth day.

The wise man should diligently avoid the second, third, and fourth lunar days as well as the *parvan* (the junctions of the phases), while observing the remaining days; likewise, if [the fast] is undertaken during the dark fortnight, he should avoid the sixth and the eleventh days.

One should diligently avoid the eighth, the ninth, the new moon day (darśa), and the thirteenth lunar days; other lunar days are considered suitable. Alternatively, the seizure [of the breath] is held to occur according to another method, namely by means of the asterism (nakṣatra).
Āśvayuj, Rohiṇī, Puṣya, and Maghā as well.
And likewise the triad of Uttaras, as well as Hasta and Śravaṇa.
One should accept a [lunar] mansion of this kind, while another kind is inferior;
one should avoid Friday, Saturday, and Sunday respectively.
Vajrasiddhi, likewise Parigha and Śiva;
Siddha, Sādhya, Śubha, Śubhra, Brāhma, and Māhendra.
The venerable Āyuṣmān, Prīti, Saubhāgya, Śobhana,
Dhṛti, Śūla, Gaṇḍa, and Vṛddhi are said here [to be the names of the lunar days].
These are declared to be auspicious, and one should avoid other yogas;
Aries, Cancer, Leo, Scorpio,
and Aquarius are to be known as auspicious signs, and one should avoid the other zodiacal signs.
(178) Thus, one who knows the prescription of time should begin this at that specific time; and so forth.
Having determined [the time] one day prior, at the conclusion of the morning twilight;
now he states the time for the consecration with musk—
the root text:

On the eighth lunar day, on the new moon, during solar and lunar eclipses, as well as under the asterisms of Rājārka (Jyeṣṭhā), Ṣaḍaśīti (Pūrvaphalgunī), Śiva (Ārdrā), Hari (Śravaṇā), Brahmā (Rohiṇī), and Citrā in the month of Caitra,
and also on the full moon of Phālguna in the month of Phālguna, bathing Śiva with musk is prescribed.
It bestows all desired fruits, it is the state of victory, and it is the fruit of sacrifices performed in all ritual ceremonies. || 43 ||
On the birth asterism of kings, on the days of the *ṣaḍaśītika*, and on the first days of the months of Gemini, Virgo, Sagittarius, and Pisces. As it is stated in the *Niśvāsakārikā*:
"Gemini, Virgo, and likewise Sagittarius and Pisces."
In this way, other openings of the eighty-six [channels] have been fully described.

During the asterisms of Śiva (Ārdrā), Hari (Śravaṇa), and Brahmā (Rohiṇī); on the eighth lunar day, the new moon, and during solar and lunar eclipses; and specifically in the month of Caitra under the Citrā asterism, as well as in the month of Phālguna under the Phalgunī asterism—it is declared in the Āgamas that at these times, bathing with the urine of deer for Śiva is prescribed. (This is the remainder of the statement.)
