He states its fruits: it bestows all desired results, grants victory, yields the fruit of all sacrificial rites (*adhvara*), and provides the fruit of every kind of worship. Thus it is said in the *Aṃśumattantra* (p. 179):
"I shall describe the bath with musk; listen, O best of Suns."
It bestows fame, victory, merit, and subsequently grants the splendor of Māra’s enemies.

Whatever fruit there is from all forms of giving, whatever fruit is found in all sacrifices, whatever merit is found in all sacred fords, and whatever merit comes from the worship of all the gods— [all that is attained here].
A bath with musk yields ten million times that fruit;
so too on the Phālgunī day in the month of Phālguna, or on the Citrā day in the month of Caitra.
O King, [the fast is forbidden] on one's birth-star, or during the six *aśītimukha* periods,
as well as on the stars of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, and likewise on the eighth lunar day of the new moon (*abhāvāsyāṣṭamī*).
"At the time of the Great Time (Mahākāla), one should perform the bath for the sake of seizing [the breath] and so forth with the Mṛgamada mantras. Thus it is said.

Now, he states the time for the conch-consecration (*śaṅkhābhiṣeka*): On the day of the *amṛtasiddhi-yoga* of Īśa, on the new moon, during the sun’s transit (*saṅkrānti*), on one’s own birth star (*janmarkṣa*), on the middle lunar days of the fortnight, or on a Śiva-tithi, the preceptor [should perform it].
One should bathe the Lord Śaṅkara with forty-nine conches of superior, middling, or inferior quality, or with all one hundred desired ones, or even with a thousand.
The meaning is clear. Thus it has been said in the *Aṃśumat-tantra*:

"O best of suns, listen as I describe the consecration with conch water (*śaṅkhābhiṣecana*), which bestows longevity, prosperity, victory over death, destroys disease, and causes the destruction of enemies."
For the sake of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, it increases sons and grandsons;
it is declared to be pacifying (śāntika) and nourishing (pauṣṭika), and it destroys all sins.
Therefore, with every effort, one should perform the consecration with water from a conch shell during the conjunction of Rohiṇī and Saturn,
and likewise during Guru and Puṣya.
When the Sun is conjoined with Hasta, Venus with Revatī,
Mars with Aśvinī, and Mercury with Anurādhā;
In conjunction with the Soma-Vaiṣṇava [rite], for the benefit of the sacrificer,
one should perform the consecration with the conch on the eighth, the fourteenth, the new moon day, or during a solar transit, as well as on the birth asterism of the sacrificer.
It is said that the conch is of three kinds: male, female, and neuter.
That which is thick at the base is female, and that which is thick at the tip is neuter.
The root, the tip, and that which is equal [to them] are determined to be masculine;
the conch is to be known as fourfold, according to the sequence beginning with the Brāhmaṇa.
The abdomen should be light, with its lower part well-formed, its upper tip elongated, and its back even;
having thus filled out the belly, it is here called the "Brahma-conch."
A conch that is thus for a Kṣatriya is slightly yellowish in luster;
likewise, one with a long base and light weight is known as the Vaiśya conch.
Light, with a long tip and a short back—this is said to be the characteristic of a conch-shell;
hereafter follows that which originates from a conch.
A conch originating from the Tāmraparṇī is proclaimed to be the best;
that from the Gaṅgā is middling, while that from the Narmadā is the lowest.
Thus, the threefold form has been described; now the nature of the conch is being stated here.
A conch that spirals to the right is said here to be the best of its kind.
One should place that conch in the center and arrange the others around it.
One should fill [the vessel] with one āḍhaka according to the previously mentioned characteristics;
half of that is the middling size, and half of that again is the lowest.
A right-spiraling conch shell of its own prescribed size is ordained;
it should be adorned with gold, gems, and the like at the tip of its tail, and be naturally beautiful.
Having established one thousand conch shells, it is proclaimed as "the supreme";
furthermore, there is the sequential establishment of a hundred conch shells.
"Śaṅkha is forty-nine, and Kanyasa is likewise the same," and so forth.
Now, he states the time for worship for the sake of fulfilling desires— the root text says:
"Under Rohiṇī, Anila (Svātī), Uttara [Punarvasu], Guru (Puṣya), Hasta, and Maitra (Anurādhā)..."

On Mondays, Sundays, Wednesdays, and Fridays; during solar and lunar eclipses; on the fifth lunar day (pañcamī); on the two junctions of the fortnights (parvan); at the worship [of the deity]; at the end of a month, a lunar mansion (nakṣatra), or a half-month; and at the beginning and middle of the two fortnights and the two solstices—one should perform worship for the sake of desired objects.
Regarding that, he first states the asterisms: in Rohiṇī; Anila—Svātī;

in the three Uttaras (Uttaraphalgunī, Uttarāṣāḍhā, and Uttarabhādrapadā); in Gurubha—Puṣya; in Hasta; in Maitrarkṣaka—Anurādhā; on days praised by Soma, Āditya, Budha, and Guru; Asureḍita—Śukra; and during the eclipses of Āditya and Soma.

During solar and lunar eclipses, at the time of the first Śiva-pūjā following initiation (dīkṣā), during the twelve lunar mansions beginning with Citrā in each month, on the final days of each month, and on the fourteenth and eighth days of both halves of the lunar fortnight, as well as during the two solstices— these are the times for worship.
During the transits of Capricorn and Cancer, one should perform worship for the sake of desired objects at these times.
Thus it is stated in the Aṃśumattantra:
"O best of suns, listen as I describe the sacrifice for the sake of desired objects."
It bestows long life, prosperity, fame, and victory; it destroys disease and brings about the destruction of enemies.
Listen to the rules for the time of worship, which destroys untimely death, brings about the destruction of all sins, and accomplishes one's desired wishes and goals.
Under the asterisms of Rohiṇī, Anila (Svātī), Puṣya, Hasta, and the Uttarās;
and on Sundays, Mondays, as well as on Wednesdays and Fridays.
During the solstices, the equinoxes, and during lunar and solar eclipses;
on the eighth, fourteenth, and fifth days of the lunar fortnight, and at the two junctions of the lunar phases.
"On the birth-star of the patron, on the day of his monthly star,
at the end of the month, during a solar transit, or on any other auspicious day," and so forth.
(p. 183) Now, he states the time for the crowning with the diadem (mukuṭāropaṇa): Root Text:
When the sun has thus reached its northern course (udagayana), O King...
O sacrificer, favorable to the village, during the auspicious asterisms,
on the days of battle at both the beginning and the end, and on the great days of the bright fortnight, one should offer the crown for the sake of Śiva.

When the sun has entered its northern course (uttarāyaṇa), having risen, [the rite should be performed] under asterisms favorable to the king, favorable to the village, and favorable to the sacrificer— namely, under the asterism of the king,
the asterism of the village, the birth-asterism of the sacrificer, and the auspicious asterism Ārdrā— and during the period of battle.

And at the beginning and end of the battle, on auspicious and praiseworthy days during the bright fortnight (the waxing moon), one should offer a crown for the sake of welfare. As it is stated in the *Sūkṣma*:
"I shall describe the crowning with a crown; listen to that, O Prabhajana."
It bestows the fruits of long life and health, and increases one's sons and grandsons.
This merit brings about all accomplishments and is supreme for destroying enemies;
it should be performed during the period of the sun's northern course, in the bright fortnight, on an auspicious day.
In a lunar mansion favorable to the king's village, or even under an auspicious deity-nakṣatra;
or at the beginning or end of a battle, or on the day of the patron (yajamāna).
The wise one should perform the crowning with the diadem according to this rite. Thus [it is said].
The characteristics of the crown are also explained in that very same place. (p.
184) I shall describe the ritual procedure for the crown; listen, O Sadāgata!
Its characteristics are said to be threefold: the *kirīṭa* and the *karaṇḍaka*.

Now, the characteristics of the crown of matted hair (jaṭāmukuṭa) for these [deities], whether they are formless (niṣkala) or with form (sakala), shall be described. As for the crown of the forehead (taṭāmukuṭa): [it is as follows].
The rule for the number of gold pieces is as follows, according to the sequence of superior, middling, and inferior:
three thousand, three hundred and thirty, and thirty-three niṣkas.
Three hundred and thirty-three niṣkas, increased by three guñjas, is the measure for Śiva among the deities;
[this amounts to] three hundred and thirty-three niṣkas plus three guñjas.
"Except for the hundred [beads], the measurement for those on the crowns of Soma, Skanda, and others is that same measure;
or else, double or triple that measure is prescribed.
One should take pure Jāmbūnada gold according to the rules for those respective numbers," and so forth.
Now, certain specific times for optional rites (*kāmyavrata*) as set forth in the *Kālottara* in six thousand verses are written here in brief. For example, regarding the Bhūtapativrata:
"And on the fourteenth day (*bhūtā*) of the month of Phālguna, one should therefore worship the Lord of Beings (*Bhūtapati*)."
On the eighth and fourteenth days, those [observances] previously mentioned are to be undertaken.
All of those were indeed already encompassed by that very [knowledge].
(p. 185) Regarding the *skandavṛta*, that which is to be performed starting from the bright fortnight of Caitra is now described:
having fasted on the sixth lunar day while pure, one should especially worship the Six-faced One (*Ṣaṇmukha*).
Regarding the Mātṛvṛta rite: On the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, one should perform the Mātṛvṛta;
sixty-four Mothers, together with Bhairava, are to be worshipped.
Whoever worships on the ninth day of the month of Āśvayuja shall indeed possess unbroken power; of this there is no doubt.
Regarding the rite of Anaṅga:
on the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, one should draw Anaṅga upon a cloth and worship him in the midst of a flower-pavilion within a beautiful garden.
A man obtains his desires and becomes beloved by everyone;
a woman shall attain good fortune both in this world and in the next.
Or else, one should perform sacrifice month after month according to the prescribed ritual procedure.
In the month of Bhādrapada, one should always worship Anaṅga with diligence.
The Gaurīvṛta: Now I shall describe the Gaurīvṛta, which increases the good fortune of women;
one should perform the Gaurīvṛta on the third day of the bright fortnight of Caitra.
(p. 186) *Sūryavṛta*:

Now I shall explain in detail the unsurpassed *sūryavṛta*, as well as the conjunctions of lunar mansions and lunar days (*nakṣatratithiyoga*) and the conjunctions of the planets (*grahayoga*); listen now.
On the eighth and fourteenth days of both fortnights,
as well as on the asterisms Aśvinī, Rohiṇī, Puṣya, and Maghā— these three.
O Six-faced One, when Śravaṇā and Revatī coincide,
and the Sun, Moon, Āditya, Venus, Mercury, and Jupiter [are present], [that is a time for action].
Listen to what happens if the lunar days (tithis) occur according to the sequence of the constellations (nakṣatras):
if the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight falls on the weekdays starting with Aśvinī.
"In that [night], one should especially perform the rite for Śiva, the Supreme Self;
one should worship the path of his limbs with flowers for the sake of delighting Rati," and so forth.
Now, the observance of the Moon (Candravrata): if the eighth lunar day coincides with the Rohiṇī asterism, then one should perform the Candravrata.
Having worshipped Śiva according to the rules with baths consisting of the five nectars and other offerings.
The ointment, however, should be prepared with camphor or sandalwood; and so forth.
Regarding the Bhūmivṛta:
on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight, when there is a conjunction of the Tiṣya constellation and the Sun,
one should worship the Wielder of the Trident according to the previously mentioned rite and by means of fasting.
One should worship with saffron, body-unguents, and fragrant flowers;
milk-rice mixed with ghee should be offered in a quantity of one *prastha*.
One should diligently bestow a gift of land upon a devotee of Śiva;
by this foremost of offerings, one shall attain the status of a lord of the earth.
A protector of the earth should cause this [structure] named Bhūmivṛta to be constructed.
When the conjunction of Bṛhaspati with Maghā occurs on the fourteenth lunar day, that is called Devavṛta.
Having observed the fast on that day, one should worship Maheśvara, the God of gods.
According to the procedure for the Great Bath (mahāsnāna), one should first worship Mahāvatī,
and then worship Aṅgāraka with sandalwood paste and white flowers.
One should offer moving incense equal in weight to the moon;
furthermore, one should cause white garments and a horse to be given to the preceptor.
Consuming nutmegs and keeping a vigil at night is beneficial;
this is known as the Devavrata vow, which increases longevity, prosperity, and fame.
When the Svātī-yoga, presided over by Budha, occurs on the eighth lunar day,
one who has fasted according to the prescribed rules and performed the great ritual ablution (mahāsnāna) [attains the fruit].
"One should worship Virūpākṣa and likewise Aṅgāraka," and so forth.
One shall attain the station of Rājarājeśvara, which causes the great sages to rejoice;
by him, this chosen [teaching] of Rājarājeśvara has been revealed.
Regarding the Mahāvṛta:
"O child, when the conjunction of the Śukla-Śravaṇa occurs on the eighth or the fourteenth lunar day, one should perform the Mahāvṛta."
"Having observed the fast according to the prescribed rule, one should perform the great ablution," and so forth.
The fruit [of this act] leads one's fathers, grandfathers, and great-grandfathers, as well as sons, grandsons, and great-grandsons, to the world of Śiva.
Therefore, this Mahāvṛta should be performed by lords of the earth. Regarding the Viśvarūpavṛta:
when the conjunction of Revatī and the Moon occurs on the eighth day of the bright fortnight, [it is the time for the Viśvarūpavṛta].
Or when it has occurred, O Mahāsena, hear now this which was chosen [by you]: and so forth.
Whatever desires the practitioner of mantra (mantrī) may wish for, he shall attain them all;
therefore, this is proclaimed as the "Universal Form" (viśvarūpa).
"The consumption of water infused with *kuśa* grass, and then keeping vigil at night," and so forth.
Based on the conjunctions of constellations and lunar days, and through the conjunctions of the lunar days with the planets,
I shall once again explain the seasonal periods exactly as they exist.
(189) Regarding the "Son-Abounding" [constellation]: when the conjunction with Rohiṇī occurs on the eighth lunar day,
a special worship must be performed with great effort by those who desire sons.
Encompassing all desires:
when the conjunction of Jupiter occurs on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Puṣya,
or especially when there is a conjunction with the Moon, one should worship Śaṅkara.
One should offer milk-rice mixed with clarified butter to Śiva,
and worship Śiva as before with incense, lamps, offerings, and other articles.
The consumption of ghee should be performed, for ghee bestows all desires. This is the *Śivavrata*: when the conjunction of Āditya and Revatī occurs on the fourteenth lunar day.
Or, on the eighth lunar day, having worshipped Śiva as before through great yoga;
Regarding the Candravṛta: when the eighth lunar day coincides with the asterism Mṛgaśiras, one should then perform the Candravṛta rite,
diligently worshipping Śiva according to the procedure previously described.
Curd and milk should be offered as the food offering (naivedya), and milk alone should be consumed;
one shall obtain fame, health, and sovereignty—this word is not false.
(190) Bhaumavṛta:
When there is a conjunction of Mars with the asterism Aśvinī on the fourteenth lunar day,
or a conjunction with Rohiṇī on the eighth, one should perform the Bhaumavṛta vow.
O son, by worshipping Śiva with supreme devotion through the five-fold offerings (pañcopacāra) and consuming the red lotus, one shall attain sovereignty.
Regarding *Budhavṛta*:
"O Mahāsena, when the conjunction of Mercury with Rohiṇī occurs on the fourteenth or the eighth lunar day, one should perform the *Budhavṛta*."
Śiva is to be worshipped according to the prescribed rite, preceded by the great ablution (mahāsnāna);
the consumption of milk-rice mixed with ghee and accompanied by a great wick [of light] should follow.
His sons, wealth, wife, and cattle flourish; it is not otherwise. Regarding the preceptor’s observance:
when the conjunction of Revatī with Jupiter occurs on the fourteenth lunar day.
On the eighth lunar day, when it is conjoined with the constellation Tiṣya, one should perform the service prescribed by the Guru.
By consuming the fat of a tawny cow combined with the juice of *brāhmī*,
one attains mastery over speech through the power of this clarified butter.
When the constellation Śravaṇa is conjoined with Venus on the fourteenth lunar day,
that is known as Guru-vṛta; likewise, when Punarvasu is conjoined with Jupiter on the eighth lunar day, it is Siddha.
Having worshipped the Supreme Lord with extensive offerings according to one's means, one should partake of honey here; thus, one shall obtain great wealth.
Regarding the Śanivrata: when there is a conjunction of Saturn (Śaniyoga) with the Bharaṇī constellation on the fourteenth lunar day,
and likewise a conjunction of Fire (Agniyoga) on the eighth, then one should perform this observance.
Having worshipped Śiva according to the prescribed rules and partaken of curd,
Saturn, when situated in the eleventh house, indeed bestows auspicious results.
O child, if there is a conflict, that which is auspicious should be practiced for that purpose;
likewise, one should use a pair of gold pieces, coral, and pure kākara.
O child, one should carefully cause a conch shell with its star-marks, iron, and copper to be given to the preceptor in that order, according to what is available.
Thus ends the section on planetary afflictions.
Now begins the commencement of the Kṛṣṇāṣṭamī vow. Kārttikeya said:
"O Lord, you who are compassionate toward living beings, please describe the specific vows month by month for the entire year."
Īśvara said:
When one observes the fast of eating only at night on the eighth day of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa,
one should worship Rudra, known by the name Śaṅkara, together with Bhavānī.
One should perform worship specifically above one's own mantra, honoring Īśvara with the *bindu* and the Goddess by the name Mahāśaṅkarī.
One shall obtain a hundredfold the fruit of the Aptoryāma sacrifice;
having drunk a mouthful of cow's urine, one should then consume sacrificial food (haviṣya).
O Śikhidhvaja, having worshipped Śambhu-Rudra together with Śarvāṇī in the month of Pauṣa,
one should worship the devotees of Śiva on the eighth day of the dark fortnight.
Having performed the worship of the preceptor, one should drink cow’s ghee with the three myrobalans (triphalā);
then, having eaten sacrificial food (haviṣyānna), one obtains the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice.
On the eighth day of the dark fortnight, one should worship the deity named Māghamāsīśvara,
accompanied by Ambikā, using the mantra as previously described.
O son, by worshipping Śaiva teachers, consuming milk and the three fruits according to the prescribed rite,
one shall obtain the merit of a hundred horse-sacrifices.
On the eighth day of the dark fortnight of Phālguna, one should worship Mahādeva,
accompanied by Mālinī, immediately following the daily obligatory rites.
The earth should be given to a devotee of Śiva, and the auspicious consumption of sesame seeds should be performed;
thus, the Śiva-yogins shall obtain the fruit of ten thousand Rājasūya sacrifices.
O son, on the eighth day of the dark fortnight in the month of Caitra, one should worship Sthāṇu and Mṛḍānī with ornaments made of gold and other offerings, without any stinginess regarding wealth.
By eating a slightly roasted barley grain, one obtains the fruit of ten thousand horse-sacrifices;
likewise, when one worships the deity named Śiva according to one's ability during the month of Vaiśākha along with his Śakti.
Then, according to the previously mentioned procedure, one should worship a devotee of Śiva;
having consumed the water from the *kuśa* grass, one obtains the fruit of ten thousand human sacrifices.
O son, having worshipped Paśupati together with Pārvatī in the month of Jyeṣṭha, and having performed the daily rites there according to the prescribed ritual, one should then worship him thoroughly.
Having consumed the water from a cow's horn, one obtains the fruit of a cow-sacrifice;
and in the month of Āṣāḍha, one should worship Ugrarudra together with Manonmanī.
Having consumed water infused with *kuśa* grass, one obtains the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice;
in the month of Śrāvaṇa, one should worship the Lord named Sarva together with his consort Vāmāśakti.
Having consumed lotus-seeds mixed with water, one obtains the fruit of all sacrifices;
on the eighth day of the month of Bhādrapada, one should worship the deity named Tryambaka.
Endowed with the power of Jyeṣṭhā according to the previously mentioned procedure,
one should consume bilva leaves immediately after the worship of the Guru.
By this, one hundred perfect sacrifices have been performed by him, and not otherwise;
for in the month of Āśvayuja, the Lord is to be worshipped together with his beloved.
Having consumed water infused with jewels, one obtains the merit of ten thousand *pauṇḍarīka* sacrifices;
in the month of Kārttika, one should worship the Enemy of Madana (Śiva) together with Manonmanī.
Having worshipped the Guru according to the prescribed rite, one should consume the curd of cows;
by that, O Six-faced One, ten thousand Agniṣṭoma sacrifices are considered performed by him.
At the end of the year, one should feed Brahmins who are devoted to Śiva,
honoring them with gifts of land, elephants, vehicles, and an abundance of jewels and wealth.
O Mahāsena, he who is the preceptor of those who have been chosen should be honored with supreme devotion; one does not obtain that fruit through stinginess regarding wealth.
Thus ends the ritual for the Kṛṣṇāṣṭamī.
Regarding the flour-cake (*piṣṭavṛta*):
O son, when the month of Pauṣa has arrived, on either of the two fortnights,
on the fourteenth day, the eighth day, or even on the full moon day.
Having performed the daily rites according to the rules, one should then perform the optional rites;
therein, worship with special offerings should be performed with a pure mind.
The food offering (naivedya) shall consist of one prastha of barley-gruel prepared with curd, milk, and clarified butter;
furthermore, he should feed and protect as many Brahmins as there are Rudras.
One should have a Prakṛti, measuring one span (vitasti), fashioned from barley flour,
provided with horns, a tail, and a tuft of hair, and adorned with ornaments.
It should then be given to Śiva, and thereafter to the chosen preceptor, together with a fine vehicle;
now hear the merit of such a choice.
With celestial chariots resembling ten million suns, fulfilling all desires,
crowded with hosts of Rudras, and surrounded by Rudra-maidens.
Yoked to chariots drawn by bulls and accompanied by the sounds of various songs, he goes,
together with twenty-one generations of his lineage, to where Śaṅkara dwells.

For as many thousands of yugas as there are hairs on that [person], their progeny shall likewise be honored in the families [of the donors] and they themselves shall be glorified in the world of Rudra.
Having attained proximity [to the deity], they eventually attain union;
by this rite, in the month of Māgha, [one should offer] a figure made of barley flour.
Having completed it with devotion, one shall obtain the status of a universal monarch (cakravartin);
likewise, by offering a vajra in the month of Phālguna, one shall obtain that same fruit.
Having offered an image made of flour to Śakti in front of Śiva during the month of Caitra,
one is released from the sin of killing a Brahmin and shall attain the world of Śiva.
In the month of Vaiśākha, one should offer a staff-weapon made of half-a-hand’s measure of flour before Śiva;
it should be prepared and offered at the conclusion of the worship.
One is liberated from the five sins and is glorified in the world of Rudra;
on the full moon of Jyeṣṭha, one should offer a sword made of flour to Śiva.
He is liberated from ungratefulness and goes to the world of Rudra;
in the month of Āṣāḍha, one should offer a noose made of flour to Śiva.
He who offers a banner made of flour before Śiva is liberated from all misdeeds accumulated in this life.
By following the prescribed rite in the month of Śrāvaṇa, one shall attain imperishable liberation;
he who gives a mace made of flour in the month of Bhādrapada [attains the same].
Having obtained a treasure, one is glorified in the world of Śiva;
and in the month of Āśvayuja, [one should fashion] a trident half a cubit in size made of flour.
It should be offered before Śiva; it removes the sin of foeticide.
During the month of Kārttika, one should then offer that discus (cakra) before Śiva.
In the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, a lotus made of flour burns away the sins committed over seven lifetimes, just as fire consumes fuel.
One should give [the offering] to Śiva according to the prescribed rite and shall attain all sovereignty;
thus have I proclaimed the practice of eating only at night (nakta) for all those who are chosen.
Having completed the daily worship, one should perform the optional worship;
now hear briefly the livelihoods for the poor and the helpless.
Beginning from the month of Kārttika, one should observe the practice of eating only once a day until the end of Āśvayuja; hear now the fruit of his merit.
One is honored in the world of Rudra for one hundred and fifty divine years,
starting from the month of Kārttika until the end of Āśvayuja.
One should observe silence during the twilight hours until the stars appear;
at the end of the body, such a person goes to the world of Rudra together with their kinsmen.
He rejoices there in that world for thirty thousand divine years;
at the end of that time, he shall certainly attain Yoga through identity with Śiva. One should worship him thus.
Listen now to the fruit of merit for one who observes the practice of eating only at night (nakta), beginning from the month of Kārttika until the end of Āśvayuja.
There, in the world of Rudra, he dwells for many tens of thousands of years;
at the end of that time, through the yoga of knowledge, he shall obtain the fruit of all sovereign powers.
In the month of Kārttika,
[he] remained without food and observed silence for that entire period, month after month, until that limit.
He shall dwell in the world of Rudra for as many years as there are Manus,
provided he observes a fast on both fourteenth lunar days.
Beginning from the month of Kārttika until the end of Āśvayuja,
[one attains] the world of Rudra— [and there is] auspiciousness.
Beginning from the month of Kārttika for the duration of a full year, on the eighth day of the bright fortnight, one should observe a fast; hear now the meritorious fruit thereof.
He too shall dwell in the world of Rudra for as long as fourteen Indras [reign].
Regarding the Kedāra enclosure, the Kāmika states:
"Now I shall describe in detail the supreme Kedāra enclosure."
One should avoid the intercalary month when the sun is in transit through Virgo.
On the fourteenth day that occurs during the bright fortnight of the month of Proṣṭhapada,
one should perform the rite known as Kedāra.
Whether performed on a sacred festival day or at other times, this most excellent of all rites yields immediate fruit; so it was proclaimed by Gautama.
And at midday, one should worship Śiva on that day as is appropriate;
by him being pleased in mind, Gaurī’s anger is pacified.
The Kedāra vow, performed on the fourteenth day of the month of Proṣṭhapada (Bhādrapada) and under the constellation Pūrvaphalgunī, is proclaimed as the unsurpassed Gaurī-vrata.
He obtains sons and grandsons who increase his lifespan and fame;
for the sake of attaining knowledge and detachment, he shall ultimately attain the state of Śiva.
In this very way, during the dark fortnight, up to the eighth day—
[the merit is] a hundredfold greater than that.
Thus, on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, the fruit may be like that of the bright fortnight;
by performing it on both, a human being obtains a fruit multiplied a thousandfold.
One who desires auspiciousness should diligently perform the prescribed rite month after month;
[thus] one shall obtain the fruit... [and so forth].
Saffron, agallochum, betel, a moon-bright seat, a vehicle,
beautiful ornaments there, or whatever bed one desires in the mind.
One who desires auspiciousness should offer [this] every month before Śiva;
it attains inexhaustibility as long as Brahmā and the ten directions endure.
Whoever, having performed the rite of *vṛta*, offers the fruit to Śiva—
by him the eternal state is attained.
Thus ends the section on specific times for recitation.

Thus, for the pleasure of those whose intellects are adept in ritual action, [the author] composed this ocean of Śaiva scriptures, beginning with the Kāmika, just as [the gods] created the oceans for the sake of the gods.
May this heart-pleasing nectar of the discernment of time, now attained, never be seized by those wicked men who are as excessively crooked as demons and whose sole vision is for faults. (47)
Thus ends the *Śaivakālaviveka* composed by the venerable Nigamajñānaśivācārya. (p.
200) Commentary:
This is a unique excellence of expression, arising from the unfolding of a most pure intellect through the study of all the Śaiva Āgamas of the Great Lord of Aruṇagiri;
it is heard as a singular masterpiece among compositions of graceful words.
Vīti Gaṇapati Bhaṭṭa respectfully explains this.
Thus ends the commentary on the *Śaivakālaviveka*, composed by Gaṇapati Bhaṭṭa, the ornament of the Śrīvatsa lineage. Om. Peace.
The auspicious connection:
the section on place and time.

In the *Īśānaśivagurudevapaddhati*, within the *Siddhāntasāra*, in the twenty-sixth chapter of the *Kriyāpāda*: now, concerning the construction of a temple for the purpose of the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) of the *liṅga*.
The cycle of activities beginning with plowing and so forth should be known; it is now being described.
In this matter, one must especially consider the attainment of a virtuous place and time;
for a seed sown in a fertile field at the proper season grows well.
And that [temple], which bestows the desired fruit through rites such as the sprinkling of water,
[is established] in a temple endowed with the proper characteristics, once the activities beginning with the plowing of the ground have been accomplished.
When the *liṅga* has been installed according to the prescribed rite in a distinguished place and at an auspicious time, Śiva manifests his presence for the welfare of the practitioner.
In this regard, the period of the northern solstice is fixed for activities such as plowing;
the months should not be deficient, the fortnight should be the bright one, and the lunar days (tithis) should be auspicious.
Those [days] which are free from the Parvan, the Aṣṭamī, the Viṣṭi, and the Pratipad, as well as the Karaṇas— excluding Viṣṭi, Śakuni, and Catuṣpada— [are auspicious].
Excluding the Nāga and Kiṃstughna yogas, the days, drekkāṇas, and degrees of the Moon, Mercury, Jupiter, and Venus are commended and grant happiness.
The ascendants and aspects of Jupiter, the Moon, and Venus are praised; whereas the ascendants, days, and decanates of malefic planets, along with their aspects, are not.
All the planets that have gone to the Lagna (ascendant) are auspicious;

malefics having gone to the third or sixth houses are not desired, while elsewhere they bring auspiciousness. All [planets] situated in the eighth house are undesirable, yet Venus is auspicious even there.
The Moon in the second, fifth, and ninth houses;
Mercury in the seventh, ninth, and fifth houses;
and Jupiter in the second, seventh, fifth, and ninth houses—these bring about auspicious results.
The constellations Saumya (Mṛgaśiras), Āditya (Punarvasu), Aśvinī, Tiṣya (Puṣya), Hasta, Pauṣṇa (Revatī), the three Uttarās,
Rohiṇī, Śravaṇa, Svātī, and Maitra (Anurādhā) are indeed the auspicious lunar mansions.
One should abandon that which is released by a planet, conjoined with a planet, or aspired to by a planet.

For example: if a meteor falls during the tenth lunar mansion from the Sun, there will be an earthquake; on the seventh [day], the Brahma-staff (brahmadaṇḍa); on the fifteenth, it is fruitless; and on the twenty-first, death occurs from Venus in the seventh lunar mansion, and likewise from Rāhu in the eleventh. From the lunar mansion conjoined with Saturn, [death occurs] in the tenth, sixth, or twentieth [day].

The *khaṇḍanakṣatras* beginning with *Khā* (Kṛttikā) are to be avoided. From Mercury (*Budha*), the eighth, eighteenth, twenty-fourth, and third asterisms are called the *mahākaṇṭhakas*. From Mars (*Bhauma*), the fifth, seventh, ninth, fourteenth, and third asterisms [are so named]. From Jupiter (*Guru*), the ninth is called *rogākhya* (the disease). The *jvālāgnis* [beginning] from Jupiter’s [position]... [are as follows].
And [these] are to be avoided.
Furthermore: In Aśvinī, Citrā, Rohiṇī, Dhaniṣṭhā, and likewise in Uttarā;
in Jyeṣṭhā and also in Pūṣa (Revatī), the conjunction with the Sun and other planets is called "burnt" (dagdha).

Likewise, the eleventh is burned by the twelfth, the fifth by the second, the eighth by the ninth, when they are conjoined with the Sun and the other planets respectively. Also, Anurādhā, Jyeṣṭhā (Vaiśvadeva), Śatabhiṣaj, and Aśvinī are [burned] by the Moon and the Bull (Vṛṣabha).
Indeed, when Hasta is conjoined with the Sun and other planets, they become *mṛtyu-yogas* (fatal conjunctions).
Likewise, Maghā, Viśākhā, Ārdrā, Mūlā, Śatabhiṣaj, Rohiṇī,
and Uttarāṣāḍhā are *viṣa-yogas* (poisonous conjunctions) when conjoined with the Moon and other planets.
The conjunction of Arka with Agni on the fifth lunar day, and of Soma with Citrā on the second.
On Tuesday, Rohiṇī and the full moon; on Wednesday, the seventh lunar day with the southern asterism (Pūrvaphalgunī);
on Thursday, Jyeṣṭhā and the first lunar day; and on Friday, the sixth lunar day and the Vaiṣṇava asterism (Śravaṇa).
On a Saturday, the conjunction with the eighth lunar day under the asterism Revatī is the Mṛta-yoga; one should avoid these.
On the third lunar day, the asterism Rohiṇī (Prājāpatya), on the sixth, the asterism Mṛgaśiras (Saumya), and on the [twelfth], the asterism Puṣya (Tiṣya) [are to be avoided].
On the tenth day, the Dvādaśī [muhūrta] is auspicious; on the fifth, likewise Śravaṇa;
on the seventh, Pauṣṇa; and on the eighth, that known as Yāmya—these are called Ugra.
Citrā and Viśākhā belong to Agni; Ajaikapād and Vaiṣṇava (Anurādhā) belong to Viṣṇu; Śatabhiṣaj belongs to Uḍumbaras; Āhirbudhnya (Śravaṇa) and the two Aśvins (Aśvinī); and likewise Bharaṇī.
Rohiṇī, Ārdrā, and the lord of the Apsarases (Punarvasu)— these twelve lunar mansions, including the empty ones and the trees, are to be avoided in the months beginning with Caitra, respectively.
Niṣkambha, Śūla, Gaṇḍa, Atigaṇḍa, Vajra, and Vyāghāta—
among these yogas, [the time] is measured by three, five, six, and four *ṛtus* (seasons) respectively.
Excluding the first nine *ghaṭikās* of each of these [nine yogas], the remaining ones are auspicious:
those at the beginning of Viṣkambha and Śūla, and those in the middle of Gaṇḍa and Atigaṇḍa.
At the end of Vyāghāta and Vajra, one should abandon the stated nāḍīs;
one should also entirely avoid Vyatīpāta, Parigha, and Vaidhṛti.

One should avoid, in rites such as consecrations, the roots of the Arka and Āra trees, the stars corresponding to the number of those roots from the root onwards, and burnt or thorny wood, as well as pillars.
The asterisms of Aśvinī, Maghā, and Revatī; Jyeṣṭhā and Mūla; Bharaṇī, Āśleṣā, and Anurādhā; and Puṣya, Pūrvaphalgunī, and Uttaraphalgunī are mutually related.

The constellations Śroṇā (Pūrvāṣāḍhā), Prajeśa (Rohiṇī), Śatabha (Śatabhiṣaj), Hasta, Ārdrā, and Svāti are mutually [affected] such that one quarter of a nakṣatra is pierced by a quarter of another, and half a nakṣatra is struck by half of another.
Having understood the piercing (vedha) caused by the planets situated in these [houses], one should avoid it;
likewise, in various yogas, according to their respective numbers, when joined with the lunar days (tithis) of the two fortnights.
In this division according to the number of men, Śrīdivasa and the others are to be known;
these seven are Śrīdivasa, Vadhadivasa, Dhanārṇava,
Kali, Kālakarṇī, Vadhasaṃjña, and Varjita.

One should abandon, in sequence during the Nandā and other lunar days, the channels (nāḍīs) whose names correspond to the forms of the lunar dates: Yama, Nāga, Manapāra, and Khala, according to their enumeration.
Hārī, Sānumayaḥ, Netram, Sūnuḥ, Maunī, Kapiḥ, Paṭuḥ;
Haraḥ, Harī, Naraḥ, Saṃjñā, Mānyaḥ, Mṛtyuḥ, Paṭuḥ, Nariḥ.
A large army, an unstable place, clay suitable for those seeking a name,
and the sage Jarā at a distance— one should avoid these and those who have the appearance of bears.
In the constellations beginning with Aśvinī, two ghaṭikās at the end of the [total] number of ghaṭikās of the sentence must be avoided;
likewise, two ghaṭikās at the end of the constellation and five nāḍikās at the end of the day.
At the end of a month, two days should be omitted; at the end of a solar transit (ayana), three days.
One should avoid the fortnight and the end of the year in rites such as consecrations (*pratiṣṭhā*). [The sequence of the months is:
Nāga, Anābhi, Vara, Kopa, Nīla, Nīra, Naga, and again Naga.
Araṃ, dayā, svaraḥ, krūraḥ, pāpaḥ, bhūyaḥ, nayaḥ,
bhayam, nārī, priyā, naraḥ, nīpam, nāram, deyam, dvayoḥ, hayaḥ.
The "Vāra," "Diśā," and "Vara" are said to be the poisonous nāḍīs;
in the asterisms beginning with Kṛttikā, one should avoid these four nāḍīs at the end of the [respective] statements.
One should know that even a half-blow [is neutralized] by the slow songs of the *vesara* [drum], while *śambhu*, *guru*, *pathija*,
*naya*, *kaṇṭaka*, *sākṣāt-śiva*, *guru-pada*, and *gulika* are to be understood through the application of the eighth parts of the days of the week, beginning with Sunday.

The Yoginīs, beginning with Brahmāṇī, are to be known in the east and other directions through the [elements] earth, air, water, and peace; [the deities] Khyāti and others, as well as Vahni, Durgā, and so forth, are assigned to the lunar days (tithis).
During the seizing of the ground, processions, and so forth, as well as during the acceptance of the foundation stone and similar rites,
one should always proceed while avoiding travel directly toward the Yoginī.
In the three sets of ten lunar days beginning with the new moon (amāvāsyā), the lunar days are numbered as nine, ten, and one;
these correspond to the sky and the netherworld (rasātala).
One should not perform auspicious rites in the sky or in the netherworld (pātāla),
for these and other such defects have been determined by the science of astrology (jyotiḥśāstra).
One should avoid the five defects, the half-moon, the sixty-four gateways (ṣaḍaśītimukha), as well as the eclipses, the equinoxes, the transits (saṃkrānti), and the solstices.
A day free from all defects is not easily found by itself;
therefore, one should resort to a lunar mansion (lagna) that possesses many virtues and only few defects.
The Jupiter situated in the ascendant pacifies one hundred thousand defects;
Venus pacifies five thousand, and Mercury pacifies five hundred.
Therefore, when a benefic planet is strong and situated in the ascendant,
one should perform activities such as plowing for the sake of increasing the status of both the doer and the one who causes the deed to be done.
When auspicious conjunctions are possible, one should perform the installation and other rites;
for example: the Mūla constellation on a Sunday with the second lunar day, or the Śroṇā constellation on a Monday with the first lunar day.

On a Tuesday, the third lunar day with the constellation Āhirbudhnya (Śravaṇa); on a Wednesday, the eighth lunar day with Kṛttikā; on a Thursday, the fifth lunar day with the constellation Aditi (Punarvasu); and on a Friday, the fourth lunar day with Phalgunī.
On the seventh lunar day, the conjunctions of Saturn and Svāti are immortal and auspicious;
so too are Hasta, Mṛgaśiras, Aśvinī, Anurādhā, Puṣya, Pūrvāṣāḍhā, and Rohiṇī.
The Siddhi yogas conjoined with the days of the week, beginning with Sunday, are remembered as auspicious.
And it has been said by others: "The [nakṣatras] Jvalana, Pavana, Citrā, Revatī, Vāruṇa, Phaṇi, Hari, and Nṛti— each one of these in sequence [is associated with the eight directions]."
If Nandā coincides with the conjunction of the Sun and Mars, it becomes Parayoga, which is the cause for the accomplishment of all undertakings. Thus [it is said].

Therefore, at a time endowed with merit— whether all or some of the following are present as appropriate— the rites beginning with plowing and ending with consecration should be performed; [namely] the month, fortnight, lunar day, *karana*, asterism, day of the week, *yoga*, auspicious planets, planetary divisions (*aṃśaka*), *horā*, *drekkāṇa*, aspects, and ascendants (*udaya*).
One should perform the ritual actions.
Thus ends the section on place and time.
